But, but, but… There are 30 NFTs scattered around the game, collectible but not tradable (so of dubious use, I'd add).

2.title: 🥽ff.15.3 Digital events
2.content:
The pandemic forced us into digital events (like Billie Eilish's session). But I find it more fascinating to use an already virtual world (like Fortnite) as the setting for an event that, until a few years ago, would only have happened in real life.
Showing up with the latest impossible-to-find skin surely boosts your chances to copu… cooperate with someone cool on the next drop from the sky!

3.title: 🔢ff.15.4 Let's crunch the numbers!
3.content:
As you'll have figured out by now, I like throwing numbers around. Quantifying trends.
More time in the metaverse by 2030? That's what an ARK estimate of average global time spent online vs. offline seems to say. While in 2010 we were 90% in "real life", it's estimated that by 2030 we'll spend more time online.
Revenues will consequently skyrocket. From 500 million in 2020 to 800 in 2024 (+13.1% a year). But if we count all the infrastructure needed, the metaverse could be a 2.5 trillion dollar business in 2030 (world GDP will be 150 trillion).
captions: From RoundHill Investments

4.title: 🤍ff.15.5 Off-White versus the Louvre
4.content:
Virgil Abloh, the recently departed graphic designer and founder of Off-White, worked a lot on the intersection between the real and the digital.
In a detailed manifesto, Abloh lays out the steps for creating a "Skyscraper" (capable of taking down the Louvre), a digital place of avant-garde and artistic stimulation.
Thanks to an internal token, the work done and the "decentralised participation" in the project would be recognised transparently and easily for all artists.

5.title: 🎥ff.15.6 Gorgeous renderings
5.content:
If the metaverse is going to be this important, meta-physical 3D renderings will be the order of the day. For immersive and completely "new" realities.
LHC Studio has some beautiful videos along these lines, tastes of possible metaverses. Imagine these strange shapes through an Oculus headset!

0.title: 💰ff.16.1 Many trillions of dollars
0.content:
McKinsey estimates that to reach the COP26 climate goals we need to find 9 T$ (by T I mean trillions, a thousand billion dollars = 10^12 $) of investment a year, which is about a tenth of global GDP (100 T$) and 10 times the funding raised in this direction in 2021.
The "green premium" is the extra price to pay to offset the CO2 emissions produced. This contribution is the light-blue bar in the chart below. These costs are estimated for 2030 and add to the black bar, the baseline estimate for 2030 (there will be better efficiencies, so "base" costs will tend to be lower - today's price is shown by the dashed line).
A few things that jump out:
The green premiums of cement and steel are 50 and 25% respectively (producing these two materials "costs" us 10% of global emissions). Ethylene will cost practically the same in 2030 as it does today. The same will happen for paper, although in this case the green premium is smaller.

1.title: 🌉ff.16.2 The cost of infrastructure
1.content:
Technological developments, but also infrastructure: another report by Goldman Sachs on COP26 tackles the cost of the infrastructure needed to keep warming to "only" 1.5 °C.
50 T$ from now to 2050 (up to 3 T$ in a single year). That's the bill for infrastructure alone: next-generation power plants, charging stations, adapting and maintaining infrastructure, and CO2 capture systems.
If we break investment down by type (adding up the contributions from now to 2050), we see that 30 T$ will go to new renewable energy facilities (8 T$ for solar, 13 T$ for onshore/offshore wind).
captions: Annual infrastructure cost, broken down by type (peaking around 2035 at about 2.5% of world GDP)

2.title: ⚫ff.16.3 The (black) market for CO2
2.content:
To fund this spending, one idea is to tax pollution (and so make emissions paid for like physical waste, which is what happens with the TARI, Italy's waste tax).
Two fortissimo problems
The market is anything but "fair", with prices ranging from 7$/tonne (China) up to more than 150$/tonne (Sweden). The European area sits at about 75$/tonne. "Avoided" emissions. Right now companies can say "I'm polluting much less than I potentially could" and so receive CO2 emission credits that offset their emissions (traditional offsets). A bit like being allowed to eat a hamburger a day because I'm giving up a monthly trip to New York...
€50/tonne. McKinsey hopes for at least this level of tax on CO2 emissions to fund the costs of the transition.
In rich words:
A carbon pricing or emissions trading scheme could create incentives for individual stakeholders to reduce emissions. At a carbon price of €50 per tCO2e, an additional 21 percent of required capital, on top of the 40 percent already in the calculation, could be unlocked through 2050. A carbon price of €100 per tCO2e could unlock another 10 percent, giving more than 80 percent of all capital expenditures, including infrastructure, a standalone investment case. The remainder would require carbon prices of over €100 per tCO2e to create positive investment cases. How the European Union could achieve net-zero emissions at net-zero cost
The good news: in Europe we got to €80/tonne fairly quickly. Will the world follow?
captions: Tax (€/tonne) on CO2 emissions in Europe (blue), California (yellow) and South Korea (green).

3.title: 🆕ff.16.4 Which startups to watch?
3.content:
Optimising technologies matters too, so let's take a closer look at some start-ups and at investment in fast-growing companies.
40 billion of the 700 estimated in 2021 was raised by start-ups or fast-growing companies. Growth was 20% every four months, a 3x increase compared to 2020.
The three main sectors (mobility, energy, and food and water) raised 90% of the funding; the most important companies are Northvolt, Rivian (mobility) and Helion, Commonwealth (nuclear fusion).
The other categories, including emissions capture, raised less money but saw a much bigger increase (10x) compared to 2020.

0.title: 🇳🇴 ff.17.1 Norway is obsessive
0.content:
Allow me to introduce a monster: Kristian Blummenfelt. 27 years old, Norwegian, Olympic triathlon champion.
Just a few months after Beijing, he did an Ironman (roughly the distance of 4x Olympic triathlons) in 7 hours and 21 minutes. He smashed the previous record, in totally unfavourable conditions: it was raining, it was windy and, needless to say, he stopped for a bathroom break during the marathon, which he still finished in 2 hours and 35 minutes.
The New York Times devoted a detailed article to his training. Before we look at it together, let me introduce another person: the engineer Olav Aleksander Bu.
Sports engineering. Having joined the Norwegian Olympic team at the 2016 Games, right there in Rio he realised that, beyond aerodynamics and high-performance materials, sports know-how was stagnating.
From this realisation, he began diligent research, obsessively correlating physiological responses with his athletes' performance. A few examples?
He found that Blummenfelt was so mentally strong that he burned through his glycogen reserves too quickly. So, by measuring blood lactate, he found the right pace for the athlete to train longer and more consistently. He worked with a company able to measure heat dissipation, to understand how much energy was being "wasted" on thermoregulation. He had him drink a 2,000 dollar bottle with oxygen isotopes, to work out, from his urine, how efficiently he used oxygen. He studied his faeces (no, not during the marathon) to understand his carbohydrate metabolism.

2.title: 🕸️ ff.17.3 Positive social networks?
2.content:
Since we're talking about data and sport, I was reminded of a wonderful book by Sinan Aral, MIT professor of Management, Marketing, IT and Data Science.
In his analysis of social networks, which I hope to come back to in the future (fortissimo!), he also dwells on Strava, which wears the crown of social networks in sport.
As early as 2018 the Strava team noticed that group bike rides are 50% longer. Runs 20% longer, if you have someone alongside, even if not all types of runners prefer running with other people.
Sinan set out to understand more about this social effect: can we be influenced, even from a distance, by our friends' workouts?
Cause or effect? Studies like this are tricky. It's hard to find a baseline, a "control" against the hypotheses, because every social aspect can be cause and effect at the same time. Let me explain. I might run more because I see others running, or I might see more people running simply because my friends are more likely to run (because I've somehow "selected" them).
Weather-sensitive from afar. You need a random factor that alters the baseline. The book reports a study helped by the weather, a random disturbance. Starting from the activities of a runner in Arizona (where it's always sunny, so in theory the frequency of exercise should be constant), the study found that he ran less on rainy days in the Big Apple, if he had a New Yorker as a friend on Strava.
Other observations from this weather-assisted study run by Aral:
Seeing a friend run 1km more on the app pushes us to do at least 750 metres more than our usual. Seeing a friend run 10 minutes more than our standard pushes us to run 3 minutes more on average.
Ok, I'm off for a run now. Even if it's raining.

0.title: 😲 ff.18.1 Why switching your brain off matters
0.content:
Awe helps us step out of the individual perspective that stays with us most of the time, lightening the weight we give to so many worries. That's the finding of a study in Human Brain Mapping.
3 types of video (funny, neutral, awe-inspiring) were shown to two groups. One group, however, had the task of counting the number of scene changes (so it was in a state of greater concentration).
Naturally, the "task-free" group got "distracted" more easily and started thinking about its own worries (activation of the default-mode network). But not while watching awe-inspiring videos (like nature videos with breathtaking views…)
Art can trigger a similar reaction, letting us "unplug" from the ego, from "myself".
L’arte non può essere compresa con l’intelletto, ma è percepita come un’emozione che presenta analogie con lafede religiosa o l’attrazione sessuale - un eco estetico. Bonnie Clearwater,West Coast Duchamp

1.title: 🚽 ff.18.2 Artistic toilets
1.content:
Since we've mentioned Duchamp, what better way to bring him back than the ironic exhibition Best Seat in the House by the English collective Rankin?
1 person in 5 doesn't have a loo. Starting from this figure, and to raise awareness for the hygiene campaign promoted by WaterAid, the collective turned toilet seats into art. Elevating them to "the best seat in the house".
Toilets can make usfeel a little uncomfortable. Using the toilet seat as a canvas is an accessible and engaging way to put the spotlight on toilets and get people talking about them. Rankin

2.title: 🖼️ ff.18.3 Art, between artificial intelligence and humans
2.content:
While we're talking about art, where does artificial intelligence fit into all this? Can computers be artists?
In The Artist in the Machine, Arthur I. Miller discusses the creative process, giving various examples of how computers can generate art independently or assist humans, creating a new synergy.
The creative process can be split into 4 phases, according to psychologist Graham Wallas (expanding on a model by Poincaré, The Art of Thought):
Conscious thought (the necessary substrate of information and education for fertile ideas) → Fertile soil to plant the seed in. Unconscious thought (freeing the mind, letting it wander, maybe watching the videos above) → Waiting for the seed to grow. Illumination (the "aha!" or "eureka" moment, seemingly out of nowhere) → The sprout shows its first leaf. Verification (backing up the illumination with a mental framework able to do so) → Growing and tending the sprout until it becomes a full plant
Digital green thumb? But can artificial intelligence go through all these processes? Can it make a leap "outside the box"?

3.title: ♟️ ff.18.4 Artistic chess: the king of chess
3.content:
Sure, the computer is faster than humans and has a better memory, but in less "repetitive" processes, like creative ones, the machine seems inferior. As Garry Kasparov (beaten at chess by Deep Blue) put it: "I could smell a new kind of intelligence, a very strange kind of intelligence, inefficient and inflexible".
That was 1996.
Over the last 25 years, artificial neural networks have shown far greater flexibility: AlphaGo beat world champion Ke Jie by making a move that didn't mechanically follow common practice and millennia of game theory. A creative move.
"Deep, fruitful conversations between human and machine seemed like science-fiction stuff. For Go players, that moment has already arrived." Andy Okun (president of the American Go Association)
AI also figured out how to make better moves when not taught by humans, but by playing against itself and learning from scratch (see the difference between AlphaGo and AlphaZero). I'll leave you with the beautiful documentary that tells the story.

0.title: 💦 ff.19.1 Polluting flatulence
0.content:
By now it's common knowledge that cows aren't exactly eco-friendly. After China, with their ruminant stomachs and the methane they produce, they contribute an amount of CO2 equivalent higher than the United States. These emissions are also very similar to those due to transport (planes, trains, cars) worldwide.
TDLR: 🐄 = 🇺🇸 = 🚄 + 🚌 + 🚑 + ✈️
Ourworldindata breaks down food pollution into its various factors, such as land use, methane production, farming emissions, and the pollution tied to animal feed, processing and transport of the finished product.
Below, the emissions (in kg CO2eq per kg of product) of the most common foods:
Cows, if also used for milk and dairy, pollute 1/3 as much as their "beef" counterparts. Plant-based foods are on average 10 times less polluting than their animal counterparts. Hazelnuts make a positive contribution, because their low land-use impact offsets the other emissions. Milk pollutes 3 times its weight, soy milk 1/3 of regular milk. Coffee and chocolate are fairly polluting, although we consume them in smaller amounts (roughly, one chocolate bar = 0.5kg of rice = 30 bananas).

1.title: 🍔 ff.19.2 Hemingway's favourite hamburger
1.content:
Hemingway's father raised his son with one rule: "eat everything you kill". Hence his fortissimo attraction to hunting and fishing, but also his respect for animals, never preyed upon without - at the very least - the aim of eating them (porcupines and lions included). This respect also shines through in his novella The Old Man and the Sea.
Hemingway was a passionate eater and drinker. So much so that in the society notes from his home in Cuba (which lasted 20 years) we find the recipe for his favourite hamburger:
Ground beef, onions, garlic, India relish, and capers, cooked so the edges were crispy but the center red and juicy
Served in a bun, with nothing else
In short, a simple hamburger, well done on the edges and soft in the middle. The Indian spices rule. If you want to recreate it, you'll find the details here

2.title: ♨️ ff.19.3 Killer stoves
2.content:
A Stanford study found that gas stoves release a significant amount of methane, even when switched off (about 1% of what they burn).
By the numbers: the polluting effect is relatively small, since the emissions from the leaks equal the use of 0.5 million cars (out of 276 million in the United States, and about 1.4 billion motor vehicles worldwide). So we're talking about 0.2% of the pollution from US cars.
Still, molecules are molecules.

3.title: 🐖 ff.19.4 Cool sustainable choices
3.content:
The Swedish agency Everland redesigned the packaging of the products of the French green startup La Vie. The goal? To break away from the classic packaging of the "organic", "sustainable" and vegan world, in order to grow its customer base.
Using mainly pink, which recalls bacon (paired with a very vegetarian green), and wrapping the packaging in ironic and peaceful themes, Everland tries to make La Vie products more appealing (marketing-wise), maybe even cooling down the feuds between vegans and everyone else.

4.title: 💉 ff.19.5 3D-printed meat
4.content:
To make meat more sustainable, while keeping a texture and flavour as close as possible to the animal version, Redefine Meat produces its vegan burgers with a 3D printer.
Texture matters. Animal meat is made of muscle fibres whose arrangement varies depending on the cut. This leads to different cooking, consistency and flavour. Managing to replicate the marbling with 3D printing is another step towards a tasty, sustainable lunch.
Who knows what Hemingway would think of it.

0.title: 🚲 ff.20.1 The bicycle's revenge
0.content:
I don't know if you've noticed, but it seems the pandemic brought us more bicycles. At least in the Philippines. In fact, according to a World Bank survey, the bike was the only mode that saw its number of users grow.
21 metres each. Philippines aside, the good news is that something is moving in Italy too. Cycle lanes are growing steadily. Even if the data isn't up to date, you can see that on average in 2016 each person had their own 21.1 metres of cycle lane per capita (compared to 13 in 2008). For whatever the "metres-of-cycle-lane-per-capita" metric might mean.
Milan also recently approved a 240 million euro plan to boost connectivity in its hinterland (with 750 km of lanes, i.e. 0.07 metres per Lombardy resident?!). The goal: 20% of trips by bike by 2035. The challenge to Paris is on.
Below, a nice map showing the cycle lanes as if they were metro lines. Does it stop near you?

1.title: 🇮🇩 ff.20.2 Jakarta's example
1.content:
You might think that urban redevelopment aimed at more sustainable mobility is only feasible on a small scale and in "blank slate" cities with little infrastructure tied to more traditional means of transport.
In 2015, Jakarta had about 3.5 million people. Now it has more than 10. Almost nobody had a car in 2015 and only 10% of the population got around by bike. Despite this, the city had the worst traffic in the world (Rome, damn it, only seventh).
The air wasn't exactly squeaky clean either.
And yet, thanks to a series of choices aimed at favouring public and sustainable transport, with a hand from COVID:
From 2019 to 2020 bike use increased 6 times (up to 10 in some areas). The Transjakarta public transport system reached 1M rides per day. In five years, access to public transport (stations less than 500m from home) doubled, reaching 92%.
captions: Jakarta air pollution index, from CNA

2.title: ⛷️ ff.20.3 San Francisco like Cortina
2.content:
One issue with getting around on two wheels is safety, which scares many people and takes away their freedom to choose the bike.
This fun map of San Francisco shows, as if they were ski slopes in Cortina, the difficulty level (= danger) of its streets.
Speaking of "safe streets", the startup Cowboy presented its bike-friendly maps, going beyond Google's, which often pay little attention to the needs of micromobility.

0.title: 💰 ff.21.1 The magic of home-delivered salad and the Bic pen
0.content:
Tim Urban is a lovely guy. He runs the site Wait But Why (a container of deep concepts comically delivered with MS Paint graphics) and was a guest on the Lex Fridman Podcast. At the start of the chat, they talk about the complexity of the world around us.
Did Bic leave us its pens? No human knows how to build a ballpoint pen, because no human knows the techniques for:
extracting the necessary materials, forging them, developing the chemistry of plastic and ink, design and research
PS: To extract you need a shovel, which has to be built, and for plastic chemistry you need glass, fire. In short, an endless series of other steps… (Elon Musk estimates it takes at least 1 million people to sustain the complexity of the society around us, at least to create a stable civilisation on Mars)
But one artist managed to build a toaster.
Light bulbs and salad. Around the 20th minute of the conversation, Tim also asks us to reflect on the complexity of the system that makes the light appear when we flip the switch at home. It's dizzying. Just as dizzying as ordering a salad for lunch on Deliveroo and hearing the doorbell 10 minutes later, complete with Greek dressing and avocado grown - perhaps - on the other side of the world.
This technological progress is born from the interplay of technology, society and education in an interconnected world (culturally and logistically) like the one we live in. Or used to live in?

refs.2: But one artist managed to build a toaster.

1.title: 🚢 ff.21.2 The end of an era?
1.content:
And yet, since 2008 there seem to be some signs of crisis in this idyllic world. Or not? Let's take a closer look.
On the one hand, the share of global GDP tied to trade is declining. The peak was in 2008. For 10 years now this number has stopped growing, falling back to 2000 levels in 2020.
But, but, but. Maybe this number isn't the best way to quantify globalisation. Other trends have reduced "physical" trade, even though connections haven't decreased at all.
captions: The Evergreen ship stuck in the Suez Canal, from Maxar Technologies

2.title: 📡 ff.21.3 Or the start of another?
2.content:
Some features of the era that began after the financial crisis, characterised by:
Digitalisation, social media, technological developments in communication; the growth of the tertiary sector, services; the competitiveness of robots at work, which narrows the gap between labour costs in more developed countries and those in Asia; the lower impact of resources on GDP (dematerialisation); as with automation, 3D printing could lead to further localisation of production where the material is extracted.
Intangibles. If you've spent more on an NFT of sneakers in League of Legends than at the Nike store in your country, you're not alone. Much of the value of the brands and products around us is intangible (tied to the company's know-how, marketing, training, brand value…).
Investment in physical versus intangible assets has flipped over the last 20 years:
If you want to dig deeper into globalisation trends, there's of course a McKinsey study.

3.title: 🙊 ff.21.4 More interesting food for thought
3.content:
In this chat with General Richard Barrons (formerly Commander of the UK's Joint Forces Command), Azeem Azhar talked about the future of war back in 2019 (!).
Today, some of the predictions that come up in this conversation are truly incredible. Even though the focus was also on other kinds of war, seeing the "boots on the ground with militias" kind as not very fruitful and almost anachronistic
War is increasingly fought through the influence of media, trade (see sanctions) and hacker attacks. War is increasingly non-human and remote: technically, you can do terrible damage with intercontinental missiles, drones and automated processes. As in 2014, with the intervention estimated at between 3 and 15 minutes. Nations, but above all multinationals, can wield considerable soft power, leveraging the prosperity they generate (and he was amazed that after the attack on Crimea Russian oligarchs could still go shopping in London and enjoy all the related comforts)
And then, back to the fragile complexity of the world around us:
Finding food on supermarket shelves is now seen as a right. No: we need to learn about the world's fragility. It isn't guaranteed, we have to do our part for its complexity. Prosperity also comes above all from the priorities of state investment (see the percentage of GDP spent on the military). Germany has already said it will go from 2% to 4% of GDP for defence… We have to fight to keep certain freedoms. Personal resilience, on social media too. 100 years ago, people were called to arms. Today, we're called to be morally prepared and educated!!!
Tough? Don't worry: you don't need to collect all of General Figliuolo's medals.

0.title: 🕐 ff.22.1 A circadian diet?
0.content:
I recently read a great book called The Circadian Code, about how important our circadian biological rhythm is for psycho-physical well-being.
A few key points:
Our body benefits from keeping circadian rhythms, because certain metabolic or repair processes are regulated by genes that switch on according to "the phase of the day we're in".
Our body struggles to figure out what phase of the day it's in, because:
Biologically it relies on exposure to bright, outdoor light, which is what "starts the day". Since we spend so much time inside buildings, this start-of-day exposure is missing or rare. Exposure to light / screens indoors, even late in the evening, delays "the end of the day" metabolically. Digestion stretching into the late evening delays or destabilises these daily rhythms.
In short, chaotic modern life has a significant impact on our circadian cycle.
Diet and digestion. Satchin Panda argues we should follow the TRE rule: Time Restricted Eating. In particular, to help activate circadian rhythms, he suggests limiting the digestion window to 10, at most 12 hours (for any food: even a beer can restart the whole costly digestive process).
Backing this up, a study in Nature Metabolism in which mice eating the same kcal per day lose more weight if they eat within a shorter time span.
Not just mice. Some criticism of the study focuses on the fact that it's about mice. But a recent study on humans showed something similar. If we limit food intake to a single meal instead of three, fat oxidation speeds up significantly:
0.7 kg of fat burned in 11 days, when "calorie" calculations said it should have been only 0.14 kg.
A likely explanation is fat use stimulated by low insulin levels during the day.
Also, spending 12-16 hours a day in the postprandial phase (basically a state of inflammation) may not be ideal for many other risk factors (diabetes and obesity are already known to be linked to it).

1.title: 🪑 ff.22.2 Set another place (and a few kcal) at the table
1.content:
Another thing we care about is socialising. In company, we can end up eating 25% up to 50% more than what we would eat if we were alone.
Let's not even talk about what happens at Christmas.

2.title: 🥔 ff.22.3 Why eat unprocessed (and fibre-rich) food
2.content:
A few dietary tips while we're at it, with the related studies. First, a simple rule of thumb to convert kcal into "weight":
3,500 kcal calorie deficit = 0.45 kg of fat burned
Self-combustion. When we eat something, we also spend energy processing the food. Well, if the food is unprocessed (made of more fibre, for example) we can use up to twice the energy to digest unprocessed foods.
An example: to digest two 800 kcal sandwiches you burn:
With white bread and processed cheese slices: 73 kcal. With wholemeal bread and less processed cheese: 137 kcal
Since obesity in the United States is linked to an increase of 300 kcal a day over the last 25 years, this "endogenous" and "free" increase in calorie burn could help.

refs.2: up to twice the energy to digest unprocessed foods
refs.3: 300 kcal a day over the last 25 years

3.title: 🤰🏻 ff.22.4 The most filling foods
3.content:
Another way to "keep hunger in check" is the satiety index. Not all foods, for the same kcal eaten, fill you up the same way. There's a nice study that tries to figure out which foods are the most filling, for the same calories (240 kcal per portion).
A positive correlation was found with water, fibre and protein, in decreasing order, as well as serving weight. A negative correlation with fat and palatability (how much you like it).
7 times more filling: potatoes top the chart, with an index of 332, versus 47 for the croissant. 76% of foods have a higher satiety index than white bread. Oranges and apples beat bananas, if you want to feel full.

4.title: 🍹 ff.22.5 Shall we drink to that?
4.content:
Alcohol is quite a beast too:
4 bottles of wine a month, over a year, is 27,000 kcal = 48 Big Macs (one a week), i.e. about +3.5 kg. 5 medium lagers a week, over a year, is 44,200 kcal = 221 doughnuts (one every other day), i.e. about 5.6 kg.
Should we all become breatharians at this point? This newsletter is depressing, I know. Cutting down on dinners with friends, desserts or other small pleasures, and quantifying every aspect of daily life, can be alienating. I don't think it's (psychologically) healthy to follow every single point. But we do need to be quantitatively aware. For better health and lower related economic costs (= more futuro fortissimo for everyone).

0.title: 🌬️ ff.23.1 Relationships over the last 100 years
0.content:
This beautiful GIF by Flowing Data sums up, in just a few frames, everything we have to say to each other today.
It shows the % of people, by age, who are single, married or divorced. Each line is the average of a decade, from 1900 to today. The most recent decades are the least transparent ones.
More and more people aren't married (at least until 30) or get divorced (around 50). Basically, shorter and less stable relationships.
At the same time, acceptance of polygamy seems to be on the rise. Over the last 20 years, it has gone from 7% to about 20.
In this context of short and increasingly "flexible" relationships, maybe we need to talk about marriage in more detail.
captions: From Flowing Data

refs.0: acceptance of polygamy seems to be on the rise

1.title: 👰ff.23.2 Privatised marriage?
1.content:
Even though 50% of marriages end in divorce (at least in the United States), many people believe their own marriage has only a 1% chance of failing.
The lack of clarity of prenuptial vows (the private agreements signed) and the rigid legislation on the various problems that can arise in a marriage shape these trends.
In Nudge: improving decisions about health, wealth and happiness, the authors argue that privatising marriage would improve the situation. Getting married should be an experience similar to joining a sports, political or volunteering association.
People stay tied to their friends, their churches, their coauthors, and their employers for a long time. And even without a government licensing scheme or legal sanction, people take their private commitments seriously. Members of religious organizations, homeowners’ associations, and country clubs all feel bound, sometimes quite strongly, by the structures and rules of such organizations. Recall that if some kind of commitment is desirable, nothing in our proposal prevents people from making commitments through the civil union form or purely through private institutions. With respect to marriage, there are powerful arguments for privatization—for allowing private institutions, religious and otherwise, to do as they wish, subject to default rules and criminal prohibitions. We have argued that states should abolish “marriage” as such and rely on civil unions instead. If religious institutions want to restrict “marriage” to heterosexual couples, they should certainly be permitted to do exactly that. If such institutions want to limit divorce (that is, ending a “marriage”), they could do that too. The beauty of this proposal is that it would allow a wide range of experiments—increasing freedom for individuals and religious organizations alike while at the same time reducing the unnecessary and sometimes ugly intensity of current public debates. Nudge: Improving Decision About Wealth, Health, Happiness(pag. 265-269)
After all, we're so used to social newsfeeds and Netflix recommendations so personalised that the rigidity of certain traditional rituals can feel very tight.

refs.3: lack of clarity of prenuptial vows (the private agreements signed)

2.title: 🧹ff.23.3 Nobody's having s*x any more
2.content:
27% of the population under 30 is a virgin. This, apparently, is the figure from a General Social Survey study (via The Washington Post). According to the same survey, one person in three hadn't had sex in the past year (in 2018). With COVID, things hardly got better.
A slightly more scientific publication shows the following trends in the frequency of sexual activity among people aged 18-44. Each column is the two-year average from 200 to 2018.

3.title: 🔥ff.23.4 Tinder's “wall”
3.content:
Tinder was supposed to be the solution to being cooped up at home. The problem? It has a Gini index (which measures inequality, traditionally of income) worse than Venezuela's.
The Medium blog Worst-Online-Dater (the name says it all) tackles Tinder likes in a very mathematical and detailed way.
In theory, as "attractiveness" goes up, the chance of scoring on Tinder should rise accordingly. Well, it doesn't. Especially for men.
85% of likes go to the top 1% of alpha males, looks-wise (below, the Hinge data, a platform similar to Tinder).
This is an extreme version of the Pareto principle. So Tinder's algorithms don't seem to do much for building stable couples, giving those who have likes even more likes, and those who don't even more frustration.
Impossibly beautiful. If you're of average looks, the chance of getting likes drops to 1%. Good luck with the swipes!

1.title: 💦ff.24.2 They're bonds, NFT bonds
1.content:
Along the same lines, he then launched the Meta History Museum of War. Super cool!
Basically, they sold NFTs (remember the ff where I talked about them?) made by Ukrainian and international artists. Alongside the artworks, unique and "tradable", a tweet transparently recounting what happened in the war, day by day.
A chronology ofevents ofthe Ukrainian history ofmodern times, set in stone. The NFTs arefacts accompanied by personal reflections. Theformula of each NFT is clear and simple: each token is a real news piecefrom an official source and an illustrationfrom artists, both Ukrainian and international.

2.title: 💦ff.24.3 Turkey and Brazil defend their sovereignty
2.content:
In the book The Bitcoin Standard, Saifedean Ammous tells the history of the exchange of value, from barter to seashells; from gold to the dollar (today's global reserve). He argues that pegging currencies to something stable like gold or, nowadays, Bitcoin could lead to a more stable currency than leaving it to be terribly managed by a country's finance minister.
Why Bitcoin is a solution to inflation:
There will never be more than 21 million Bitcoin (the algorithm is programmed with this cap; about 19 million have been distributed so far). Nobody can control or increase their number, lowering their value, as happened instead with the dollar (and other "fiat" currencies) during the COVID crisis, which then caused the well-known price inflation (27% of the dollars on this planet were created in the last two years)
Bitcoin beats the Ruble. Speaking of war, Bitcoin and Putin: the value of the Bitcoin network overtook that of the Russian currency, after the fallout of the war.
Some currencies have lost value more than others in recent years. Especially in pandemic times. Take the Turkish lira, which in ten years went from being worth 0.45 to 0.063 € (!). Ark estimates that if 5% of the money in circulation were "captured" by Bitcoin, the value of the digital currency would rise to 3.5 times current values.

0.title: 🐖 ff.25.1 Pig heart transplants
0.content:
Le creature difuori guardavano dal maiale all'uomo e dall'uomo al maiale e ancora dal maiale all'uomo, ma già era loro impossibile distinguerefra i due. George Orwell,La Fattoria degli Animali
Did you hear about the first pig-to-human heart transplant with no rejection? To make it happen, they had to switch off a gene found in many animals, pigs included, but not in monkeys or humans. In fact, gal-transferase creates a layer of an antigen that our immune system rejects, causing rejection.
Hogwash? The recipient of this donation died, probably from a bovine infection (controllable, but it got out of hand in this case).
Clearly we're only at the beginning and there are critical issues. But transplants may be a solution. To what, you ask?

1.title: 🫀 ff.25.2 The scale of the transplant problem
1.content:
The main problem is that the number of transplant requests exceeds the available organs, which are in short, fortissimo short, supply.
The Financial Times has a great report on this. In the United States alone, about 60,000 people are waiting for a transplant. Only 65% of them get one.
Which organs are most in demand? Kidneys (83%), liver (10%) and heart (3%).
Oh, and hair too, obviously. The company dNovo is working on reprogramming pluripotent cells to restore the growth of those little strands.

2.title: 🙊 ff.25.3 Translating pig language
2.content:
Being able to communicate with (or at least interpret) the signals coming from other animals could matter in many ways: ensuring their well-being, understanding how much they suffer, or holding interesting philosophical discussions.
Recently, artificial intelligence was used to sample and interpret pig grunts, recorded in situations of emotional stress or well-being. Once trained to recognise the patterns, the system was able to match the animals' sounds with their mood with 90% accuracy.

refs.2: ligence was used to sample and interpret pig grunts

3.title: 📦 ff.25.4 Amazon for pets: a bubble?
3.content:
Ryan Cohen is a very peculiar character. He reminds me a bit of Elon Musk, but at times he's even more of a living meme. Why are we talking about him? Because he made a fortune with animals.
ff is about this: trends, and how to follow them (or get ahead of them?).
Startup Stories@StartupStoriezRyan Cohen is an entrepreneur, meme-god, and chairman of wallstreetbets darling: $GME.
But long before the short squeezes and 🚀🚀 of 2021, Cohen set out to revolutionize the pet market with@Chewy🐶
The story of@ryancohen’s underdog (get it?) effort to take on Amazon 🧵9:00 PM ∙ Dec 21, 202140Likes8Retweets
Founder of Chewy, the Amazon of pets, he's now an executive at GameStop. A perfectly logical career move, since nobody lives a dog's life more than gamers.
Ok, that wasn't funny.
It's interesting how interest in pets also exploded during the loneliness of the pandemic.
But, but, but… Just as Zoom and Peloton "burned" all the value they'd accumulated over the last two years, Chewy's value followed the same trend (down 50% since the start of the year).
This leads to an interesting thought: are the digitalisation of shopping, the hours in front of the computer, the metaverse and cryptocurrencies just the result of a huge pandemic boredom, or did the future speed up thanks to COVID-19?
For sure, by "riding" the pandemic wave, Cohen made big money. Maybe, though, rather than following trends, you need to predict them and get out once they're a given. Inflated.
With ff we try to trace possible futures before they become visible to most people.

0.title: 👧 ff.26.1 Genuine (virtual) influencers
0.content: Apparently, there are fully digital influencers. That alone is a trend nobody saw coming. To fight the perfection of social media (which is limitless when control over the character is total, given its digital nature), Jesse Zhang created Angie, a virtual influencer with imperfect skin who often cries, embodying the insecurities typical of her age.

1.title: 0️⃣ ff.26.2 (Almost) zero-impact websites
1.content:
Even if the endless scroll of social media feels free, besides paying for it with our data, it also has an impact on energy emissions. To remind us of this, an Amsterdam design studio redesigned the Volkswagen website to make it more sustainable.
By removing colours, high-definition images and animations, they got down to 0.02 grams of CO2 emitted per page view, about 100 times less than average.
100 YouTube pages = two plates of rice. YouTube's emissions per page view, calculated by websitecarbon.com, are 1/100 of the emissions needed to produce 150g of rice.

2.title: 🌾 ff.26.3 The superfoods that will save the planet
2.content:
Rice, by the way, is eco-friendly. Wheat, which yields only once a year and constantly needs replanting, slightly less so. A recently proposed alternative is Kernza (Thinopyrum intermedium). Unlike wheat, this special-K is perennial and produces seeds cyclically.
Patagonia (which apparently also makes beer) used it for an alternative Pale Ale.

3.title: 🪁 ff.26.4 Startups for male fertility
3.content:
Behind every great building there's a… well, you know the joke. The things below aren't SpaceX's next rockets. They're not d*cks either, but a container for what can come out of them.
Legacy is a Boston startup specialising in DIY kits for cryopreserving and storing sperm. Your right hand, every guy's eternal partner, will be happy to hear it. Oh, it costs $195.

4.content:
The environmental issue tied to aviation and long-haul travel (by plane) is a very delicate one. We'll talk about it in a future ff. Even though super-luxury is anything but green, Led Zeppelin could make a comeback. Or rather, just the zeppelins (read: airships). Led never went out of fashion.
Ocean Sky Cruises is planning expeditions flying over Antarctica for a candlelit dinner with a view of polar bears. If the ice holds up, of course.

0.title: ⚈ ff.27.1 The New York Times' pixels
0.content:
Over the last few years, The New York Times has been very attentive to the pandemic. I was struck by its report on Bergamo and the deaths of the first wave, with images taken directly from L'Eco di Bergamo and its countless pages “of the dead”.
To remember the million dead, it tried to visualise them as pixels. Each dot, a human life. Used to being bombarded by billions upon billions of pixels every day, stopping on each black dot (a human life!) and giving it the time it deserves is incredibly hard. But that seems to be exactly what it's asking of us.
Here's the cover for the 500,000 dead. Already with the pixel theme, laid out vertically by day. Showing the progression of the pandemic.
Here instead is the age breakdown of the million dead. 650 thousand over 65.
And here are the waves of pixels. Half of the deaths came after vaccines were created (remember the not-so-high vaccination rate in the United States: 61% fully vaccinated, dropping to 31% for the third dose).
The page is interactive and, as you scroll, the pixels build a map of the geographic distribution of deaths.

1.title: 🖱️ ff.27.2 Scrolling and deaths
1.content:
Axios created another beautiful visualisation to put the victims and numbers of the pandemic in context: as you scroll this page, the dead pile up, as shown in the chart in the corner.
In January 2021 the death toll reached that of World War II (for the United States).
In September 2021, that of the 1918 pandemic (675 thousand). The US population has tripled since 1918, so 1.6M COVID deaths would mean a similar mortality rate. At 1M deaths today, we're not far off.

2.title: 💬 ff.27.3 The Washington Post's unfinished sentences
2.content:
The Washington Post, on the other hand, presented a project with a series of unfinished sentences. It doesn't aim to show every detail of the problem, but asks us to stop and read a few stories. It's frustrating. Because the opening page looks like this:
As you start reading, the sentence is cut off halfway. We don't know how it ends. Interruptions are perhaps one of the things we find hardest to handle mentally. Our brain is a prediction machine, always trying to anticipate what will happen.
Only by hovering the mouse over the sentence do we see how it would have been completed, had the person in question not died. Had the sentence of their life not been colonised by a virus that spread to every corner of the planet.
This Futuro Fortissimo ends here. With few articles. No futurism. Just the request to stop for a moment, to remember what was the darkest moment of the 21st century. And what other problems could arise in a similar way if we don't stop exponential curves in time.
P.S. We'll also talk about how COVID-19 spurred research and progress in medicine, but now is not the time.

0.title: ☢️ ff.28.1 Artificial intelligence for nuclear fusion
0.content:
Nuclear fusion has been predicted for decades, as we discussed in 🎼 ff.12 Sun, heart and love.
This time it's different! (?) A few months ago Nature published the use of neural networks to control the position and shape of the plasma in a nuclear fusion reactor. In practice, control of the plant's operation (with magnetic actuators) was handed to a Deep Reinforcement Learning system. Replacing complex physics calculations that have to happen extremely fast, AI can “learn” to manage the system beforehand and be much faster in execution.
A plasma snowflake. With this system they obtained various types of plasma, including non-spherical and less conventional shapes (a snowflake). Exploring its geometric properties is one of the fundamental steps towards finding the fusion process able to generate more energy than the system uses.
In rich words:
We successfully produce and control a diverse set ofplasma configurations on the Tokamak à Configuration Variable1,2, including elongated, conventional shapes, as well as advanced configurations, such as negative triangularity and ‘snowflake’ configurations […]. Tokamak magnetic control is one ofthe most complex real-world systems to which RL has been applied. This is a promising new directionfor plasma controller design, with the potential to acceleratefusion science, explore new configurations and aid infuture tokamak development.

1.title: 🧆 ff.28.2 Finding the bean in the jar
1.content:
X, the moonshot factory, is a Google-linked company that does cool stuff.
Project Mineral is one of the most interesting projects: it uses a mix of robotics, image recognition and biology to improve agriculture, monitor harvests and map new crop varieties to boost biodiversity and nutrition.
The grass is always greener. Of the 30,000 known edible plant species, only 1% is cultivated by humans. We don't know what nutritional value 99% of known plants could offer (because the analyses are missing). Project Mineral aims to close this knowledge gap.

2.title: 🗺️ ff.28.3 Google Maps cuts emissions
2.content: Google has implemented an eco-friendly routing system on Maps. By avoiding traffic jams, and therefore more time with the engine running, it already helps cut emissions. It has also recently added options for bikes and e-scooters and started integrating charging stations for electric vehicles into routes, encouraging their use and reducing “dead battery” anxiety. Google estimates these features could avoid 1M tonnes of CO2 emissions (the emissions from using 200,000 cars) every year.

refs.5: encouraging their use and reducing “dead battery” anxiety

3.title: 🩺 ff.28.4 Wear your vest (or are you feeling lucky?)
3.content:
Google has launched a data management platform called Care Studio, which presents the doctors of the future with a given patient's health data, ensuring simple, AI-assisted access. There's a short video showing how it works.
Nest Hub, not just a voice assistant. Speaking of wellbeing, Nest Hub 2, Google's mini-tablet for the smart home, can monitor the sleep-wake cycle with 3D radar and help disabled people with communication difficulties express themselves or make themselves understood.

0.title: 👶 ff.29.1 We're not having kids any more
0.content:
Apparently, even though in some parts of the world the population is booming (remember 🎼 ff.13 Populations and pollutions?), Elon Musk is extremely worried because people aren't having children.
No kids, no future (on Mars). To populate Mars, you first need a stable demographic base on Earth. With the right share of young people able to “support the economy”.
Elon Musk@elonmuskWe should be much more worried about population collapse5:02 PM ∙ Jan 18, 2022193,003Likes20,155Retweets
The global average fertility rate per woman has fallen from 4.5 children (!) to about 2.4 over the last 60 years.
And the projections for 2100 aren't rosy, with China and India below a billion inhabitants and countries like Japan halved. Don't worry, because in Nigeria they'll “keep at it”.
Why is this happening? What can we do to reverse the trend? A Washington Post journalist, the singer Grimes and a book on the next 500 years give us some ideas.

1.title: 👩‍💻 ff.29.2 Being a mum is a job!
1.content:
A crucial issue around motherhood is its cost. In an ever more individualistic, capitalist, profit-driven world, even motherhood gets quantified.
1700 feeds. Alyssa Rosenberg, a Washington Post journalist, tracked every breastfeeding session she did in her first 6 months of motherhood. They're the little dashes below.
She then calculated the wage she should receive if every feed and caregiving stint were paid at the US minimum wage, including living costs (basically, the milk produced). Considering the average US wage and roughly 2 and a half hours a day, the total cost over 6 months comes to 13,000 dollars.
Vitalik Buterin, father (lol) of Ethereum, also weighed in on the wage asymmetries between men and women that follow childbirth. If the 13,000 dollars were counted, they'd probably be smaller.

2.title: 💰 ff.29.3 Elon Musk's girlfriend proposes paying mums
2.content:
Elon Musk's ex-girlfriend (mother of the infamous human being X Æ A-Xii, a name as unique as it is rare) also spoke out on the issue. She proposed a MaternityDAO, i.e. a Decentralized Autonomous Organization to give credit to mums all over the world.
In a few points, here's what she proposes:
Capitalism doesn't give motherhood its fair value: a well-raised, educated, healthy, sporty child will one day be a priceless source of progress for society. Although “pro-life” welfare measures exist (baby bonuses, to be clear), they often do a poor job of capturing the dynamics of a child's growth that benefit society. Having children is one thing; raising them as model citizens is another. A MaternityDAO could address these problems with quantitative measurement tools. Based on how “well you raise your child” and their positive impact on society, the mother would receive proportional recognition and rewards.
Obviously the line between utopia and dystopia is thin and fragile. Measuring a child's positive impact or ranking their growth can easily veer into undemocratic systems like the “social credit” ranking we find in China. But it's important to think about how to improve welfare with the new possibilities technology gives us.

refs.2: dit” ranking we find in China

3.title: 🧫 ff.29.4 Unconventional motherhood: wombs “in glass”
3.content:
In a sense, though, the market has already started “compensating” motherhood: in surrogacy cases (I hate the Italian term “rented womb”, to be honest), the surrogate mother providing the service is handsomely paid by a biologically infertile mother.
Almost 1000 mothers dead. Even where a mother can handle a pregnancy, despite medical progress, still today around 1000 mothers can die in a single year in the United States. What's more, although the champions of pain see labour pains as essential and “natural” for such an important moment, I'm sure some women would gladly do without the physical limitations, risks and pain of pregnancy.
Speaking of dystopia, The Handmaid's Tale imagines a future where a male-chauvinist government subjugates the few fertile women (the Handmaids) to “bend the female body and its reproductive functions to its own ends”.
Rented wombs? Yes, but non-human ones. A 2021 study in Nature showed it's possible to grow physiologically stable mouse foetuses in extra-uterine cultures (rotating glass vials). A solution that may make people wrinkle their noses at first, but that could bring considerable social, demographic, psychological and economic benefits.
Maybe one day we'll manage to see reproduction in a demystified way, free from all the religious/magical/ritual flavour we carry around today. That is, as a mere biological process, like eating, sleeping, having sex.
Oh, in case this analysis wasn't enough for you, there's more here.

0.content:
Before diving into DALL-E 2's art, the explainer.
DALL-E is a name that blends the art of Salvador Dalí and Disney's cute little robot. It's an artificial intelligence developed by the OpenAI folks (the same ones who beat the world GO champion; we talked about it in 🎼 ff.18 Between digital art and AI) able to generate images consistent with a text input.
DALL-E can also place, in a given image, any kind of object we want, like a dog in a museum. And it does so by adapting the style to the location:
For now the model is accessible only to a few people, given the ethical issues that could arise from its misuse.

3.title: 👂 ff.30.4 Understanding Picasso
3.content:
Another Twitter user suggested using the software's regression ability (when it's asked, for example, to show the dynamic steps from one image to another) to analyse Picasso's sketches.
Starting and ending on the artist's drawings, what's shown in between is a wandering / imagining of intermediate phases between the two forms. Thanks to DALL-E, then, we see the creative mental process that might have led Picasso from one idea to the next. The simplifications and “prototypes” between the various sketches.
Sarebbe molto interessante preservare, a livello visivo, non lefasi ma le metamorfosi di un immagine. In questo modo, potremmo scoprire il percorso seguito dal cervello per materializzare un sogno. Pablo Picasso,1935

4.title: 📈 ff.30.5 The improvements in just one year
4.content:
What's phenomenal about artificial intelligence is the speed of its development. For years people have predicted that the physical (quantum) limits of Moore's Law would halt progress in computing power. The reality is that humans keep inventing loads of ways around them.
In one year, DALL-E (now version 2.0) improved its results, reaching 4 times the resolution. Seeing is believing.
“An avocado-shaped chair”.
DALL-E 1
DALL-E 2
The next step? Probably video creation. Imagine the power of a tool that can depict, for example, any film plot that comes to mind. And maybe do it in an afternoon.
The creator economy of the future will put today's influencers to shame.

0.title: ⚈ ff.32.1 How much do phones pollute?
0.content:
Let's start strong.
Considering all the vehicles and electronic devices produced worldwide, it turns out that every year, to make cars/laptops/smartphones, we use:
🏎️ 7 EJ  | 💻 4.5 EJ | 📱 0.25 EJ
EJ = exajoule = 10^18 J. From a quick estimate (if I haven't made mistakes), every day humanity consumes (by eating, at about 3000 kcal/person) 0.1 exajoules. In a year, 36 EJ. This number doesn't account for all the waste and inefficiencies in the energy>food conversion; it's just the calories eaten.
Anyway, taking into account the longer product life (after all, we don't change our car every two years, the way we do when a new smartphone comes out with yet another extra camera), the differences in the energy used to make them shrink:
🏎️ 0.7 EJ/year | 💻 0.45 EJ/year | 📱 0.1 EJ/year
Of course, then you have to use them. And in use:
a phone uses 30 MJ (megajoules) in 2 years, 3-8% of the energy needed to make it, depending on how you charge it (with wind power or by burning coal). a car uses 500 GJ (gigajoules) in 10 years, 5x what it took to make it (100 GJ per car).
Bottom line: in a year, getting around by car you use 3000x the energy you use to power your phone.

1.title: 🍷 ff.32.2 Let's drink to that (or maybe not)
1.content:
Among the trends analysed in the book, Vaclav also dwells on wine consumption.
Our grandparents had strong stomachs (especially in France). Apparently wine consumption in France peaked in 1926, at 136 litres per capita a year. So two big, full glasses each, every day. In 2020, despite the pandemic, the French drank more or less just one glass every two days.
This trend probably reflects the growth in options and alternatives (like spirits and fizzy drinks) and doesn't tell us much about the intake of alcohol molecules in absolute terms.

2.title: 🐔 ff.32.3 Chicken run
2.content:
60% of food goes to feeding animals (in North America). Meat's climate impact is well known. Another interesting number is the one just mentioned, on the impact of feed production. But not all animals are equally efficient at converting feed into protein.
For 1kg of protein, you need:
7kg of feed for a chicken (15% efficiency); 20-30kg of feed for a cow
Not necessarily vegan. Since the global distribution of animals for meat production is currently:
🐖 40 % | 🐔 37 % | 🐄 23 %
if the percentages became:
🐖 40 % | 🐔 50 % | 🐄 10 %
we could produce 10% more meat with no greater climate impact.

3.title: 💉 ff.32.4 Vaccines beat the stock market
3.content:
Vaccines are the best investment there is. At least the pentavalent vaccine, which is good practice to give every newborn before 12 months, at a cost of about €1.
Half of Italy, almost 25 million people. That's the estimate of deaths prevented over the last 10 years thanks to vaccines. If you factor in the medical costs avoided and the economic output linked to these survivals, each vaccine is estimated to generate at least €16. Including other economic output linked to these people's survival, you can get to about €44. Against €1 spent (these days, not even a coffee).
The International Monetary Fund relaunched this message in relation to COVID-19 too.

refs.1: message in relation to COVID-19 too

4.title: 🚗 ff.32.5 Electric cars: green or not?
4.content:
Electric cars are green, but a lot depends on how we power them:
Norway, for example, produces 95% of its electricity from hydropower; France 75% from nuclear; In China, India and Poland, on the other hand, electric cars are often coal cars.
These are the emissions for the EU-28 area and Norway (Italy pollutes, for the same electricity produced, 10x what Norway does):
Toxic (not the Britney Spears song). Producing an electric car creates toxic materials equal to 3x those linked to traditional cars (due to heavy metals). Still, we can learn to manage this toxicity and, maybe, electric cars will speed up the transition to a more sustainable electricity mix.
Below, a summary table from a 2018 article that considers all the CO2 emissions linked to electric vehicles compared with conventional vehicles (CV in the chart). The number next to BEV represents the energy mix (3 is Norway).
40 times less green. As you can see, compared with electric vehicles in Norway, traditional vehicles emit 40x the CO2.

0.title: 🧠 ff.33.1 The philosophical and cognitive value of trees
0.content:
The connection between humans and plants has historically been very close. The tree has always been at the heart of many cultural aspects: from Adam and Eve to medieval theories of knowledge, all the way to search and optimisation algorithms (like the decision tree). Plant branchings have inspired and helped humans to define themselves, to understand the world and themselves.
Shannon Mattern, an anthropology professor at The New School for Social Research in New York, traced the history of this relationship in the short essay Tree Thinking.

1.title: 🍁 ff.33.2 CO2 collectors
1.content:
Plants, besides capturing CO2 during photosynthesis, keep it locked up for a shorter or longer period (in the carbon of bark and leaves). A Science study by the University of Zurich calculated that we could plant 0.9 million hectares, with a potential storage of 200 Gt (gigatonnes) of carbon (each year we emit about 30). When a tree dies, though, part of the captured CO2 is released back into the environment as it decays.
Peat-what? And yet peatland (see the image below to get a rough idea of what I mean) is much more efficient at holding CO2.
Here are the Gt of carbon “held” in:
Forests | 8% of land | 272 ± 23 Gt of carbon; Peatlands |2% of land| 415 ± 150 Gt of carbon
If you want to dig deeper, here's a great newsletter:
Climate Tech VC🌎 Peaty blinders: in bog we trust #101Happy Monday! Outside of great potential for puns, peat also contains more than 3x the carbon as forests on a hectare basis. Despite it taking longer to form, its stewardship and carbon removal capacity is at odds with its’ use as a cheap fuel alternative. Innovation in its preservation is burgeoning, though its carbon credits markets are still relative…Read more4 years ago · 12 likes · 1 comment · Sophie Purdom and Kim Zou
Two more interesting ideas on this:
Dendra uses a mix of drones, AI and satellite analysis to optimise efficiency and biodiversity when planting. Carbo Culture is working on creating biochar able to stabilise captured CO2 and keep it from escaping through rotting.

refs.5: Climate Tech VC🌎 Peaty blinders: in bog we trust #101Happy Monday! Outside of great potential for puns, peat also contains more than 3x the carbon as forests on a hectare basis. Despite it taking longer to form, its stewardship and carbon removal capacity is at odds with its’ use as a cheap fuel alternative. Innovation in its preservation is burgeoning, though its carbon credits markets are still relative…Read more4 years ago · 12 likes · 1 comment · Sophie Purdom and Kim Zou

2.title: 🏭 ff.33.3 Plants modified to capture CO2
2.content:
Plants are lazybones. Plants don't go all out to capture CO2. For example, even when there's plenty of sun, they slow their metabolism so as not to run out of other nutrients like water. So the conversion efficiency from CO2 to organic matter, which is then “held” as in the figures above, is low.
Some researchers are using innovative genetic techniques (read CRISPR) to increase the conversion of CO2 into stabilised carbon. Mark Zuckerberg (and his wife Chan) recently funded the Innovative Genomics Institute. This California institute, founded by CRISPR pioneer Jennifer Doudna (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020), is where much of the research on CRISPR applications is happening (we'll come back to it in more detail in an ff).

refs.0: Some researchers are using innovative genetic techniques (read CRISPR) to increase the conversion of CO2 into stabilised carbon

3.title: 🧮 ff.33.4 Computational moulds
3.content:
To close the circle between knowledge, algorithms and plants, let's talk about Plasmodium. It's a mould that has been used to find the shortest path connecting various regions (solving the famous Traveling Salesman Problem and showing great computational parallelisation skills).
Transport networks are ubiquitous in both social and biological systems. Robust network performance involves a complex trade-off involving cost, transport efficiency, and fault tolerance. Biological networks have been honed by many cycles of evolutionary selection pressure and are likely to yield reasonable solutions to such combinatorial optimization problems. We show that the slime mold Physarum polycephalum forms networks with comparable efficiency, fault tolerance, and cost to those of real-world infrastructure networks—in this case, the Tokyo rail system. The core mechanisms needed for adaptive network formation can be captured in a biologically inspired mathematical model that may be useful to guide network construction in other domains
In plain words. The researchers placed food to represent the cities to be connected and light gradients (which repel the mould) to define obstacles and topological barriers. In this way, a mould recreated the Tokyo rail map, and did so while showing control over transport speed and other parameters that define the main links. In short, a system like this can be used to calculate and design stable networks given certain operating conditions/limits set by the researchers. As if it were a computer, but it's a mould that simply wants to survive as best it can.

0.title: 🏙 ff.34.1 Ever more city dwellers
0.content:
It's a fact: we increasingly live in urbanised, “non-rural” areas, which many nations define as settlements of 2,000-10,000 people. As a percentage of the population:
🇮🇹 70 % | 🇺🇸 80 % | 🌐 55 %
Who wants to be a millionaire. For me, “living in a city” means a much bigger settlement. Let's say a million people. If we take that number as the definition of urban areas, the percentages change:
As you can see, the share of “true city dwellers” is relatively stable worldwide (except for China). In Europe it's below 20%. In Australia and the United States, 60% and 40% respectively.

1.title: 🚦 ff.34.2 Rethinking cities: mobility and traffic
1.content:
Even if most Italians live outside settlements of 1M people, they often travel to these nerve centres for work during the day. And we know it well, given the amount of traffic (especially between Pero and Cormano). COVID and remote working have improved things a bit. But how much?
TomTom (does anyone still use it?) does an interesting analysis and has loads of data broken down by country and city. Below, a snapshot of Rome.
After the return to “post”-COVID normality, Rome's traffic is below 2019 levels. From 24 minutes of delay (in the morning, 21 in the evening) it went to “just” 17 minutes in 2021.
10% of pollution from queues alone. The site estimates the amount of CO2 due to congestion. In Paris, for example, of the 13.8 MT of CO2 a year linked to mobility, more than 10% could be avoided without queues (maybe with flexible working hours or remote working?). In Am(mi)sterdam emissions are 10 times lower, because everyone cycles.

2.title: 🚦 ff.34.3 Rethinking cities: liveable spaces
2.content:
Speaking of Amsterdam and the Netherlands. In the '70s the Dutch were staunch supporters of cars and turned 900-year-old canals into roads.
U-turn. Then a series of projects strongly discouraged car use and gave space back to greenery and canals. This before-and-after gives an idea of how the city has been transformed again and made more liveable.
Then there are those who ask Artificial Intelligence to do the same using street images from Google Street View. AI opens up new visions that, in our concrete-covered habits, we can't conceive.
AI-generated street transformations@betterstreetsaiHindley Street (Adelaide, Australia)6:00 PM ∙ Aug 8, 2022136Likes7Retweets

3.title: 🥵 ff.34.4 Rethinking cities: heat
3.content:
With last summer's heatwaves (don't you miss it a bit, apart from the Jova Beach Party?), we realised it's better not to hold the Ferragosto barbecue in the city.
The European Space Agency (ESA) collects infrared images showing ground temperatures in a handful of European cities. It's fascinating to see 10-degree gaps between green areas (like Parco Sempione) and railway stations or covered markets (Milan's Fruit and Vegetable Market, presumably a shed with lots of air conditioners).

4.title: 1️ ff.34.5 It's all a monoculture
4.content:
Finally, let's get philosophical, fortissimo, right?
Homogenising space for cars. Journalist Thalia Verkade and urban planner Marco te Brömmelstroet argue in the Guardian that cities are yet another example of monoculture and homogenisation.
Just as we now grow very few plant varieties (with the resulting problems of pest epidemics wiping out harvests), we devote loads of urban space to a single factor: mobility. Roads (rather than spaces for relaxation, sport, culture and socialising) fill every corner of the city.
In rich words, as they write:
… just as swathes of our countryside were repurposed for farming, over the past century our city streets have been optimised for one goal: to move people around as quickly as possible, unhindered by anyone using public space for other purposes. This has its benefits — who wouldn’t argue that it is useful to be able to get from one side of a city to another quickly and efficiently — but they have come at a cost. Our shared urban environment, which used to be for everyone, is by and large dominated by moving and parked cars.
Cars infect every corner of our cities. And yet there's never enough parking, though there's always enough traffic. Who'll find the solution? Tesla with Autopilot or some micromobility startup?

0.title: 📈 ff.35.1 Projections for the wellbeing market
0.content:
Health matters. Especially when you consider that 20% of US GDP goes on medical spending and that, recently, China overtook the average American in life expectancy.
In ff.17 Sport (and the people who poop it) we saw Strava data showing a more active post-pandemic world population. McKinsey has a nice report on the strong growth of the wellness market ($1.5T).
Mens sana in corpore sano. As the chart below shows, “feeling good” is mostly about health, followed by personal care and clothing, fitness, diet and sleep.
It's interesting to note how COVID raised “awareness” of health (actually mostly in developing countries):

1.title: 🕛 ff.35.2 Smartwatches and more
1.content:
Spending in the wellness category obviously includes wearables, devices we carry with us all the time that monitor various aspects of our physiology. Here's the split between smartwatches, wireless earbuds, smart bands and “other”:
Other? What's in this category? Some notable examples:
The Oura Ring is a ring that measures HRV, heart rate variability (some smartwatches do it too, and it's not clear which is more accurate). HRV indicates how much fatigue you've built up. So it suggests to elite athletes the kind of training compatible with their recovery.
Supersapiens, meanwhile, offers a blood glucose monitor. This lets athletes “never run out of fuel” by suggesting when to eat. It can also be used to assess the glycaemic response to various foods.
Speaking of glycaemic responses: Zoe does exactly that. It sends a kit for various physiological measurements while suggesting a precise diet, to see how the body reacts to it. And there's huge variability from one person to another, and not just genetic.
Nothing grows from diamonds… The variability is linked to the microbiome, the microbes in our gut. So the kit also includes a poop collector to send by courier (Bartolini, out of spite) so Zoe can correlate the microbiome with the physiological responses above.
Battery dead? No problem: recently, devices have been proposed that can transmit information without chips or batteries, using only smart materials.

2.title: 💸 ff.35.3 Lots of money in digital medicine
2.content:
In 2021 startups raised an extraordinary amount of funding (which collapsed in 2022 due to far less favourable interest rates). A CB Insights study gives an overview.
The five health companies that received the most funding (3 billion in total out of 38 invested in the US):
Devoted Health (for finding health insurance); Medlinker (the site is in Chinese, so who knows); Magic Leap (advanced 3D headsets, with medical applications); Neumora Therapeutics (more targeted/customised brain drugs); Hinge Health (digital straps or bands for posture/movement problems)

3.title: 💤 ff.35.4 Super-sleep and super-focus
3.content:
7 easy pieces to sleep well and stay focused:
(1) Get sunlight by going outside as soon as you wake up (pyjamas are fine) (2) Wait a couple of hours before your first coffee (3) Drink water as soon as you wake up (4) Train early in the morning (within 3 hours of waking) to boost productivity at the start of the day (5) Practise partial fasting, with low carbs (but… I'm starving!) (6) Practise non-sleep deep rest for 30-90 minutes when physiology (and digestion) slow productivity down, especially in the early afternoon. (7) Minimise exposure to bright light between 22:00 and 4:00.

4.title: 🌳 ff.35.5 Leopardi's L'infinito according to AI
4.content:
Nature is another fundamental part of feeling good. I think because of the relationship
nature = outdoors = more light
Being outdoors, daylight inputs are well separated from the artificial ones of indoor spaces, and our body manages to restore important circadian rhythms (we talked about it in 🎼 ff.22 Do we eat too much?)
Nature, greenery, also keeps us away from screens and social media. That makes us feel good too.
If you can't find “green all around”, don't worry. Artificial Intelligence can recreate it for us. I fed passages of Leopardi into Wombo Art. I find some of the AI's artistic interpretations of the world-famous poem fascinating.
Sempre caro mi fu quest’ermo colle,e questa siepe, che da tanta partedell’ultimo orizzonte il guardo esclude.

0.title: 🐒 ff.36.1 Examples of superintelligence?
0.content:
Between DALL-E, algorithmic recommendations, Alexa, Roomba and Neuralink, Artificial Intelligence is ever more advanced and pervasive. And so concern grows about the effects these technologies could have on society, the economy, human psychology and, above all, our futuro fortissimo.
Reading thoughts. Neuralink, one of Musk's many labours, uses electrodes implanted in a monkey's brain to get it to play Pong.

1.title: 🦉 ff.36.2 The super-tome on the singularity
1.content:
A book I'd start from to discuss the topic is Superintelligence by Nick Bostrom.
Swedish, a philosophy professor at Oxford and co-founder of the Future of Humanity Institute, Bostrom deals with the singularity, i.e. the arrival of an artificial intelligence superior to human intelligence and beyond human control.
The author first asks how we'll get there: by simulating the brain, or by simulating the evolution of neural networks (from the very first neuron to the assembly we find in our heads). Or superintelligence could emerge from networks of individuals and companies (is Apple conscious?) or from genetic modifications of our brains (the least likely hypothesis).
Will we be the lambs? Then he discusses AI containment strategies (disconnecting it from the internet, for example, or severely limiting its resources/computing speed). Containing a superintelligence could be harder than expected (like Hopkins in The Silence of the Lambs). After all, if it's a superintelligence, by definition it would have escape strategies and powers of persuasion beyond our imagination.
Finally, Bostrom asks which universal and moral values to instil in it. What final goal should we give it? And how do we stop it from interpreting it in some absurd way, turning us into paperclips?
The singularity is already here:
Alcune centinaia di migliaia di annifa, nella preistoria umana (o ominide), la crescita era così lenta che ci voleva circa un milione di anni perché la capacità produttiva umana aumentasse sufficientemente per sostenere un ulteriore milione di individui. Nel 5000 aC, in seguito alla Rivoluzione agricola, il tasso di crescita era aumentato al punto che la stessa quantità di crescita richiedeva solo due secoli. Oggi, dopo la rivoluzione industriale, l'economia mondiale cresce in media di quella cifra ogni novanta minuti. Nick Bolstrom
The singularity in CO2:

2.title: 🗣️ ff.36.3 A good chat
2.content:
Lex Fridman always has interesting guests. Keeping up with him is very hard: he does a couple of podcasts a week, 2-3 hours each.
In this episode he talks with Ray Kurzweil, futurist and inventor of various speech recognition technologies. His next book, The Singularity is Nearer, updates his predictions on artificial intelligence.
Forget the Maya, mark 2029 in your diary. That's the date for reaching the singularity, defined as the moment when a human can't tell answers given by AI from those of a Sapiens (passing the Turing test). I also recommend the film Ex Machina on this topic.

3.title: 🤖 ff.36.4 Are we already blended with AI?
3.content:
Next time you're at your desk working, put your phone in the desk drawer. Within 5-15 minutes your hand will instinctively jerk towards it. But it won't be in its usual place. For a moment you'll feel mutilated. At least, that's what happened to me.
C17 or C18? By now, it's undeniable, the phone is an extension of ourselves. It gives us access to news, the music of the moment, city navigation, stock quotes, entire encyclopaedias. We're augmented. We're Super Sapiens. We're cyborgs.
Even without electrodes implanted in the brain, this connection is changing our physiology. For just over 10 years our brains have had to handle brand-new (and very high) levels of cortisol, dopamine, serotonin (etc…).
Smartphones and social media keep triggering:
The anxiety of knowing the latest news; The desire for approval; The search for social validation
In The Atlantic, Jean M. Twenge, a psychology professor at San Diego State University, argues that smartphones have destroyed a generation, iGen.
The scientific paper and its observations:
Teenagers who spend more than three hours on their phones show a 35% higher risk of suicide. More harm to themselves than to others, in social media isolation. In 2011 (for the first time in 24 years) the suicide rate was higher than the homicide rate among teenagers. A problem for girls. Depression symptoms rose by 21% for boys, while for girls we're at a 50% increase between 2012 and 2015.
Below, some correlations (not proven causal links) between the iPhone's release date and social phenomena of interest (image from Have Smartphones Destroyed a Generation?).
In short, we need LookUp more and more: the startup created by a dear friend that rewards us when we look up from our phones.
Extra reading (Nature paper): The effects of smartphones on eyesight, neural activity and our comprehension skills.
