0.title: 🌵 ff.37.1 Will it end like Westworld?
0.content:
There's a magnificent TV series: Westworld. Written by the Nolan brothers, with Hopkins and Aaron Paul (Pinkman from Breaking Bad, to be clear), it's about a Wild West theme park populated by unfeeling automatons, where you can unleash your most visceral impulses: sex, drugs, war. Over the first season, though, the humanoids seem to show clear signs of consciousness. I won't spoil anything else.
This series is just one of many narratives imagining the coexistence with robots that might await us, proof of how much this aspect of the future fascinates and frightens us. A future that is, after the latest Tesla AI Day, in my view closer than it seems.

1.title: 🤖 ff.37.2 Tesla AI Day
1.content:
By now I think you all know Tesla doesn't want to stop at self-driving cars and robo-taxis. At Tesla AI Day 2022 (by now my favourite tech event) Musk presented major developments on Optimus, perhaps the most advanced humanoid robot in development.
Unlike Boston Dynamics' robots, Tesla wants them to move without coding every single movement. Musk wants to be able to give general instructions and leave the details to artificial intelligence. 73kg in weight, a 2.3kWh battery (roughly the energy of 2000 kcal), actuators to mimic fingers, knees and shoulders. The cost: $20k, in line with robot price projections for the coming years (though “humanoid” ones are more expensive, around $150k according to Christian Hubiki)
I'm torn on Musk's approach. A humanoid robot can be advantageous:
Better integration with the world around us; Safer human-machine interactions
At the same time, though, I have some doubts:
Trying to mimic every joint can be hard to develop and costly in energy; Wouldn't a robot too similar to us scare people, slowing its adoption?
Tesla has on its side great efficiency in scaling production and the know-how built up from electric cars (image processing, optimisation search algorithms, …)

2.title: 🎮 ff.37.3 Haven't you tried NVIDIA?
2.content:
Sorry for the terrible pun above (in Italian, “Non ci hai NVIDIA?” sounds like “Aren't you jealous?”).
NVIDIA also recently held its annual conference, another event worth following, and not just for fans of Battlefield and GPUs ever better at simulating reality.
Different twins. To develop next-generation robots, you need to study their movements in detail, ideally in a fully virtual environment (digital twin). So simulation helps robotics, and the experience built up on Battlefield can come in handy.
On the hardware side, NVIDIA presented chips like the Jetson Orin Nano, which can be a common interface for all devices. It's a sort of Lego for artificial intelligence, a generic chip able to handle navigation and the smart management of sensor inputs.
Robotic metaverse. The intersection of these trends, where the line between digital and real blurs more and more, is obviously the metaverse. NVIDIA, with its Omniverse and the suite of tools/partnerships it has built over the years, is well positioned to seize the “meta” opportunity.

3.title: 📈 ff.37.4 Robots ever more widespread
3.content:
A Republic founded on labour. Let's now broaden the effect of robotics on society, which we'd discussed in 🎼 ff.9 Automation.
Industrial robot installations relative to their cost have accelerated nicely in recent years:
China rules the roost, with almost half of all installations (2020 data):
And here you'll find the projections for 2030. Robots, today used mostly in manufacturing, will spread as autonomous vehicles and move into services (food, retail, cleaning, …).
Italy installed 11.6k of the 400k robots worldwide, with one of the biggest growth rates (+50%) in Europe compared with 2020.

0.content:
We've already mentioned the crazy Tim Urban in a previous Futuro Fortissimo (🎼 ff.21 The magic of salad delivered to your door). On his blog he collects truly peculiar questions and answers.
In 2014 he started from one figure: 241 trillion dollars (the sum of the value of all the money, all the stocks, all the private and public buildings on Earth).
How do we quantify $241 * 10^12? He tried to visualise this number by turning it into blocks of gold, $100 bills or one gigantic potato.
In $100 bills: we'd have a stack almost as high as the Moon.
In gold: things are more manageable, with a cube 63 metres per side, compared below with a pyramid.
In potatoes: we get a mega tuber covering half of Long Island (179 km^3) at €0.33/kg (with inflation that number has gone up; if you're interested, here's how much a kg of potatoes costs in Italy)
In Domino's pizza: we'd cover all of Nigeria (conversion rate used: $19 for a 14'' pizza, corresponding to 52 cm^2). Luckily Domino's pizzas that big don't exist, especially after the closure in Italy.
If you're curious about the exact calculations, I'll point you to the hilarious article.

1.title: 💰 ff.38.2 COVID and inequality
1.content:
But how is the pizza shared out? If we cut it into 9 slices and 100 people represent the entire population of the Earth:
1 takes 3 slices | 9 take another 3 slices | the remaining 90 share the last 3
A pandemic of inequality. Right after COVID, the richest 1% of the world's population accumulated more wealth than the poorest 90%. Inequality.org is a good site for more on this. The temporary “citizen's income”, i.e. the support showered on those who lost their jobs because of COVID closures, should have helped with inequality, right? Wrong.
The blanket handouts amounted to 400 billion, against 4500 billion invested in corporate assets (thus supporting the richest 1% of the population). It's true that money invested in companies then trickles down into society. But the first to receive the money are the most advantaged. Let's see why.
The Cantillon effect. Imagine receiving a million euros in a remote village. You spend it, build yourself a lovely house and eat delicious food, paying the other villagers, who will “feel” the money injected into the system.
Spending it first, the amount of “lovely houses and delicious food” isn't a limit. When the other villagers want their share, though, there isn't enough for everyone, because production hasn't adapted to the increased demand. “Lovely houses and delicious food” will cost more, and the wealth accumulated will be smaller. It reminds me a bit of the rising inflation going around.

2.title: 👁️ ff.38.3 The cryptocurrency to reduce inequality
2.content:
Much of the value of Meta, Google and Amazon is their network effect: Facebook makes sense because it creates and offers connections. This is intangible value, with no physical counterpart like an advanced machine or a super-powerful chip. So it isn't produced, nor does it generate a complementary physical economy around it. It's just built into the company's share value, which is owned by the (often richest) 1-10% of the population.
Retina as a wallet. To try to redistribute part of the wealth tied to these networks and to the internet, Worldcoin proposes bringing every citizen on Earth onto the blockchain, scanning their eye and giving them a unique economic passport and equal access to the most basic technologies.
Recently, major investment funds invested ($100M) in this technology. Worldcoin expects to scan an average of 350-1400 people a week (starting from a base of 60k users). For comparison, “crypto” users number 400M (from Crypto.com, 2021).

0.title: 🍝 ff.41.1 It's all in the filling
0.content:
Write the recipe for casoncelli alla bergamasca
Casoncelli alla bergamasca are a typical dish of Bergamo cuisine. Here are the ingredients and the method to prepare them:
Ingredients:
500 g 00 flour; 250 g ricotta; 100 g butter; 100 g smoked pancetta; 100 g grated parmesan; 1 egg; 1 onion; 1 celery stalk; 1 carrot; 1 garlic clove; 1/2 glass white wine; Salt and pepper to taste.
Method:
In a saucepan, sauté the finely chopped onion, celery, carrot and garlic with a little butter. Add the diced smoked pancetta and brown for a few minutes. Deglaze with the white wine and let it evaporate. In a bowl, mix the ricotta with the grated parmesan, the egg, salt and pepper. Roll the pasta out very thin and, using a pastry cutter or a glass, cut out discs. Place a little filling in the centre of each disc and fold the casoncelli into half-moons, sealing the edges well with your fingers or a fork. Cook the casoncelli in plenty of boiling salted water for 3-4 minutes, then drain and dress them with the pancetta sauce prepared earlier. Serve the casoncelli piping hot, topped with a sprinkle of grated parmesan. Enjoy your meal!

3.title: 👩‍🍳 ff.41.4 Parodi who?
3.content:
I have in the fridge: pasta, eggs, pork loin fillet, milk, cheese, peppers, beans, apples, cream, lemon, avocado, salami. Can you suggest two recipes, a first course and a main course, starting from what I have?
With the ingredients you have in your fridge, you can make two tasty recipes, for example:
First course: tagliolini with salami and peppers. To make this recipe, start by dicing the salami and peppers, then sauté them in a pan with a little oil. Meanwhile, cook the pasta in plenty of salted water and drain it al dente. Add the pasta to the pan with the salami and peppers and add a little grated cheese. Toss the pasta and serve immediately, piping hot. Main course: lemon pork loin fillet. To make this recipe, start by marinating the pork loin fillet in a bowl with lemon juice, salt, pepper and a little oil for at least 30 minutes. Then heat a non-stick pan and cook the pork loin fillet over medium heat for about 5-6 minutes per side, until nicely browned. Meanwhile, make a lemon sauce by melting a little butter in a small pan and adding the cream and lemon juice. Pour the sauce over the meat and serve hot, with a side of vegetables.

1.title: ❓ ff.42.2 Polluting, or pushing the transition?
1.content:
Until a few years ago, China was synonymous with smog-choked cities. With the data on electric mobility and renewable energy, this bad reputation seems to have improved a little.
Or not? China is still the world's largest CO2 emitter (1/4 of total emissions), and emissions are estimated to peak only in 2030, with net-zero by 2060. It's also still the largest builder (52% of the total) of coal plants, with 91 GW in 2021 (these absolute numbers should always be weighed against the size of the economy and population)
But it has also invested more than any other country in the energy transition ($266B, 2.4x the US):
5x and 17T. Economically, to reach net-zero China needs to invest a total of $17T (so, with $266B, in 2021 it invested 1.5% of the total) and increase current renewable output by a factor of 5x.
captions: Investment by country (in billions of dollars) in preventing climate change (2021).

2.title: 🐌 ff.42.3 A spanner in the AI works
2.content:
Supremacy in electrification suggests an all-Chinese future. But on topics like artificial intelligence the situation is a bit different:
Technological (and military) development is tied to artificial intelligence. Artificial intelligence is strongly tied to the computing power needed to train it. The technical know-how for building graphics cards/compute nodes for training is in US hands (NVIDIA, AMD). In the last year a full-blown embargo on American products began, to slow down China's computing power and technological/AI development.
It's interesting to note that, in the long run, this will have an effect similar to what we're seeing in microchip manufacturing: the United States and Europe are building independent semiconductor factories. China could do the same with AI.
The Taiwan case. In short, every state is trying to be as independent as possible. If the benefits of globalisation were to disappear, trade and interdependence between countries would shrink, raising the risk of tensions and, eventually, wars. What's happening with TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co) should ring an alarm bell ($40B invested in the US by them in the last year)

0.title: ☑️ ff.44.1 The modern fallacy of time in boxes
0.content:
4000 Weeks opens with a historical excursus. In the Middle Ages, when time couldn't be measured, all human activities were dictated by natural rhythms. There was no point trying to optimise the apple harvest (maybe with KPIs or market analysis): you had to wait for them to ripen. Same with milking cows.
Today, instead, time is a continuous flow, made of minutes, hours, days. Time today is a conveyor belt that never stops, with boxes to fill every hour that otherwise go unused. Wasted. Tim Urban, fittingly, visualises the 4000 weeks like this:
And so come the deadlines, the 25-5 Pomodoro methods, the productivity guides (which exploded after the pandemic, didn't they?).

1.title: ♾️ ff.44.2 The infinitude out there
1.content:
Even if these boxes existed, how could we ever fill finite boxes with the infinite objects (and experiences) around us?
The digital world doesn't help:
The alternative way to spend your time, where to go on holiday, which film to watch is ready in the next Instagram story, the next online article, the next TripAdvisor review. Alternatives are served up in 15-second TikToks and infinite feeds, where even if we try to fill a box with something, to focus on one experience, a few seconds later we're on a different app, with a different thought, trying to squeeze in something else.
Burkeman argues that the anxiety of choosing, of defining a box, is philosophically inseparable from Heidegger's concepts of “being” and “existence”.
To overcome the anxiety of our present, we need to accept our own finitude and the finitude of the real world, which, unlike virtual worlds and metaverses, is the only one that can truly materialise and “be”.

2.title: 🏠 ff.44.3 Settling down steadies you
2.content:
Decided? Not by chance, in Italian decidere (to decide) shares its root with uccidere (to kill) and recidere (to cut off). Cutting. Removing opportunities.
We don't know how to do it: every kind of commitment, of tie, scares us. It means ruling out other opportunities.
Not that this message is new, mind you. Kierkegaard (Heidegger's close intellectual relative) was already talking about it in 1843 (which is as far from us as 2201). Do you think anyone will remember this newsletter in 2201?
La sua libertà di scelta non rappresenta la sua grandezza, ma il suo permanente dramma. Infatti egli si trova sempre difronte all'alternativa di una "possibilità che sí" e di una "possibilità che no" senza possedere alcun criterio di scelta. E brancola nel buio, in una posizione instabile, nella permanente indecisione, senza riuscire ad orientare la propria vita, intenzionalmente, in un senso o nell'altro. Søren Kierkegaard,Aut-aut
That said, it must be said that Kierkegaard, a never-sated womaniser, didn't have Tinder. Otherwise who knows how many more books he'd have written.

3.title: 🖼️ ff.44.4 Wasting 3 hours in front of a painting
3.content:
One of the book's messages is that the constant search for new stimuli and time optimisation is a way to escape the anxiety of standing still. It's a way not to think about our essence, our finitude, our mortality.
So the author reports an assignment that Jennifer Roberts, an art history professor at Harvard, gives her students every year: stare at a painting for three hours.
Certeforme d'arte impongono vincoli temporali al loro pubblico in modo piuttosto ovvio: quando guardi, ad esempio, un'esibizione dal vivo deLe nozze di Figaroo una proiezione diLawrence d'Arabia, non hai altra scelta che dedicare all'opera il tuo tempo. Oliver Burkeman,Come fare per avere più tempo? Time management per comuni mortali
Personal note. I don't know about you, but more and more often I find myself not finishing a film. Leaving it halfway. “I'll finish it later”, I tell myself, gripped by the anxiety of doing something else.

refs.1: stare at a painting for three hours

4.title: 4️⃣ ff.44.5 4 ways to find a cure
4.content:
I like to suggest solutions after defining a problem. The author suggests:
Atelic activities (like walking, cultivating hobbies, activities with no ultimate goal where you can't “fail”); Setting reasonable, finite goals (I work on 🎼ff for half an hour, then I've done my bit for today!); Keeping a done-list (to remind us how much we've already achieved); Avoiding forcing carpe diem: focusing too much on living in the moment is itself a fallacy, like trying to fall asleep by thinking hard about falling asleep.

1.title: 🚀 ff.46.2 Astronomical costs
1.content:
Fear has blocked funding, research, deployment and cost reduction. Here's the energy mix (split into emoji) for the US in 2021:
US ENERGY MIX | 61% fossil fuels | 19% nuclear | 9% wind | 3% solar
Even though the United States has a good share, nuclear energy has effectively been stagnant since the '80s:
Moore's law's close cousin (actually a generalisation of it) is named after aerospace engineer Wright: Wright's law (1936). It says that the more we produce something, the better we get at making it, and so the faster and cheaper we become.
The cost of regulation. Well, for nuclear this doesn't seem to work. The cost of nuclear energy has grown (an effect entirely linked to regulation). Before 1980 the cost was $1175/kW. At an inflation rate of 2-3%, today it could cost a few cents per kW. Instead we're above $5000.
Nerd corner. The cost of producing one TJ (but also the energy of a heartbeat or of the Cretaceous meteorite)
$/TJ | diesel 26k | natural gas 12k | coal 7k | uranium 20 (no k!)
Winter is coming. Meanwhile, China will build 150 plants over the next 7 years (60% of global growth) and overtake the US as the country with the largest nuclear system. In Europe, on the other hand, apart from France, the picture is sad. Germany, for example, is closing many plants, and only a crisis like the war in Ukraine led to some measures being postponed.
We can't depend on socio-health/geopolitical upheavals (see COVID → remote working) to make the future happen!
Here's a breakdown with numbers on production around the world.
🇺🇸 91.5GW | 🇫🇷 61.3GW | 🇨🇳 50.8GW | 🇯🇵 31.7GW | 🇷🇺 29.6GW
captions: Since around 1990, US nuclear generating capacity has been flat: 102 GW
Instead of falling, nuclear costs are rising sharply. Probably because of super-restrictive regulation.

2.title: 😭  ff.46.3 Wasted years
2.content:
If nuclear had replaced coal and gas, we'd have avoided 9.5 million deaths and 174 Gt of CO2 (that is, if the 1960-1976 acceleration had continued).
Social and regulatory resistance has led to an embarrassing delay in nuclear research: while quantum mechanics and the Standard Model describe the behaviour of electrons and subatomic particles superbly, our understanding of the interaction between atoms still has big gaps (despite the field's venerable age of 80 years).
We should already have nuclear batteries. And guess what? Your iPhone wouldn't need charging and your Tesla would have a range of 2 million km. Storrs Hall, Where is my flying car? A memoir of future past
In conclusion. Recent developments in fusion are exciting (but it'll take time). Meanwhile, why not appreciate the potential of what we already have? The uranium dissolved in the oceans is enough to supply 10 kW (US per capita consumption) to 10 billion people for 10,000 years (and current technology is close to extracting uranium from seawater economically).
Can we go back to believing in the future? Can we drop the mindset of mandatory cuts, degrowth and sacrifice?

0.title: ⚽ ff.49.1 We're getting rounder
0.content:
Nutrition and diet are a complex topic, hard to unpack in a newsletter, also given the non-trivial connections between:
Genetics; Microbiome; Meal timing; Amount of fiber and micronutrients; Type of exercise / training level of each individual; Other aspects we'll try to throw into the pot in this 🎼ff.
Let's give it a go anyway. And let's do it with a number that sticks. After all, this is Futuro Fortissimo. Obesity mortality worldwide is rising:
5.3% (1990) | 8.5% (2019) | +3% in 30 years
The share of obese adults has also nearly doubled over the last 40 years. Give or take a country, the whole West is following a not exactly positive trend.
captions: From 1975 to today, Italy went from 10 to 23 people (out of 100) with obesity problems. In the US, 37.

1.title: 👅 ff.49.2 BMI, BMR (they're not raspberries)
1.content:
These charts, though on different scales, remind me terribly of those from February 2020. In a (post-)COVID era, can we talk about another, quieter and slower pandemic? If so, what is the “obesity virus”?
Let's start with the basics. With the PCR test.
BMI, body mass index. The well-known index, a cold, hard number, tells us whether we're under/normal/overweight. On 🎼ff we give numbers a personal, “understandable” spin. So here's a range for various heights:Height ! 18 - 21 - 25 |————————————————————————150 cm  ! 41 - 47 - 56 |155 cm  ! 43 - 50 - 60 |160 cm  ! 46 - 52 - 64 |165 cm  ! 49 - 57 - 68 |170 cm  ! 52 - 61 - 72 |175 cm  ! 55 - 64 - 77 |180 cm  ! 58 - 68 - 81 |185 cm  ! 62 - 72 - 86 |190 cm  ! 65 - 76 - 90 |
BMR, basal metabolic rate. It's how much our body burns just to survive, at rest. Here's the first dose of variability: BMR can range from 1100 kcal up to 2500 kcal a day. 63% depends on how much muscle you have, 26% on unexplained individual factors (!).
It's also influenced by age, sex and (needless to say) BMI:
captions: The main factor correlating with BMR: your lean mass, i.e. muscle.
BMR by age and sex. Women are the circles, men the triangles. At 50, BMR is 10-15% (200-300 kcal) lower than at 20. Paper.

refs.0: BMR can range from 1100 kcal up to 2500 kcal a day

2.title: 🍔 ff.49.3 Diets and pollutants
2.content:
We've seen the trends and laid the groundwork for measuring our bodies. Now let's try to understand why we're getting ever rounder.
Chicken and Doritos. The first suspect is obviously diet. Pew Research collected the changes in the American diet over the last 40 years. People take in 400 kcal more, eat twice as much chicken and fewer potatoes (even counting fried/bagged ones).
Calories in - calories out. This simple little rule is a good starting point. After all, the correlation between BMI and calories consumed is clear.
And yet there's a non-negligible spread at equal calories consumed (maybe because, for example, digesting food takes more or less energy depending on meal size, amount of fiber and macronutrients?).
Fats or carbs. Both macronutrients have been blamed for the pandemic. And yet one study found no difference between a mostly fat-based diet and a carb-based one. Backing this up, the diet (3000 kcal) of the super-healthy Maasai (a nomadic people between Kenya and Tanzania) is 66% fat.
Then there's the decline in carb consumption in recent years.
In short, tinkering with macronutrient percentages doesn't seem to have much effect. Fiber, on the other hand, helps lower BMI (for example by adopting a whole-food plant-based diet).
But is there more?
A Chemical Hunger is a read with food for thought, even if, I admit, at times a bit far-fetched (the discussion on Y Combinator).
Let's put more meat on the fire (but don't eat it!):
Eating 10,000 kcal a day leads to weight gain, obviously. Once the over-feeding period ends, though, people return to their original BMI. The potato diet, which makes you lose weight and the urge to eat. In Australia sugar intake has dropped by 20%, but obesity keeps rising. The inverse correlation between obesity and altitude above sea level. Processed foods are linked to a higher risk of premature death and even dementia, due to their low fiber content and the many added ingredients for long-term stabilisation. Fats and sugars make us release a whole lot more dopamine, after all.
captions: Breakdown of calories consumed by food type (American diet 1970 vs 2010). Flour-based products went from 400 to 600 kcal. Fats are rising too.
Share of overweight or obese people vs daily calorie intake. The underlying linear trend is clear.

The record for reversing epigenetic ageing (5 years). Some people have taken diet care to the extreme (ranking first in the Rejuvenation Olympics).
Bryan Johnson. 45 years old (on paper) and founder of Braintree, acquired by PayPal in 2013 for 12 billion. He proposes the Blueprint method to slow down ageing (or reverse it). If you follow the previous link, you'll find the obsessive tracking of every aspect of his physiology.

0.title: 🤔 ff.50.1 The oddness of the last 50 years
0.content:
In 2011 Tyler Cowen, an economics professor at George Mason University, published the famous book The Great Stagnation, arguing that the last 50 years have seen techno-economic stagnation. Then there's a website, WTF happened in 1971, that collects charts thrown off kilter since that year. I'll pick three at random.
Inflation looks out of control (here the last 300 years):
US public debt has exploded to today's $32T ($94k per citizen or $234k per taxpayer):
And house prices have followed the same trend (here Amsterdam):
But, but, but. The last 50 years have been very, very peculiar. Economic boom, spread of education, population explosion, the digital world and the chip revolution. And, more recently, the pandemic and lockdowns, the subprime crisis and the “.com” one.
Too many issues to find a single explanation. But let's look at one possible contributing cause: monetary policy. Money printed whenever needed.
captions: Inflation rate (Consumer Price Index, CPI) in the United States, from 1770 to today.
House prices in Amsterdam (1620-2020).

1.title: 🪙 ff.50.2 Gold, silver, myrrh, beer and Bitcoin
1.content:
The golden age. Columbia economist Saifedean Ammous, in The Bitcoin Standard, points out that the technological progress of the 20th century (symbolised by the belle époque) coincided with the implementation of the gold standard, the monetary system that guaranteed the conversion of each country's currency at a precise rate.
Below, the value of various currencies against gold, with a clear plateau between 1920 and 1970. Then, a sharp, massive devaluation.
A future that devalues. OECD data, after all, show that from 1990 to 2015 the global annual increase in currency was 7.2%. Here's the situation in the US.
currency devaluation → less faith in the future → less investment → less growth → stagnation
To restore faith in the future, Ammous proposes Bitcoin as the new standard. Its decentralisation and intrinsically limited supply (21 million) would ensure that nobody manipulates the reserves, stabilising the value of all currencies.

refs.0: Here's the situation in the US.

2.title: 💻 ff.50.3 Technological stagnation
2.content:
It's not that there's been no progress in the last 50 years. Quite the opposite. Here we try to be optimistic and positive first and foremost. But technological stagnation in some sectors is undeniable.
The strange case of Dr Eroom and Mr Moore. The cost of developing drugs doubles every year (due to the big pharma monopoly or to the regulation demanded by a society more frightened than attracted by a technology).
We landed on the Moon in 1969 and only today, after Musk came up with re-landing rockets to slash costs, are we dreaming of it again.
Despite the many PhDs (which, however, aren't growing the way they did before the '70s), “basic” scientific progress has stalled (in the early 1900s quantum mechanics and relativity; today we've been stuck at the standard model and string theory for decades).
Vaclav Smil, in Growth: From Microorganisms to Megacities, collects many logistic charts showing the saturation of efficiencies in many mechanical systems (mostly invented in the early 1900s and still not replaced by new developments).
In short, in plain words:
We wanted flying cars, instead we got 140 characters. Peter Thiel, co-founder of PayPal and Palantir.
But is it fair to compare different paths of technological development? Again according to Thiel:
Today the word technology means information technology, while in 1960 it meant space travel and nuclear. It's hard to say whether it's better to have an ever snappier smartphone (or one that takes photos a million times better) rather than a flying car.
futuro_fortissimo_newsletterA post shared by VeI2ax (@futuro_fortissimo_newsletter)
My take:
The space/nuclear technology argument is a bit misleading. During the Cold War (or World War II) the acceleration and deregulation were so strong that some technologies arrived “early”. Moore's Law (Wright's law applied to chips) is the most famous precisely because chips were the first example of scalability and a positive loop between process and result (better computers → better chips). Given how easy it was to reap the fruits of Moore's Law (and the considerable benefits involved), the money was invested there. Today, PC performance gains are ever smaller (an example of diminishing marginal utility?) and computing power is fuelling positive loops in other fields (genetics, robotics, AI).
captions: Energy conversion efficiency from thermal sources, United States.

refs.0: The cost of developing drugs doubles every year
refs.1: PhDs (which, however, aren't growing the way they did before the '70s)

3.title: 🌟 ff.50.4 Consumers, but not of energy
3.content:
Another sign of stagnation is energy use. Per capita energy consumption (I stress “per capita” given the population explosion of the last century and a half):
Possible explanations:
Dematerialisation and digitalisation; Greater efficiency; Remote working; Limits imposed by the cost of energy
Unlimited gigs. Points 1-3 show we're using energy ever more efficiently. But a major bottleneck on energy consumption is its price.
Especially after the recent events in Ukraine, petrol pump prices and ENEL bills have changed Italians' habits. Energy is not yet as accessible as computing power or GBs of internet data.
🎵 Final notes
Does it make sense that, in 2023, we still have to heat our homes sparingly, drop by drop?

0.title: 💚 ff.51.1 Storytelling for green
0.content:
Green: a symbol of hope, bucolic, organic, natural. Calcutta would want it “all around”. Let's face it, it's also a bit easy. After all, who'd want “some Lampugnano” all around? Better wide open spaces, “sovrumani silenzi e profondissima quiete” (superhuman silences and deepest quiet).
Science agrees too. Walking in green spaces helps against depression, thanks to reduced mental rumination, or maybe because we breathe in a molecule that knocks down cortisol. And Japanese medicine counts shinrin-yoku, forest bathing, as a cure.
But, but, but. A line from The Eight Mountains made me think a lot. When the city folk meet Bruno, the protagonist's mountain friend points out:
“[…] siete voi di città che la chiamate Natura. È così astratta nella vostra testa che è astratto pure il nome. Noi qui diciamo bosco, pascolo, torrente, roccia, cose che uno può indicare con il dito. Cose che si possono usare. Se non si possono usare, un nome non glielo diamo perché non serve a niente.”Paolo Cognetti,Le otto montagne
So I start to suspect that, in our digital/anthropic frenzy, we're idealising nature. And, as a result, the issue of climate change.
So let me try to spark a somewhat “against the grain” reflection on climate, using numbers and percentages. Shades other than 1/0. Other than all or nothing. Other than black and white.
captions: Differences in blood flow in the prefrontal cortex (linked to mental b******t) between patients after a walk in nature vs in the city.
In Japanese medicine the concept of forest bathing, shinrin-yoku, is elevated to a cure.

1.title: 🛐 ff.51.2 Ecology = religion?
1.content:
Perhaps nature is the religion of the 21st century. Climate change the God who controls us, and sin is what we feel when we eat one steak too many.
In Dark Green Religion, Bron Taylor (professor of religion and nature at the University of Florida) tries to articulate the theme in more detail.
He cites the thinking of a naturalist, John Burroughs, who draws important parallels between nature and spirituality.
Non andiamo in Chiesa tanto frequentemente come i nostri genitori, ma ci immergiamo nel verde molto più di loro, quasi identificando gli alberi come un tempio laico. John Burroughs,The Gospel Of Nature.
By elevating ecology to a religion, we could act irrationally, forgetting the need for critical thinking and quantitative analysis. Let's look at a glaring example.
(Green) peace be with you. Greenpeace, according to its co-founder, has become an ideological monster. Born to raise awareness about whaling and atmospheric nuclear tests, it ended up protesting unscientifically against chlorine (Carthago delenda est).
captions: The leafy cathedral right outside my home, at Passo Zambla (Bergamo).

refs.1: Greenpeace, according to its co-founder, has become an ideological monster

2.title: 🔥 ff.51.3 I'm your heretic dream
2.content:
I found an episode of the podcast that intrigues me most, Lex Fridman's, uncomfortable but also eye-opening.
In his typical 4 hours, Lex talks about climate change and its socio-economic impact with Bjørn Lomborg (author of False Alarm) and Andrew Revkin (21 years at the NYT). Some takeaways:
Contrary to popular belief, “extreme” events aren't increasing: we're better at monitoring them and they hit more people because of the urbanisation of critical areas (COVID exemplifies both: molecular tests, and densely populated areas that amplify the damage at equal risk). Cutting temperatures and CO2 isn't the only solution: we can use better prevention and monitoring systems (an earthquake can have totally different effects depending on the precautions taken). Every dollar spent on education brings a 45x return; invested in fighting malaria and tuberculosis (1.5 million deaths a year) 42x; on climate change 10x. In numerical terms, climate change could bring a 0.7-2.4% annual reduction from now to 2100 (for the US), so at most we're talking about the cost of legal disputes (2.4% of GDP in 2016).
Let me repeat: climate change is a serious issue and needs to be studied in detail (if you like, here's a 40-page summary from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change).
Population ageing, diet, lifestyles, mental health, bureaucracy, wage distribution and migration: all issues that can impact socio-economic development (positively or negatively) more than climate change.
Olympus. If the analogy with religion holds, perhaps we should at least move from a natural monotheism to a social polytheism, weighing in due proportion every aspect of our complex, stimulating and ever faster society.
🎵 Final notes
Coming soon: a world religion that forbids smoking, travelling more than 1000 km a month, eating meat, burning wood.

Democracy trembles. Democracy and modern institutions are so fragile. The earthquake in Turkey showed that some nation states can't even count people, assess the state of buildings or assign property.
The concept of the Nation-State is also cracked by citizens able to cross borders digitally, work remotely, move money around blockades (as is happening with the war in Ukraine).

And so we're back to talking about cryptocurrencies. But aren't they “like, so 2021, bro”? No. Even though Bitcoin is worth half its peak (partly because of the FTX mess), they're more relevant than ever.

1.title: 🏙️ ff.52.2 Centralising pays off
1.content:
Centralisation or decentralisation? Let's add a piece to today's Futuro Fortissimo: cities. Or rather, centralisation. McKinsey helps us out this time too, pointing out that half of world GDP in the 2010-2020 decade was generated in 3600 regions (covering 1% of the planet).
Cities could also help us contain climate change, since they seem to pollute less (cutting the travel needed to reach services and pushing people to live in smaller homes, with lower consumption).
Services are increasingly centralised too. Companies controlled by a handful of individuals can choose to dethrone the President of the United States from a social network or control our access to news and information.
The film Her. With the arrival of ChatGPT and the like, sexuality, psychological support and friendship will also be managed digitally (Replika, the PEGI 18 bot that sends you (for a fee) hot pics).
The problem? 6529, a CryptoPunk active on Twitter, comes to the rescue with a reflection on the growing need to decentralise. He uses New York taxis to make his case:
6529@punk65291/ On Taxis
Or how the world is centralizing all around you, but why you, fellow citizen, have probably not thought about it at all.

2.title: 🌐 ff.52.3 Founding your own nation
2.content:
Homemade nations. Balaji Srinivasan (former CTO of Coinbase and general partner at A16Z) proposes a solution to these problems in his recent book The Network State, freely available online (don't worry, it's also summarised in one sentence, 1000 words, one image, or a short essay).
Not everyone is Trump. Balaji starts with a couple of reflections:
The probability of becoming President of the United States is far lower than even that of becoming a billionaire. Only 45 people have made it, because of bureaucratic/legislative/demographic eligibility limits. Many nations (and their monetary reserves) are much smaller than the Bitcoin and Ethereum networks.
So Balaji offers a guide to founding and building a digital state:
As easily as you found a startup, you can think about building a startup society. All it takes is a Discord group of people who believe in certain rules (ideally a simple diktat, like “100% vegan” or “long live abs”). Around this rule, people can coordinate to reach a higher goal (with tokens that incentivise working in that direction). Thanks to the value created by the internal economy, the digital world can start spilling over into the real one. In the “long live abs” example, you'd start with gyms, then buildings and whole cities, accessible only to members holding the token. Then you need to connect the various physical nodes with decentralised protocols and social interactions powered by augmented reality. At this point the network could monitor its users' economy and demographics. Its legislative and institutional capabilities would then lead to pressure for recognition by national bodies.
🎵 Final notes
In the future, we'll need a visa to enter a vegan restaurant. And woe betide us if in the last 12 months we've passed through the state recently founded by the Berettas.

1.title: 🥇 ff.53.2 Pro athletes to the rescue
1.content:
Iñigo San Millán studies the intersection between athletes' metabolism and cancer. Head of Performance of the UAE-Emirates cycling team, he's the coach of champion Tadej Pogačar. I find him fascinating, as usual captured perfectly in a TED Talk.
Since you're all mega-busy, a mini-summary:
Carbs and sugars are blamed as the greatest evil. Yet the brain uses only those, and athletes take in up to 100g an hour. When we estimate the impact of diets/treatments, the “healthy person” used as a benchmark is the average Westerner, a bit overweight and sedentary. Instead, athletes should be the benchmark. To study the impact of fuel (diet, drugs) on the engine (physiology) we should use an F1 Ferrari, not a '96 Cadillac that's been sitting in the garage for ages. The key to our survival is respiration. Cellular respiration. Mitochondria. Many diseases (like diabetes) are linked to their dysfunction (because, being sedentary, we don't activate them at all). If mitochondria don't work properly, lactate and hydrogen ions build up, which the body fights with insulin. After two months off, athletes' mitochondria lose half their ability to burn lactate. Imagine what happens in a population stuck at 4000-5000 steps a day.
Gels, lactate and tumours. About 100 years ago, Nobel laureate Warburg hypothesised that cancer cells attacked mitochondria. Why? He noticed a huge, massive build-up of lactate in diseased cells (even in the presence of oxygen, as if the mitochondria weren't working well). The direct-attack theory has been disproved, but the focus on lactate's role is correct.
Back to Dr. Millán. He re-examined the Warburg effect, hypothesising that the same lactate that has to be metabolised efficiently to conquer the Tour de France could promote the development and spread of cancer.
This is beautiful. Just as space research or F1 gave us GPS and the KERS system, sport could solve the drama of cancer.

2.title: 😷 ff.53.3 From COVID to cancer
2.content:
Another example of how a crisis can be beneficial: COVID vaccine technology can be applied to cancer treatment. BioNTech develops mRNA vaccines that bind to markers on tumour cells, stimulating the individual's immune response.
This approach requires analysing the DNA of each patient's tumour cells (neo-antigens). Once the sequence is identified, you can “write” the matching mRNA able to bind to them.
Ouch, it hurts. AI doesn't hurt. AtomicAI is one of the most active companies in this field. A bit like AlphaFold with proteins, its PARSE algorithm speeds up the identification of RNA structures to develop new drugs.
🎵 Final notes
In the future, we'll have blood tests able to detect traces of tumours. If present, after screening their DNA, we'll be given a vaccine to wipe them out. Syringe injections will be as common as pills are today.

0.title: ✊ ff.55.1 How does it feel, inside a revolution?
0.content:
Before any other reflection, I recommend Lex Fridman's ever-timely podcast with the founder of OpenAI.
When is it a revolution? Hard to say, but when the efficiency of the best-paid job in the world improves by 50% overnight and there's growing convergence (ARK Invest's annual report) between AI and other technologies, maybe we're close.
The guillotine. With the steam engine we delegated physical activity; now we're handing mental activities and memories over to digital. Just as for an 18th-century farmer physical labour was everything and a tractor was unimaginable, if AI takes away our mental faculties, what human dimension will we discover?
Meditate, people, meditate! Gyms and Ironmans stimulate the sedentary bodies of most workers: no feudal lord ever dreamed of running an ultra-trail or doing an everesting. In the same way, mindfulness and meditation (already on the rise, and not by chance) could become ever more important. Perhaps humans will fall back on the irreducible: their consciousness.
But, but, but. Let's not take even consciousness for granted, since computers are already reconstructing what we're seeing.

1.title: 🕳️ ff.56.2 We are already geoengineers
1.content:
Agriculture raised atmospheric CO2 to 280ppm. Glacial cycles predicted 240ppm for pre-industrial levels. 6000 years ago the Earth's average temperature was 1 degree higher than in the 19th century and, without agriculture, Canada would have been covered in ice.
Containing the ozone hole is perhaps the textbook example of geoengineering. Its dangerous thinning was stopped by banning chlorofluorocarbons (and other ODS, Ozone Depleting Substances). NASA reminds us of the UV-blasted world we avoided thanks to the Montreal Protocol.
And smog? Our CO2 and sulphate emissions are already changing the climate (in an uncontrolled way). Very bad geoengineering, so much so that sulphites emitted in the Northern Hemisphere cause droughts in Africa.
captions: We stopped the very dangerous decline, but we're not at pre-DDT levels.

Given the immense (solar) energy reaching the Earth, tiny variations (like the amount of reflected light) make geoengineering easy to implement. At the same time, they make the balance precarious.
☀️ Solar radiation   | 170k TW      |☁️ Reflected radiation | 50k TW (30%) |🏭 World production | 15 TW (1/10k)|
How much is 170k (thousand!) TW? A waterfall one kilometre high running along the entire equator.

3.title: 🌧️ ff.56.4 Controlling the rain
3.content:
Oliver Morton, a senior editor at The Economist (no small fry), published The Planet Remade, an excellent book on the subject.
Plenty of food for thought to get past the Promethean/catastrophist dichotomy and think rationally about controlling the climate. Geoengineering is neither a magic fix nor “unnatural”, but one more tool to consider with care, responsibility and humility.
Ballare può servire se ci crediSarà il più primitivo dei rimediLa danza della pioggia degli indianiDanze tribali come gli africaniJovanotti,Dobbiamo inventare qualcosa
In Wyoming, between 2008 and 2016, they tried to make rain. The result? Roughly a 10% increase in precipitation. The boldest will scream “chemtrails”, but after yet another summer of drought in the bed of the Po, maybe they'll accept this extreme option.
Other possible solutions mentioned:
Controlling reflected radiation (a Nature article by Harvard scientists proposing sulphate aerosols); Fertilising the oceans with iron and urea to boost plankton (more controllable, but more expensive, 12 experiments already tried); Capturing CO2 from the atmosphere (Climeworks) or, better still, from ocean water.

In a few days I'll be on the start line of the Padua Marathon. It'll be my first official one, but during the red-zone lockdown, staying strictly inside my municipality, I'd already covered the distance by running 6 laps of my charming hometown, Gazzaniga.
Modern pilgrims. Running past the 78 statues of illustrious figures linked to the city in Prato della Valle, I'll probably reflect on the millennia-old history of this race (unless the cramps have already taken over).
Sport is part of my daily life, partly as a response to family trauma. It can help fight depression and become a new religion. The members of this sect speak in code (VO2 max, BPM). They greet each other mid-run with reverence, as if they were priests.
Corriamo perché gran parte della vita è frustrante e futile, e solo contrastandola con qualche sorta di dolore, che richiede tempo, fatica e mesi di sforzi ripetitivi - lontani da amici, famiglia, birra e sanità mentale - siamo in grado di fare un atto di sfida alle Moire che complottano sulla nostra vita. Spesso questo può comportare disagio o addirittura dolore, una sensazione di alienazione dalla nostra normale zona di comfort che ci ricorda la nostra mortalità e ci fa rispettare le nostre capacità e limiti. Correre è l’equivalente laico del servizio domenicale. La maratona è l’equivalente odierno del pellegrinaggio medievale. If you can't run a marathon, your health is shaky. That's the provocation on Twitter from Alan Couzens, an expert performance coach. Replying to a doctor who claims marathons are among the most pointless activities known to humanity, he points out:
Alan Couzens@Alan_CouzensUnpopular opinion:
If you're not fit enough to run a marathon right now (without negative consequences), you're not fit enough. Dr. Eli David@DrEliDavidUnpopular opinion: Running marathons is the most pointless activity known to humanity. 7:03 PM ∙ Jan 28, 2023705Likes53Retweets
Remember that we should study the Tour de France to cure diabetes? Well, if you have a VO2 max of 50+, your risk of dying from any cause is 4 times lower. That's Alan's starting point. A VO2 max of 50+ means, for a 75kg person, running a marathon in 5 hours. That is:
42 km in 5 hours = 7 min/km = 8.5 km/h = 7 cal/min = 2100 kcal
VO2 what? VO2 max is the maximum oxygen uptake (ml/min/kg) a given person can sustain. Basically, the body's “horsepower”. The higher it is, the better your cardiovascular/metabolic fitness. One way to measure it is the Cooper test.

With chapters sorting objects and activities by g/kg/t of CO2 emitted, the author calculates the impact of: a mortgage, a road accident, the education system, etc…
10 tonnes. If every citizen emitted this much CO2 (I'll skip the CO2eq distinction for simplicity), we'd see a 40% rise in emissions (forget 1.5°C) compared to the 51 billion kg of CO2 in 2020 (📉 ff.1.2 From 51 billion to 0).
Average tonnes of CO2 per citizen: 🇺🇸 | 28🇦🇺 | 30🇬🇧 | 15🇨🇳 | 3🇲🇼 | 0. 1🌎 | 7
The average European emits 15 tonnes. According to the author, even being very careful about food and lifestyle choices, it would be hard to get below 3 tonnes: there are so many “fixed costs” tied to a “first world” standard of society, between available services, education and healthcare.
€2,700 or 150 t of CO2. That's the cost of a human life, considering the number of deaths from climate change (see also ⚫ff.16.3 The (black) market for CO2). In practice, UK citizens are worth about 5% of the GDP they generate.

1.title: 🕹️ ff.58.2 Emissions Minecraft
1.content: If you want a visual idea of what 10 tonnes look like, gaze at the Po Valley from the Orobic Prealps (but if you can't, there's a game, Seeing CO2).

2.title: ⛲ ff.58.3 Going to Niagara Falls (from New York)
2.content:
To show the level of detail the author reaches in calculating emissions, which are very often indirect and “invisible”, here's an example.
kg CO2eq for New York - Niagara Falls53 | Bike (on bananas)120 | Horse carriage250 | Bike (on cheeseburgers)330 | Train500 | Small efficient car1100 | Plane
The bike and health. The bike is the greenest solution, but only if you don't get run over along the way (though dying could be green, especially if you get cremated). On the other hand, cycling helps reduce the number of heart bypasses needed (each operation 1 t of CO2).
A car can be greener than a train (if you share the ride, filling every corner of the cabin), but a road accident can end up emitting (through the damage caused and the traffic) 50 t of CO2 (5 years of life in emissions).
Volare, oh-oh. Even if the plane doesn't look so bad, the 2-3x factor is what takes us from the global average to European per-capita consumption (and beyond). Then, emissions at high altitude have a bigger impact on warming (1.5-2x).
If you have time, take the carriage.
captions: Ignasi Monreal

3.title: 💲 ff.58.4 Spending a dollar
3.content:
Money emissions. On average, spending a dollar contributes 100g-1kg (or at most 10kg). So a starting point for polluting less is probably frugality. Or a life of excess at 30 t, offset with 140 euros in reforestation projects and by investing in renewables (!!!).
kg CO2eq per dollar spent on-220 | Reforestation project-2   | Solar panels0. 1  | Financial or legal advice0. 5  | Buying a car0. 6  | Food4    | Electricity bills6. 5  | Petrol10   | Air travel

4.title: 📉 ff.58.5 Happy degrowth or tech growth?
4.content:
On the one hand, less excess and waste is desirable, but it's neither the only nor the main solution for a fortissimo future.
The “fixed costs” of welfare, education and healthcare would account for half of global emissions if every citizen reached “first world” standards. Eating only grasshoppers and locking everyone indoors isn't an option, I think.
We need technology. For example, with solar/wind energy you can offset your emissions and set your mind at rest about your everyday choices. Although producing a turbine generates 30 t of CO2, over 20 years it prevents 500 (i.e. 20 or 40 years of emissions with an American/British lifestyle).
🎵 Final notes
In the future, with careful tracking of consumption and investment in renewables, every citizen will collect ecological credits to spend on plane tickets and Florentine steaks with a clear conscience.

0.title: 🐸 ff.59.1 Stagnation? Hardly!
0.content:
Born in France in the mid-1800s, positivism is the cultural glue of technology. Dismissed as a short-sighted pursuit of the useful, lacking ethical/psychological analysis, it is undoubtedly the cultural foundation of the technological society we live in.
Back to 1971 and the supposed technological stagnation (🎼 ff.50 WTF happened in 1971?)? According to Works in Progress, it's a big fat lie:
GDP doesn't capture progress. With technology we achieve more while spending less, in a deflationary drop in consumption (energy included). Digital for free. There's a famous study showing that the value of digital services can reach €25,000 a year. That's money we don't spend (and that doesn't land in our pay packets) but that we should take into account. Online, we don't spend. The data on spending on online services got me thinking. Even though we now spend a quarter of our day in front of a screen, we're particularly stingy online.
By the way, if you'd like to buy me a digital coffee (I drink a lot of them) you can click here. Or simply share this newsletter. Share
Once writing is invented, you have to learn to read! Increasing computing power has been the main focus of the last 30 years. Let's say we focused on optimising the ink and the writing. Now, thanks to training and boomers being replaced, we can start writing books! It's time, as the Progressive Policy Institute argues, to “smash” the Great Stagnation.

refs.1: the value of digital services can reach €25,000 a year
refs.2: we now spend a quarter of our day in front of a screen

1.title: 🗃️ ff.59.2 Social pressure and bureaucracy
1.content:
You can study technology with an evolutionary theory: just as a species evolves based on external pressures (or their absence), technological development goes hand in hand with society's acceptance/resistance.
Technological co-evolution. QWERTY is far from the optimal keyboard layout, but we adapted and now changing it is a mess. Another example of society-technology interaction is the nuclear freeze after Fukushima and the rethink after the invasion of Ukraine.
If you want to dig deeper, I suggest the book Come saremo by Telmo Pievani and Luca de Biase.

2.title: ➕ ff.59.3 Why telling positive stories matters
2.content:
In the newsletter Not Boring, Packy McCormick points out that, despite the fact that:
AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) is around the corner; we're sending ever bigger rockets into orbit; we're reprogramming T cells to fight tumours (!!!)
all around us there's nothing but fear and negativity:
La ricerca spaziale è vista come un passatempo per miliardari. Le centrali nucleari stanno chiudendo in tutto il mondo. I progressi nell’AI suscitano timori di perdita di lavoro e di essere trasformati in clip di carta. I progressi nella biologia sintetica fanno pensare a focolai incontrollabili e alla minaccia del bioterrorismo. È difficile biasimare le persone. Lo show più discusso in TV al momento -The Last of Us- si svolge in un mondo in cui, secondo NPR: “il cambiamento climatico ha alimentato la diffusione di un nuovo patogeno, che si diffonde in tutto il mondo infettando gli esseri umani, trasformandoli in zombie e controllando il loro cervello
Elliot Hershberg@ElliotHershbergThe fact that we can hot-wire a patients own T cells to attack certain types of tumors is absolutely incredible.
And the thing is, we're just scratching the surface when it comes to cell therapy. 8:00 PM ∙ Feb 7, 2023172Likes19Retweets
The ever brilliant Balaji Srinivasan, at the height of the pandemic, published The Purpose of Technology, a hymn to positivity, calling for creative, progressive scientists who care about outreach. Real stars.
Scienziati e ingegneri, progressisti piuttosto che conservatori tecnologici, devono imparare a scrivere, pubblicare e dirigere. Dobbiamo costruire consapevolmente un ecosistema mediatico decentralizzato guidato dalla tecnologia. Non tweet, ma articoli. Non articoli, ma video. Non video, ma lungometraggi. E non film, ma un’intera libreria di contenuti originali Netflix, un ecosistema mediatico tecnologico parallelo pieno di contenuti ispirazionali per i progressisti tecnologici. Una vita intera di contenuti che sostengono la moneta immutabile, la frontiera infinita, l’intelligenza artificiale e la vita eterna. Balaji Srinivasan,The purpose of Technology
Chaudhri, the heart of the design and software behind the invention of the iPhone, shares this idea too and lists his heroes and sources of inspiration. Young people need a Maradona of technology to cheer for. Of positivity. Neil deGrasse Tyson isn't enough.
I want to find meaning. Here's futuro fortissimo's: to stimulate, to spread knowledge, to prepare society for the fortissimo future. In short, future-forming.
🎵 Final notes
In the future, a newsletter like this one, with its interactions in terms of reads and shares, will provide direct compensation based on the path the shared information then produced, sparking inventions and new connections.

0.title: 🤠 ff.60.1 The Westworld of self-driving: SF
0.content:
Are we there yet? Like many technological developments, self-driving has seemed ready to conquer the roads for years. Some trends start slowly, then become the norm in no time (see electric vehicles).
A child's dream is to go to San Francisco. Like Westworld in the HBO series, San Francisco is a parallel amusement park, a window onto the future. I wish some of these experiments happened closer to home. Instead, we get the Privacy Watchdog and the ChatGPT saga.
Cruise (General Motors' self-driving unit) launched its plan for a 24/7 robotaxi service. Self-driving is here (with Baidu and Waymo too). But the numbers are insignificant. And since only Tesla has scaled production consistently, we're waiting on them for the big leap in adoption.

1.content:
Robotaxis. Tesla (at $182 today) is valued by ARK at $2,000 a share in 2027, with a final value equal to 3x today's Apple ($2.6T). Much of the market value is tied to robotaxi adoption ($613B in hypothetical revenue in 2027; Apple's revenue in 2022 was $394B).
Nerd corner. Below, a detailed breakdown of the model (with bear and bull estimates) put together by the financial research group.
Anyway, numbers aside, here's an Uber driver doing a dress rehearsal of his own replacement. Listen to the comments of the tourists who get in. A bit like riding the Blue Tornado for the first time.

2.content:
There's a section on self-driving in ARK Big Ideas 2023 too (yes, despite the rejection after 5 interviews with them, I'm particularly fond of Cathie).
Fewer vehicles sold, but used more. That's the trend ahead of us. It won't make sense to buy a car and leave it parked 96% of the time. So self-driving will make more money for the owners of the taxi service than for the companies building the vehicles.

4.title: 💀 ff.60.5 Fewer deaths on the roads?
4.content:
A road accident can pollute as much as 10 years of an average European's emissions (⛲ ff.58.3 Going to Niagara Falls (from New York)).
But are accidents on the rise? Honestly, I thought so (distracted by smartphones; data below only goes up to 2015, though). But if we normalise deaths per million inhabitants or per miles driven, fewer people die on the road.
Here are deaths per 100,000 people (including motorcyclists, pedestrians and cyclists) for some developed countries.
Better autonomous? On Tesla's website there's a quarterly summary of miles driven before an accident. From 500k (US average) it goes up to 4-6M (a 10x improvement).
California collects all the accident reports involving self-driving cars (111 in 2021). On the streets of San Francisco, in the same year, 37 people died (drivers, pedestrians and cyclists) out of 13,000 accidents.
🎵 Final notes
In the future, digital nomads will work in a self-driving van, circling the globe again and again, like the train in Snowpiercer.

0.title: ⚖️ ff.61.1 Measuring pollution in hours of life
0.content:
We saw (🎼 ff.58 Do bananas pollute too much?) that Mike Berners-Lee proposes 10 tonnes of CO2 a year as a global per-capita target (i.e. a 50% cut for the average European).
If I don't measure, I don't know. With a CO2 “salary” to spend each month, and clear costs on every activity, maybe we could hit the target. So let's break that number down.
10 t/year → 27 kg/day → 1 kg/h → 20 g/min
1kg CO2/h. In practice, if an activity keeps us busy longer than its CO2-to-time conversion, it's green. For example, a banana is 4 minutes of pollution. And I usually eat it, and it fills me up, for longer than that.

1.title: 🕗 ff.61.2 Emissions converted into time
1.content:
A detailed table with the emissions of practically everything (taken from the book). Below, 10 examples (in minutes/hours) of the conversions we just talked about.
04  | banana06  | 100g rice18  | porridge with milk18  | pint of beer22  | daily emails30  | one km by car32  | egg60  | bottle of wine2h  | hamburger2h  | one km by car (in traffic)
If we take these numbers and factor in the quantity and frequency of a given activity, we get a cumulative analysis over the year.
Above, countless other contributions are missing (household consumption, building a house, mortgage, healthcare, other food). In short, there's little room for frugality, short of near-total, unrealistic renunciations at scale.

refs.1: a cumulative analysis over the year.

2.title: 🥩 ff.61.3 Meat or asparagus?
2.content:
Being vegan is respectable: both for the environment and for a person's health (🍔 ff.49.3 Diets and pollutants).
But, but, but. I don't like the all-or-nothing approach of the vegan diet. Moderate meat consumption can be acceptable (one extra month of emissions in the 10-tonne model; with today's European average of 15 t, we're talking about just two weeks).
Diet profile | kgCO2/day | t CO2 per yearLots of meat | 7. 2 | 2. 62Little meat  | 4. 5 | 1. 70Fish only  | 3. 9 | 1. 42Vegetarian | 3. 8 | 1. 39Vegan      | 2. 9 | 1. 05
-65 km by car a week. Cutting travel by this amount has the same impact as switching from a partly carnivorous diet to a fully vegan one.
Oh, and the vegan diet has its pitfalls too: asparagus.

3.title: 🎶 ff.61.4 A Spotify-style subscription for the world
3.content:
Charming as its bucolic, back-to-nature narrative may be, happy degrowth isn't compatible with the digital first world.
Offsetting and believing in progress. As we saw in 📉 ff.58.5 Happy degrowth or tech growth?, one solution is installing solar panels or wind turbines. An ever cheaper solution.
futuro fortissimofuturo fortissimo on Instagram: ”🥳 Questi grafici sono quelli che fanno sperare nel futuro! Forza, energia solare, sky is the limit!”May 25, 2023
MyClimate helps offset our emissions. For this summer's return trip to Cuba I'll emit 2.7 t, corresponding to €76 (against a ticket that cost 950).
Polluting the world as if it were Spotify. Just as we live in a house and pay (through taxes) for healthcare and education, maybe we should start thinking of pollution as a Spotify subscription for using the world (and polluting it).
The 10 t a year cost €280. No excuses.

0.title: 🔥 ff.62.1 Work has never been so important
0.content:
With the pandemic interruption breaking our habits, we also started questioning work (and its routine), perhaps realising how arbitrary certain paradigms are.
Only 40% of Americans. So 100 million people have a job taking up more than 35 hours a week. The “9-to-5” employee (if you're lucky) isn't the norm. It never was. For millennia, Weber's view of work prevailed: working to maintain the standard of living you've reached.
Copy-paste of our parents. The growth of the last 70 years may be unrepeatable. The growth inherent to the economic boom forged a genuine religion of work (and I live in Bergamo).
Everyone worked happily, in exchange for an ever better standard of living. Until today. Copy-pasting our parents, for social, demographic and economic reasons (🤖 ff.36.4 Are we already blended with AI?, a cost of living less sustainable for new generations), no longer seems to work.
study → work → marriage → house → kids

1.title: 🥾 ff.62.2 Leaving the beaten path
1.content:
In The Pathless Path, Paul Miller tells the story of his “escape” from the beaten path.
Studia. Prendi bei voti. Ottieni un buon lavoro. Poi, testa bassa e continua ad andare avanti, a chiedere di più, indefinitamente. Questo, ilDefault Path. Paul Miller,The Pathless Path
Paul Miller was the copy-paste poster boy, with stellar degrees and respectable career leaps (GE, McKinsey, Florida, New York). But then came the reflection:
Tutto andava bene, anzi era in continuo miglioramento. Eppure, ogni mattina la mia motivazione di andare al lavoro diminuiva, in un andamento inverso alla mia crescita di carriera e di stipendio.
32, Taiwan and an unhoped-for marriage. So he decided to drop everything, embracing an uncertain future of occasional freelance gigs. He then moved to Taiwan, where he met his wife, even though by then he'd written himself off as old, a hopeless single.

2.title: 🧾 ff.62.3 Taxing misery
2.content:
Money and success are the only paradigm to have survived the destruction of values of recent years.
futuro_fortissimo_newsletterA post shared by futuro fortissimo (@futuro_fortissimo_newsletter)
Misery tax. That's the tax that, according to Thomas J. Bevan, unhappy workers have to pay to keep working.
Also interesting is the concept of the “arrival fallacy” put forward by Harvard professor Ben-Shahar: the idea that the next promotion, the next raise, the next job will absolutely be what finally makes us happy.
Having enough: Kurt Vonnegut's anecdote:

refs.3: according to Thomas J. Bevan, unhappy workers have to pay to keep working

3.title: 🔺 ff.62.4 The pyramid inside all of us
3.content:
La società moderna ha perfezionato l’arte di far sentire le persone non necessarie. Sebastian Junger,Tribù. Ritorno a casa e appartenenza
There's a problem with our scale of values. Maslow's hierarchy of needs reminds us of it.
The concept of Measured Discomfort discussed by Alex Lieberman is connected to all this.

4.title: 🕹️ ff.62.5 Independence and curiosity
4.content:
What's the solution?
On one hand, more flexible hours and remote working can help (freelancers and occasional jobs have grown from 10 to 15%; the WSJ reports workers are happier, maybe because they smoke more marijuana?).
Miller proposes creativity: finding an enjoyable activity to do, regardless of everything. For him, writing. Did it bring him JK Rowling's money and success? No. But that's not the point.
By writing, Miller finds motivation and builds connections with his readers. Belonging, esteem, self-actualisation. There's Maslow's pyramid again.
futuro fortissimo is - perhaps - exactly this.

0.title: 🔦 ff.64.1 The exhibition on the void
0.content:
Returnable void. For millennia philosophy has pondered “being” and “non-being”. Matter and void. More recently, matter and antimatter, even going so far - with virtual particles - as to deny that a void is possible.
In Bergamo, Capital of Culture 2023 together with Brescia, the exhibition Salto nel vuoto (Leap into the void). Its common thread: the dematerialisation/digitalisation of art and, therefore, of life. Of being.
The retrospective has plenty of nods to the metaverse, NFTs and generative art. And so a philosophising 🎼ff is born, on the present and future of our society.
Speaking of humanism, I recently discovered Trasumanare by Emilio Dal Bo: for lovers of literature, personal growth and philosophy.

1.title: 🍎 ff.64.2 From Newton to Einstein
1.content:
Information (created ever faster with AI) is replacing the object. With the blockchain, the digital gives value to itself.
The only limit? The speed of computation and of light. In a beautiful parallel with the history of physics, Byung-Chul Han wonders whether, between the metaverse and social media, we're moving from Newton's world of “billiard balls” to Einstein's relativistic one. In this process, just as special relativity predicts, we end up “squashed”.
PS: Han also wrote The Burnout Society (see 🎼 ff.62 How to avoid burnout).

refs.0: special relativity predicts, we end up “squashed”

2.title: 🔗 ff.64.3 Just links connecting information?
2.content:
In a 1989 book, Angels Fear, Catherine and Gregory Bateson tell the story of a mother, elderly and perhaps suffering from Alzheimer's, who chimes in on discussions between her son and his group of friends, dubbed “cyberneticians”:
Voi che parlate di reperimento delle informazioni, ma che ne sapere di queste cose? Io si che me ne intendo, perché ho perso la memoria. L’unico sistema che ho per trovare le cose è di tenere un pochino di ogni cosa dappertutto.
Backup. It seems the ever more forgetful modern human is just like that: leaving a bit of information in every corner, without even having to remember where, whether in a Notion database (accessible from phone and PC, of course) or in cold newsletters full of URLs.

3.title: 👨‍💻 ff.64.4 Matrix and matter
3.content:
Cloud, Internet of Things, 5G, QR codes, augmented reality blended into the “real” one. Screens, Oculus or Apple's Vision Pro are our portals. Related: Non-things, how we stopped living the real.
Matter has been replaced by the Matrix
Urbanisation took away our greenery and animals, digitalisation our concrete and asphalt. micmer
Around us, ever more digital mental maps
La società ha sostituito a tal punto la realtà delle cose con simboli e segni che l’esperienza umana stessa è divenuta una simulazione del realeBudrillard,Simulacri e simulazioni(1981)
For example:
a tree → source of fruit → firewood → subject for an Instagram photo
Futurism, a coincidence? Matter (materia) and mother (madre) are etymologically linked. Perhaps it's no accident that Boccioni, pioneer of Futurism and of dematerialising figures, chose his mother on the terrace for the work titled (needless to say) Materia.
We can give a curious (and anachronistic) new reading to Foscolo in this sense too
Tu non altro che il canto avrai del figlio,O materna mia terra; a noi prescrisseIl fato illacrimata sepoltura. Ugo Foscolo, A Zacinto
OK. I can now wrap up this rambling collection of thoughts. I'm dematerialising.

0.title: 🆕 ff.65.1 Time = new experiences?
0.content:
Time. What a lovely topic this one is too. You find it discussed practically everywhere, from philosophy to Jovanotti's pop songs. From theoretical physics to ephemeral tissues for a cold. Ephemeral indeed.
Despite technology (household appliances, hyper-fast internet, instant messaging), we say more and more that we don't have time. Why?
DeltaT. According to one theory, time, rather than an absolute number of seconds, is marked by the amount of change between a before and an after.
The dynamic circle. One experiment along these lines showed that a circle displayed for 500 milliseconds is perceived as shorter if the circle expands/shrinks.
At the same time, as we age, there's less and less novelty, since we've piled up lots of memories and experiences. Without novelty, time seems to go faster.

1.title: 🌴 ff.65.2 A life on holiday
1.content:
I don't get it. If we're old, there's less novelty and change, so time passes faster? Doesn't that contradict everything we said about the dynamic circle?
The difference between prospective and retrospective time explains why.
In generale, un periodo riempito di esperienze diverse ed interessanti sembra breve mentre passa, ma lungo quando guardiamo indietro. D'altro canto, un tratto di tempo privo di esperienze sembra lungo mentre passa, ma in retrospettiva breve. William James,The Principles of Psychology(1890)L’attesa di un aereo in ritardo di 5 ore può essere percepita più lunga di tutta una settimana in Grecia, mentre una giornata a Atene vola. Una settimana dal ritorno dal viaggio, però, l’attesa in aereoporto è un brevissimo attimo, mentre il divertimento della vacanza si dilata incredibilmente. Dean Buonomano,Your Brain is a Time Machine

2.title: 📝 ff.65.3 Homework for life
2.content:
Freezing moments. To give value to time (and stretch it even when novelty isn't a given), storyteller Matthew Dicks suggests some homework.
Instead of spending two hours in front of the TV, consuming content that goes straight into oblivion, he suggests stopping for 5 minutes to reflect on the day.
Matthew argues that this method, originally introduced to find new stories to tell, is a genuine time machine.
5 minutes → isolated moments of the day → novelty identified → time stretched

3.title: ❤️ ff.65.4 A matter of the heart?
3.content:
Il tempo si espande o si blocca in accordo con i movimenti del cuore. Murakami,Kafka sulla spiaggia
London researchers at Royal Holloway University agree with this literary insight. In fact, they showed that a sound seems longer or shorter depending on whether it's perceived during systole or diastole.
The big explainer. Why does time last longer with the heartbeat? Maybe because in its (unconscious) processing of information (internal too), the brain receives more input during systole, building the perception / illusion of faster time.
By the way, did you know a coffee would make my heart speed up a little?

4.title: 🧠 ff.65.5 Or of the brain?
4.content:
If you want to dig deeper into the topic, Your Brain is a Time Machine by Dean Buonomano.
The brain has to handle various timescales of change: milliseconds (sound), hours (circadian rhythm), all the way to the seasons, to keep the body running properly. So it's not just a Rolex, it's a Swiss Army knife too! Why did time come about? Maybe so we could sing (or speak). To isolate phonemes. An example: in Jimi Hendrix's Purple Haze, the famous line about kissing the sky gets misheard as kissing “this guy”.
And that's all for today. I'm out of time. And I think you are too.

0.title: 📙 ff.66.1 The central dogma
0.content:
Biology is complex: a cluster of ever larger atoms (molecules, proteins, RNA, DNA, lipid bilayers, one after another, “alla fiera dell'Est” style).
Before diving into today's 🎼ff, let's at least go over the main rules of the game.
Conosco le leggi del mondo, e te ne farò dono. Supererò le correnti gravitazionali,lo spazio e la luce per non farti invecchiare. Franco Battiato,La Cura
First the egg, then the chicken. Biology's central dogma says proteins are made following instructions from RNA, which in turn is a “temporary copy” of a stretch of DNA.
DNA → RNA → proteins
In therapy, too, we have three levels of action: modifying DNA, injecting RNA (as with vaccines) or working on protein design.
The good news? We're making progress on pretty much all of them:
DNA: Prime Editing. RNA: 😷 ff.53.3 From COVID to cancer. Proteins: 🧬 ff.4.1 The structure of proteins. Drugs and molecules: the first clinical trials of AI-discovered molecules. Basically, a MidJourney for the next paracetamol.

1.title: ❓ ff.66.2 Are we getting sicker?
1.content:
Partly due to COVID, life expectancy in many countries has stalled (if not sharply collapsed), with the United States overtaken by China!
So the future of medicine doesn't look fortissimo, especially when you consider that:
Higher average life expectancy is also linked to the collapse in infant mortality (or is it?). Healthcare spending (US) has exploded over the last 50 years
Wait, wait, wait. It's not that things haven't improved. There's undeniably been a decrease in deaths from cardiovascular disease, and progress in cancer treatment is evident too (🤞 ff.53.1 Fewer cancer deaths).
But since 2012 annual progress has slowed, or even flatlined and reversed, as with cardiovascular disease.

Seasoning the recipe of modern anxiety: the endless raising of the bar.
I ran my first marathon in 2 hours 45 minutes (3:54 min/km). In sporting terms I could easily feel I'd “made it”, since only 2-3% of marathon finishers, an already small subpopulation, manage to break 3h.

3.title: 🎁 ff.68.4 Less ego and control, more flow and presence: Naval's cure
3.content:
Before the summer I left you with a 2017 (!) podcast with Naval Ravikant (here's the transcript).
It's in this pleasant chat that we find a reflection to start from in looking for a cure for modern anxiety.
Non voglio che il mio senso del sé continui a svilupparsi e diventi più forte man mano che invecchio. Voglio che sia più debole e più smorzato in modo da poter vivere molto di più nella realtà di ogni giorno. Accettare la natura e i suoi limiti. Apprezzare il momento presente, come si fa da bambini. Naval Ravikant
Brad Stulberg, ex-McKinsey optimiser and author of Peak Performance, now proposes the concept of groundedness. Which is really Verga's oyster ideal adapted to our hyper-distracted, anxious days.
Here are the suggested exercises:
Accept your current state, remind yourself you're doing your best to be your best. Once you've acknowledged how things are, anchor yourself to them, committing to focus your attention on the present. Help yourself by seeking movement, action, which often comes with flow; that way your mind won't wander into the past or plan the future (even a fortissimo one).
Science seems to back this message of anchoring to the present: activity in the posterior cortex, linked to anxiety, drops when we accept the situation we're in. As also seen in 💚 ff.51.1 Storytelling for green.
Refer a friend

0.title: 🐱ff.69.1 From Schrödinger's cat to qubits
0.content:
The idea for this newsletter came from Google's recent article: Sycamore-70 beats Frontier.
Frontier is the biggest “classical” supercomputer (in Tennessee). Compared to the previous Sycamore-54, in two years Google achieved an improvement of 7 orders of magnitude (10,000,000x)!
In practice, one second of quantum computing is now comparable to a year of “classical” computing on the world's biggest supercomputer. Clear?
Don't touch the cat (Schrödinger's): it can help us understand quantum computers. Until we measure (disturb) the system, the atoms (even those making up the giant feline) are “undefined”.
And what does this have to do with the supercomputer? Let's use the Financial Times illustrations. To solve a maze, we have to try a series of <1> (turn right) and <0> (left). As the forks multiply, we end up with an exponential number of possibilities.
That's in the “classical” world, the world of “big things”, of Newton's billiard balls.
An atom (qubit, quantum bit), on the other hand, can represent a superposition of <1|0>, <right|left>.
Like the cat that is <alive|dead> before we open the box and check on it (disturbing the wave function with an experimental measurement).
Simplifying a lot. Since each qubit represents both-right-and-left at the same time (until we measure), we don't have to program every combination of <right>/<left> to find the way out. That's all (bit).

1.title: 🧼 ff.69.2 Quantum foam
1.content:
Another quantum consequence is, as we've seen, that the void doesn't exist (🔦 ff.64.1 The exhibition on the void). In fact, if an area were completely empty, we could say there's no matter (or energy, E=mc2) there. But saying the energy is exactly zero goes against Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.
The void is a quantum foam. As in On Space Time Foam by Tomás Saraceno (2013, Hangar Bicocca). A project between art, the Big Bang, string theory and human beings, just the way we like it on 🎼ff.

2.title: 🍏 ff.69.3 The quantum Apple?
2.content:
Rigetti Computing is trying to take quantum technology commercial (it recently went public on the Nasdaq, NASDAQ: RGTI -85% since trading began).
The pandemic had given a big boost to start-up/venture investment, with its push towards digital (for example, TDOC, which offers remote medicine). 2022 brought something of a return to earth (VC from $170B to $70B).
Not for quantum technologies, which saw private investment grow by $2.35 billion (McKinsey's Quantum Technology Monitor 2023).
The 10 companies that received the most investment. Which will be the quantum NVIDIA?
As for public investment (projections and announcements), China is pushing hard (in billions): 🇨🇳| 15🇪🇺| 8. 4🇺🇸| 3. 7
