3.title: 🤔 ff.69.4 What uses and dangers?
3.content:
But what are the applications of this technology, and the potential dangers?
Improving traffic in the port of San Francisco (SavantX). Monitoring brain scans to understand autism (SandboxAQ). Destroying VISA, Mastercard and maybe even Bitcoin
Bitcoin and VISA in danger? Yes, because the cryptographic systems underpinning today's financial system (and Bitcoin, Elliptic Curve Cryptography) can be solved (like the maze) in a finite and ever shorter time (Shor's algorithm).
If computers that you build are quantum,Then spies of all factions will want 'em. Our codes will all fail,And they'll read our email,Till we've crypto that's quantum, and daunt 'em. Peter Shor,Nobel per la Fisica 2023 proprio per studi su questi temi

1.content:
Analogue was simpler. As a kid, I'd buy a CD (for the price of a month of Spotify) and wring it dry for months in the car. I subscribed to Internazionale, which I read, distraction-free, cover to cover.
Today I can't listen to a whole album on Spotify even once. Unless the artist, like Mike Posner, explicitly asks me to in Introduction.
A little exercise. To slow down a bit, I suggest listening to A Real Good Kid all the way through. As in Greek tragedies, the album gives voice to the very human suffering of those whom society (and social media) makes us see as “invincible heroes”. Among them, the tragedy of Avicii, a dear friend of the artist.

2.title: 📚 ff.72.3 If the Library of Alexandria had 100 books
2.content:
Too many books? According to Naval, yes (from the podcast mentioned here: 🎁 ff.68.4 Less ego and control, more flow and presence: Naval's cure). So much so that people end up reading dozens of personal finance books without ever leafing through Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations, for example.
Back to the classics. Pick 100 books and understand them deeply: that's the provocation from illacertus on X.

3.title: 🇬🇷 ff.72.4 From multitasking to the Greek classics (and arete)
3.content:
As with books and CDs, we need to extend the philosophy of ONE to our whole being: one screen, one tab, one activity, one thought.
La persona che si concentra su un compito e lo porta a termine, anche se lavora in modo un po' lento o obsoleto, batte l'eterno ottimizzatore che salta da uno strumento all'altro e spera sempre che un nuovo pezzo di tecnologia lo aiuti a completare ciò che ha iniziato. James Clear,3-2-1: On seizing the day, perseverance, and focusing on one task at a time
So we come to the third nod to Greek classicism, a pillar of our humanist culture.
Nell'antica Grecia, una virtù morale primaria era l’arete(ἀρετή), l'eccellenza raggiunta nell'applicazione della presenza completa nel proprio mestiere. Brad Stulberg,The Practice of Groundedness
And that's all for today. Remember, UNO colour at a time (or red-colour-change).

0.content:
Yes, I'm a bit obsessed with cryptocurrencies. And in this 🎼ff I'll explain why.
All that glitters isn't gold. The senseless rally of DOGE, the meme coin Elon Musk pitched as the official currency of Mars, is now just a memory.
But, but, but. The A16Z fund has introduced an index to track the health of the sector (State of Crypto Index, which combines the number of active users, projects and trading liquidity across the various blockchains).

1.title: 🤖ff.73.2 The AI–Bitcoin convergence
1.content:
The charts seem to show stagnation. What's changed recently? AI, ChatGPT and MidJourney. As discussed here:
A few takeaways:
The economy of converting money into compute time is exploding (along with the energy needed, so much so that Microsoft is considering nuclear reactors). VISA/Mastercard take up to a month to process payments for these services, but companies like OpenAI offer instant access to compute. The compute-time/hardware mismatch (hardware that can also be used to mine BTC) becomes a dangerous inefficiency in the system. What's more, VISA/Mastercard aren't accessible to everyone. Even verified users with accounts on these networks have seen their access blocked (privacy watchdog, anyone?). In these cases, the blockchain was the only way in.

2.title: 👍ff.73.3 A financial VPN
2.content:
In short, crypto guarantees access to ever more essential digital services, like a financial VPN.
No wonder Worldcoin (👁️ ff.38.3 The cryptocurrency to reduce inequality, backed by OpenAI founder Sam Altman) has reached 2.2M users.
Another reason crypto is the future is demographics. ChainAnalysis's map shows global adoption is high in India and Nigeria (2 billion people in 2050).
Not just individuals. Entire nations crushed by inflation could get financial revenge (Javier Milei, a candidate in Argentina, is leaning precisely on these themes).

1.title: 📙ff.74.2 A short cultural dictionary
1.content:
Ignorant. Because of the geo-graphical distance (of their alphabet) I didn't know much about what, in the '70s - despite its defeat in the war - was the world's second-largest economy. Matt Alt comes to the rescue in Pop ポップ, with historical and cultural insights.
He tells, for example, of the biggest bombing raid in history (9 March 1945, 100k dead) or of the incredible economic rebirth driven by tin toys (Mattel, after all, chose Japan to produce Barbie).
Light and shadow. The book offers two concepts that condense Japan's charm and contradictions.
kawaii (可愛い), lit. cute; describes something charming, vulnerable, childlike or lovable. You often find it in cartoon illustrations with round, oversized heads (Hello Kitty, Pikachu).
otaku (おたく), a young person obsessed with a particular hobby or interest (esp. comics, cartoons, video games and computers). In Japan, though, it describes socially isolated people. A nerd shut away at home, running from reality.

refs.1: Mattel, after all, chose Japan to produce Barbie

2.title: 🈵ff.74.3 I'm Japanese!
2.content:
The series The Man in the High Castle imagines a Second World War without nuclear bombs, after which the East prevails and the streets of San Francisco are dotted with kanji (漢字).
Silent invasion. But, culturally, are we sure that's not how it went? Pasolini lamented an Americanisation of culture after the economic boom of the '60s.
Millennials (and maybe Centennials and Screenagers too) grew up in front of a PlayStation, after lunch with Dragon Ball, Naruto, Detective Conan or One Piece. They communicate in emoji and live more and more on social networks (the story of 2chan), to escape a reality that feels ever tighter.
In short, Americans my foot. We're Japanese!

0.content:
Remember when, between an episode of Dragon Ball and Naruto, they'd show us Tesmed ads? No? Let me unlock a memory for you.
Now, in a decidedly more scientific way, people are trying to do exactly the same. But with the brain.
Trans…what? With surgically implanted electrodes we've made giant strides against Parkinson's, but transcranial stimulation can be less invasive. These are devices that, placed on the outside of the skull, help with post-stroke rehabilitation, as motor support or as a treatment for depression!
If you want to dig deeper: review and market forecasts (N1, the first device from Musk's Neuralink, could generate $200M by 2030, and clinical trials have started for patients in certain categories).

1.title: 😴ff.75.2 Neural lullaby
1.content:
Thanks in part to AI, we're learning to read thoughts, understand sleep, measure consciousness. On that note, an embarrassing video of micmer straight from 2019.
If the video wasn't enough and you don't have a Jigglypuff handy, relax, there's Somnee.
It uses transcranial stimulation, that very one, to promote sleep (scientific principle). Basically, the device shifts the distribution of brain waves, bringing it closer to the one linked to a sleep state.
Like a relaxing massage, but for the brain.
↑ β-waves → wakefulness ↓ α-waves → sleep
Insomnia, er, in sum. Better than melatonin!

2.content:
Yes, I know. As with Tesmed, these stimulators look like a solution to a problem we created ourselves:
But if, for psychological, economic or social reasons, some people can't break out of the harmful loop of modern life, it's good to offer solutions.

3.title: 👮ff.75.4 Thought police
3.content:
In his book Exponential, Azeem Azhar discusses the chasm opening up between regulation and technology. Neural chips throw more fuel on the fire already stoked by AI, social media, robotics and climate.
He talked about mind control with Nita Farahany (professor emerita at Duke University, North Carolina).
A few reflections:
Collecting brain data, a growing interest with $1 billion in investment. The possibility of monitoring (and modifying) thoughts (see Orwell: thoughtcrime and 1984). The need to open a discussion on mental privacy

0.title: 🦠ff.76.1 What's left of COVID?
0.content:
COVID is, for the most part, a distant memory. I see the lockdown period like my 2 years in the Netherlands: a sealed, isolated compartment of life in which I was a completely different person.
But what's left of COVID? Let's start with a few charts, which always capture reality in an instant.
In short, lockdown brought us closer to chess, to remote working and, as a result, to comfy tracksuits.
In-between seasons. In the trends, some seasonal swings are bigger than the COVID peak. Homemade bread, yoga and cycling are back where they started (and with them, Peloton)

1.title: 🧖‍♂️ff.76.2 The hobby boom
1.content:
A lockdown of time. During confinement, hobbies spread, a trend that began back in the 1800s with the better living brought by the industrial revolution. So much so that 1 American in 2 took up a new hobby (and went into debt for it).
If Barbero isn't enough for you, here's the history of hobbies.

2.title: 🫁ff.76.3 And the physical effects
2.content:
Yes, some trends have passed. But the psycho-physical mark COVID left is very much current.
65 million. The number of people with long COVID. The scars left behind: a mix of shortness of breath, poor concentration, insomnia and bad sleep quality.
Long-Covid Europe lets you play Minecraft with a character weakened by COVID. It's a provocation between the real and the digital, reminding us we can't escape what happened through Zoom and VR.
Oh, related: Nature discusses how the microbiome of babies born during lockdown was altered (and remember how much we are our microbiome, so much so that Zoe links it to the glycaemic response, 🕛 ff.35.2 Smartwatches and more).

3.title: 🐛 ff.76.4 Turned into a cockroach?
3.content:
Bruno Latour (whom we bumped into in 🧼 ff.69.2 Quantum foam) proposes a philosophy of lockdown.
Ska-ska cockroaches. According to the philosopher, lockdown turned us into a cockroach, as happened to Gregor Samsa in Kafka's Metamorphosis. Not because it physically confined us within four walls, but because it mentally confirmed our materiality.
Expanding on Down to Earth: Politics in the New Climatic Regime, Latour argues that lockdown brought us down to Earth, reversing the push towards inert space that began with Galileo, continued with Ariosto and culminated with NASA and Musk.
Stiamo iniziando a renderci conto che non abbiamo, che non avremo mai, che nessuno ha mai avuto l’esperienza di incontrare “cose inerti”. Bruno Latour,After Lockdown
A SpaceX-style landing? The impossibility of living “inertly”, “above the Earth” is the lesson of the pandemic. COVID, with its mucus, plunged us into Gaia's mud. Into Gregor's exoskeleton.
Non è giusto spingerci a tornare sulla Terra, se non ci dicono dove atterrare per non schiantarci. Bruno Latour,After Lockdown
And that's all for today. Back to isolating myself (in art).

0.content:
OK, we've talked about the crisis of the “boomer” value system:
marriage (🎼 ff.23 Privatised marriages), fertility (👶 ff.29.1 We're not having kids any more), the default path of study>work>house>family (🥾 ff.62.2 Leaving the beaten path).
Even taking into account the explosion of post-pandemic weddings (i.e. the ones not celebrated during lockdown), the trend seems pretty clear:
And kids, don't even mention them. So much so that in Taiwan the number of pets has overtaken the number of children (🎼 ff.74 I'm Japanese!).
Since these topics are by definition our future, let's try to explain what's going on.

1.content:
Hand me those Meloni (melons). Giorgia Meloni claims the demographic crisis is tied to the collapse of traditional family values. Yet a study using a European survey on family values (EVS) tried to check whether this correlation with fertility rates actually exists. It found the opposite:
All the fertility rates here.

2.title: 🤑ff.77.3 Or of money?
2.content:
Pope Francis argues it's more of an economic issue. But with what I spend on Michelin-starred dinners, trips to the other side of the world and Ironman entries, I could probably support a child.
It looks like “money” is just an excuse.
Or is it? Housing, the expense that weighs most on young people's lives and the conditio sine qua non for having a child, has recently become a problem.
But over the last decade affordability was far higher than in periods like the '80s. So this doesn't seem to be the main reason.

3.title: 🛠️ff.77.4 Or of emancipation?
3.content:
Does the career woman have no time for kids? It's not an easy question, so much so that this year it earned Harvard's Claudia Goldin the Nobel Prize in Economics.
The fall in fertility doesn't seem tied only to the rise in working women. At the start of the 1900s, true, almost no women worked. But in the 1800s, 60% of women were in the fields with their husbands.
After giving birth, new generations of mothers are more and more often going back to work and taking on higher positions.

My take. We're in a new world compared to that of the 1800s and the baby boomers, with new and unexplored assumptions about values, money and society (number of children, of homes owned, of families under one roof)

0.title: 👨‍🏫ff.78.1 A school for life?
0.content:
Let's face it, school curricula are more and more a thing of the past: years memorising names, dates and poems that we now pull up with Google and AI. As if that weren't enough, students keep getting worse at maths and reading, AI keeps getting better.
But that's fine. Maybe these benchmarks are a thing of the past too. And I wouldn't worry that we'll stop writing code; after all, nobody today complains about not doing 4875 x 29 with pen and paper.
Physical education, not mental. In 13 years at school desks, topics like emotional education and wellbeing are non-existent or handled superficially, for example:
the idea that wrong thoughts can be fixed by thinking about something else (when it increasingly seems we need to act, to respond with the body); the idea that “feeling that we feel” emotions, being aware of them, is the starting point for changing them (when in fact we need to be able to give them a name)
No wonder digital psychologists (on ChatGPT too) and Netflix content are trying to fill this immense emotional void inside us.

1.title: 👥ff.78.2 Stutz's shadow
1.content:
Breaking the theatrical “fourth wall” several times, director Jonah Hill brought his sessions with psychotherapist Phil Stutz to Netflix.
Stutz starts from accepting the inevitability of work, uncertainty and pain. We can't escape physical entropy (that one, yes, we did learn at school).
With sketches and drawings, he invites us to depict the problem, giving it a shape, a name. That's where the solution begins (literally, by solving it).
Corpore sano → Mens sana. Among these drawings, the pyramid of life forces. It has a physiological base, starting from the body's wellbeing.
Finally, the concept of the shadow: the past self we're ashamed of and hide from others. Stutz asks us to talk to our shadow, apologising to it and acknowledging its influence on our present insecurities.

2.title: 🏞️ff.78.3 Pánta rheî
2.content: Anyway, even if we take it philosophically (Heraclitus-style), we don't like change. Around us, though, it's happening more and more often:

3.title: 📚ff.78.4 Reading, lightly
3.content:
How can we accept change? With a book by Brad Stulberg (whom we met in 🎁 ff.68.4) maybe? After all, reading can be psychotherapy too.
In Master of Change, Heraclitus' idea of the river is expanded:
Just as water molecules will never be in the same spot again, the riverbanks too are eroded and constantly changing. The riverbed, though, tends to stay the same. In the same way, we all need to set a limited number of values (3-5) on which to base a dynamic resistance to change. These values must be diversified. We need several sides, several independent interests. Depending on the “seasons” or the “rainfall” of a given period of life, we'll switch them on like so many streams. By identifying with what we believe in, rather than what we own, we're less fragile in the face of external events (which can take away relationships, health, money).

4.title: 🗣️ff.78.5 My personal take
4.content:
A concrete example. Two of my values are sport and financial independence. They guide my everyday choices. When I do things that feed these values, I feel good.
What's more, specific values teach general rules of life, of existing. For example:
improvement also comes from the dips (the rest day without training); it's important to stay in the game (surviving a black swan event or a cramp at the least expected moment); progress is invisible (you can't see muscle growth after a single workout)

3.title: 🎄ff.79.4 The Christmas tree effect
3.content:
Unwrapping the year. Thanks in part to Spotify Wrapped, Christmas and the end of the year come with a renewed bout of introspection. More and more, a moment to stop and take stock.
But what can Christmas teach us?
More is worse. American journalist David Epstein, 40, compares our brain to an over-decorated Christmas tree (The Christmas Tree Effect):
In Texas, road safety awareness signs increased mental load, causing more accidents. The US Army had to cut down the gear issued to soldiers, which was weighing them down too much.
Over-decorating doesn't seem healthy.
Labor limae. Faced with a problem, we look for a new product, a new diet, a new subscription/service. Leidy Klotz, in Subtract, suggests subtracting, removing, simplifying.
This Christmas we could write a special letter: asking for something to be taken away. P.S. To go with Trading Places, I suggest Netflix's documentary Minimalism.

0.content:
Lux Capital is already writing 2024 into the history books. Let's see why.
2023 closed with renewed optimism about the future, symbolised by Marc Andreessen's The Techno-Optimist Manifesto.
Over the top and idealistic. As every manifesto should be. Here are the lines that struck me most.
Crediamo che l’Intelligenza Artificiale sia la nostra alchimia, la nostra pietra filosofale. Stiamo letteralmente facendo pensare la roccia, la sabbia, il silicio.
Crediamo in una spirale crescente. L’energia come motore della civiltà. Più energia abbiamo, più persone possiamo sostenere. Crediamo sia possibile generare energia in modo gratuito, tanto da arrivare a darla per scontata come una penna, nonostante una penna sia tutt’altro che un oggetto semplice (così come è internet). Dobbiamo rendere scontato ogni oggetto fisico.
Crediamo che la popolazione mondiale possa raggiungere i 50 miliardi di persone e diffondersi su altri pianeti.
The incredible growth of world wheat production.
Il nostro nemico è la stagnazione. Il nostro nemico è l’anti. Anti-meritocrazia. Anti-ambizione. Anti-conquista. Anti-grandezza. Il nostro nemico è la burocrazia, la veto-crazia, la deferenza cieca delle tradizioni.
The Christian Creed? To wrap up, a list of “secular saints” (it made me smile):
[…] Andy Warhol, Bertrand Russell, Jeff Bezos, Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, John Galt, Paul Collier […]
Ah, I'd barely finished writing the newsletter when George Hotz (geohot, the nerd behind the first iPhone jailbreak) weighed in too.

0.title: 🦖ff.82.1 Mass extinction?
0.content:
500 million years ago, the Cambrian explosion. Perhaps a new organism able to produce oxygen “suffocated” the other life forms that lived by breathing CO2.
Today, CO2 is scary again. AI-driven emissions are growing: one exchange with ChatGPT equals an hour of LED light, one DALL-E image a smartphone charge.
Will computronium be the next form of life? Will CO2 get its revenge?
But, but, but. Doom and sensationalism aside, here on 🎼ff let's try to dig a little deeper into the question:
Comparing ChatGPT to LED light is misleading. In one case we're talking about the first example of a mass technology, in the other the result of a century of improvements (compared to the tungsten filament). Even if ChatGPT uses 10x a Google search, how many other Google searches does it prevent?
What's more, MIT points out that AI's energy consumption can bring benefits and that efficiency solutions already exist:
rolling out Small Nuclear Reactors (Microsoft's proposal), optimised management of computing resources
Nerd corner. The report on projections of internet energy consumption.

0.title: 🌇ff.83.1 Generating a sunset
0.content:
In 🎼 ff.81 2024 in the history books we saw that 2024 could go down in history as the annus mirabilis of handing over our cognitive abilities.
The steam engine took away physical effort; computers and AI, the mental kind. What's left for us? Maybe consciousness. Feeling human (✊ ff.55.1 How does it feel, inside a revolution?).
Tutto può essere tolto ad un uomo ad eccezione di una cosa: la sua libertà di scegliere come porsi di fronte ad ogni situazione. Viktor Frankl,L’uomo in cerca di senso
Our consciousness is non-negotiable. It will never be taken from us.
Generative consciousness. Ever noticed that a sunset never looks as good on your smartphone as in real life? Well, the real-life sunset is a construction of our brain, which condenses the imperceptible flicks of our eyes between light and dark areas into a single impression. Natural HDR.
captions: Illustration by Margaret Cook (1913)

1.title: ⚠️ff.83.2 Pay attention!
1.content:
Consciousness is choosing what to focus our (ever more bombarded) attention on.
L’attenzione è un discriminante intenzionale e impenitente. E’ un continuo chiedere cosa sia importante in questo preciso momento per registrare solo quello. Alexandra Horowitz
Transformers? Attention is precisely another trait AI and the human mind share. ChatGPT is a transformer, first proposed in the famous paper Attention is all you need.

2.title: 🧠ff.83.3 Language and thought
2.content:
Autocomplete. Large Language Models (LLMs) amazed us with their “emergent” abilities (like translating, writing code, putting together recipes), even though they were only trained to predict the most likely word to complete a sentence.
Language, thought, building the world: a tangle with a whiff of Wittgenstein.
I limiti del mio linguaggio significano i limiti del mio mondo. L'immagine logica dei fatti è il pensiero. Il pensiero è la proposizione munita di senso. Ludwig Wittgenstein,Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
Language and thought are so connected that Orwell, in 1984, talks about Newspeak, the language introduced by the totalitarian regime to control its subjects.
Arthur Koestler, the Hungarian anti-totalitarian writer, tries to rebel like this:
Il linguaggio può diventare uno schermo tra il pensatore e la realtà. Per questo motivo, la creatività inizia laddove il linguaggio finisce. Athur Koestler

3.title: ⏸️ff.83.4 Why writing and thinking matter
3.content:
Buried under texts “vomited” by GPT, Tim Ferriss answers his son's question on his blog: does writing still make sense?
Yes, because when we write:
We stop and focus our attention (there it is again!). We understand: without giving voice to our thoughts, we live in the mere hallucination of understanding concepts. We grow attached to the text we produce. A text we then also have to re-edit and cut. Writing teaches us to let go of what, a moment earlier, was our finest result (I say this after rewriting this point at least 5 times).

4.title: 🔎ff.83.5 Understanding the brain with AI
4.content:
In this merry-go-round between AI and the human mind, here's Anthropic, a company founded by OpenAI defectors.
In a virtual “vivisection” of the thoughts of Claude, their ChatGPT, they noticed that certain clusters of “neurons” fired depending on the context (sport, numbers, DNA sequences).
Black box. The goal of these studies is to better understand GPT's outputs, since one criticism of LLMs is their randomness and poor reproducibility.
What's fascinating, though, is that thanks to these models we're above all understanding how our own brain works. For example, by understanding how LLMs have internalised the concept of time.

0.title: 💀 ff.86.1 If you don't move, you die
0.content:
If you move, you lower your probability of dying from any cause over the next ten years.
As the chart shows, all-cause mortality drops by up to 50% as metabolic fitness (MET) rises.
MET what? Metabolic equivalents are the unit that measures our body's metabolic consumption.
1 MET = 3.5 ml/kg/min O2 (the O2 consumed just to stay alive)
Below, oxygen consumption by type of exercise (dashes) and the population distribution of VO2max, which drops as we age (lines).
Running at 16 km/h equals 16 METs, for example. Walking, 3 METs.
To not die (or to die with lower probability) you need to rack up at least 15-30 MET-hours of activity a week.

0.title: ‍💨 ff.87.1 A short history of breathing
0.content:
Feuerbach (reviewing Jakob Moleschott's Popular Treatise) claimed that we are what we eat.
Food, chewing, breathing. This connection floored me: chewing less because of processed food, our palate has changed shape over the last two centuries, bringing problems like snoring (related: the effects of bottle-feeding versus breastfeeding on breathing and teeth alignment).
So are we what we breathe?
James Nestor explores the subject in the phenomenal Breath. A few takeaways:
Taping your mouth shut at night (or during workouts) leads to better sleep/performance. The amygdala, more than the brain's fear centre, looks like a CO2 sensor. So much so that the famous impossible-to-scare patient SM was terrified by a single breath of CO2. Email apnea is a thing: we're so caught up in notifications and multitasking that we forget to breathe (is that why sport, meditation or singing, which force us to breathe, prevent stress?).
In short, a book you should not read in one breath.

1.title: 🦠ff.92.2 One more organ: the microbiome
1.content:
The microbiome (the layer of microbes lining the gut) is increasingly linked to mood, blood sugar and disease.
After all, if you think about it, the gut is where food spends most of its time in our body. So microbes control how fast molecules like sugars enter the bloodstream (and therefore the glycaemic response).
So much so that analysing (no pun intended) poop can win you the Olympics (Blummenfelt, world champion triathlete: 🇳🇴 ff.17.1 Norway is obsessive).
I Contain Multitudes by Pulitzer winner Ed Yong raises gut microbes to the level of our “own” cells. So much so that growing up without microbes is impossible (for example, they regulate blood pressure).
And the beans? Like other unprocessed foods, they're rich in fibre. And fibre fosters a healthy, diverse microbiome (and, as a result, less inflammation).

0.title: 🤰ff.94.1 How to get pregnant?
0.content:
In past issues we talked about obesity (🎼 ff.49 The pandemic of the 21st century). It's a delicate, tangled subject, just like the rest of human biology.
Stigmatising fat leads to social and psychological problems, like bulimia. Deborah Clegg explains why a bit of fat matters, especially on women's hips.
The highlights:
Fat cells are a source of oestrogen and regulate ovulation, so much so that without them a woman's cycle and fertility shut down. The fat that builds up after menopause is in fact a “third ovary”, rebalancing the missing oestrogen. Soy and sprouts contain substances similar to “ovarian” oestrogens and can help fight the effects of menopause. Good and bad fat cells: the “white” ones are flexible and release the fat inside them more easily. The waist-to-hip ratio identifies obesity better than BMI.
Fast food, then? Not so fast: eating at McDonald's and eating little fruit lower fertility. During pregnancy and afterwards, though, better to overdo it a little: breastfeeding a baby takes up to 400 kcal a day.

1.title: 🍔ff.94.2 Good fats and bad fats
1.content:
A bit of fat is good for you. But which kind?
Food and diet are a tangle of chemistry, biology and physiology. The nutrition facts on a food label aren't enough. Especially for fats.
Compound Interest sums up the 5 categories of fat:
Trans fats are to be avoided: the rise in cardiovascular disease. Thanks to their C=C double bonds, polyunsaturated fats can have antioxidant properties and lower cholesterol.
Oil Pokédex. Flaxseed oil is “super effective” in omega-3s (but the short ones, read below). Because of its high saturated fat content, on the other hand, better steer clear of the “coconut-bello”.
As I said, though, there's a lot of chemistry involved. Temperatures and reagent ratios have to be precisely controlled. If you took up home baking during lockdown, you know.
So much so that:
If we overheat “good” oil (extra virgin, polyunsaturated) we turn it into trans fat, silently doing ourselves a lot of harm (all it takes is “flipping” the C=C bond in the carbon chain). Polyunsaturated fats are good for you, but too many omega-6s compared to omega-3s maybe not.
To dig deeper (it's long, I warn you), the Dynomight blog.

2.title: 🚬ff.94.3 Omega-3s like cigarettes?
2.content:
OK, I've thrown more meat on the fire and the question “which fats?” is even more tangled.
A simple answer, if you have to pick which fats to take: “long” omega-3s.
In this phenomenal podcast (we'll come back to it), Rhonda Patrick points out:
Taking 1g of omega-3s a day (50g of salmon) can have the same effects as quitting smoking. The biggest benefits come from “long” omega-3s (=EPA and DPA), found in animal sources (fish). The “short” omega-3 variant (=ALA) found in seeds and vegetarian diets, even if partly “lengthened” during digestion, isn't enough. Vegetarian or pescatarian? To hit the target simply and consistently, it's worth taking a supplement (just one, promise, not like 💊 ff.49.4 The superman who takes 100 pills a day)

2.title: 🔑ff.95.3 Digital private property
2.content:
That's how Chris Dixon of the A16Z Crypto fund makes the case for a new internet in his brand-new book Read Write Own.
What is web3? And above all, what are web1 and web2?
web 1 | read + open protocols like the ones still used today by email (SMTP) and websites (HTML) - systems with no organisation and no financial incentives for users web 2 | read and write + centralised databases and user-friendly platforms - free speech but no control over the means of distribution/algorithms web 3 | read, write and own + decentralised databases with blockchain (the web2 advantage) + immutable rules that reward user participation (with tokens) and make funding easier
A good summary of the book is the chat between the author and Balaji (ex-CTO of Coinbase, 🌐 ff.52.3 Founding your own nation).

3.title: ✍️ ff.95.4 Reinventing writing and printing
3.content:
Writing and newsletters on Substack could be a first example of the shift to web3. Let's see why.
Since newsletters are emails, running on an open protocol as we've seen, Substack can't lock in its writers if they want to move to other services (a copy-paste of the email list is all it takes).
Gutenberg or Telepass? Writing sits at the heart of another analogy. Just as the printing press broke the Inquisition's grip, blockchain gives network neutrality back to users/influencers/brands, who are forced to pay more and more for the same traffic on social media.

4.title: ⛓️ff.95.5 What does blockchain solve?
4.content:
Asking what blockchain solves is like asking: “what does steel solve?” Chris Dixon, Read Write Own
Beyond censorship and “marketplace taxes”, here are the weak spots of today's online world:
Boxing. AI packs content harvested online into boxes/FAQs/chats, taking monetisation away from the original sites. Deepfakes, ever more convincing, undermine the credibility of online content (🍝ff.85.4 Carbonara and cryptocurrencies, verifymedia)
and the opportunities:
Tokenisation. In gaming, mods are the order of the day (League of Legends is a remix of a Warcraft III map). Blockchain rewards user creativity and contributions in a predictable way (Edenhorde, the collaborative Lord of the Rings that gives value back to users)
Interoperability. Moving contacts, content and purchases from one platform to another with zero friction (as mentioned, see the Substack example) Bureaucracy. The example of Etherisc, which refunds your plane ticket in 10 minutes

1.title: 🫂ff.97.2 The touch famine
1.content:
This very “touch famine” is at the heart of Out of Touch by Michelle Drouin, professor of psychology at Indiana University.
Michelle proposes a to-do list of relational (not individual) exercises:
Try to hug or touch someone (even just an animal) for 20 seconds a day. Nurture old relationships and friendships as much as possible, but if they're not reciprocated, look for new ones. Make the most of technology: the phone, but for a call or a personal message. Or use ChatGPT or Replika.AI for a conversation, even a purely introspective, self-analytical one.
This focus on relationships rather than on the individual brings us back to 🔺ff.89.2 Maslow's pyramid 2.0.

2.title: 🩵ff.97.3 Caresses against stress
2.content:
Abbracciamoci forte e vogliamoci tanto bene.Fabio Caressa
OK, but let's not wait to win the World Cup again before we hug. Because touch is life. Let's look at the science.
Unlike when we touch inanimate objects, we all squeeze a human being in the same way (at a speed of 5cm/s, the one that stimulates “slow” touch neurons)
Slow neurons and fast neurons. The two types of neurons our skin is equipped with: fast ones to respond to stimuli like pain, slow ones to convey the gentleness of a caress.
Rangan Chatterjee (whom we met in 🦁ff.90.1 Scappare da un leone o una notifica) notes that during childhood a mother's touch promotes stress regulation, because there's a drop in cortisol after a hug.
The physiological response is so innate that, if there's no alternative, even giving yourself a massage works.

0.content:
A driving simulator helps everyone: from Leclerc in F1 to your 50-year-old aunt who has finally signed up for her driving licence. But never as much as it helps Waymo. And autonomous driving.
Simulations are the closest thing we have to a time machine (without wheels). With ever shorter computing times, they replay thousands of possible (and impossible) scenarios.
So much so that Waymo's self-driving cars have virtually “driven” 10 billion miles, 1000x the ones they've driven in reality.
No wonder NVIDIA, born to optimise Battlefield's graphics, is now, as the simulated world has tangible effects on every technology, the most valuable company in the world.

Using language models like ChatGPT, we can create “agents”: impersonations of business or social roles that, by interacting, create virtual societies, like in The Sims or an episode of Doctor House.
By simulating conversations between patients and doctors, between diseases and prognoses, a generic GPT “did an internship” and ended up becoming better (MedAgent-Zero) than models specifically trained on the entire scientific literature (Medprompt).
In the eternal dilemma of theory vs practice, experience seems to rule.

3.title: ⚛️ff.98.4 Quantum systems
3.content:
Despite the potential of quantum computers, essential for simulating superconductors, drugs and nanotechnologies, the technology isn't mature yet (🎼 ff.69 Quantum?).
They make too many calculation errors, due to phenomena like quantum decoupling. But simulating quantum computers can help us.
But, but, but. Maybe studying qubits and Schrödinger's cats isn't necessary: Google DeepMind's AlphaFold3 (🎼 ff.4 Resurrected mammoths) has figured out quantum physics from experience.
From a text file listing the atoms present, the new version simulates the 3D structure and chemical interactions between DNA, RNA and small molecules (drugs). Before, it handled “only” proteins.

1.content:
Let's start with something “spicy”: spermidine can extend life by almost 6 years.
It's a polyamine found in peas (no coincidence), wheat, soy and polenta. Its chemical structure helps protect DNA.
Here's a table of the richest foods.
NSFW. Yes, the name doesn't lie. It's also found in human sperm. Each ejaculation, however, contains only 0.1 mg of spermidine. If you want something white, better go for tea, so protective of DNA that it can even be used to preserve sperm itself.

3.content:
Gut wellbeing and fibre: a recurring theme on futuro fortissimo, 🦠ff.92.2 One more organ: the microbiome, 🎼 ff.17 Sport (and the people who poop it).
We are not what we poop: 75% of poop is made up of microbes from our microbiome.

The spice fenugreek (trigonella) raises testosterone, but makes you sweat maple-syrup-scented sweat. Where can you buy it? Matt Clancy's newsletter (an innovation-and-society researcher at Iowa University) is called What’s New Under the Sun.
A sun now at the equinox of this summer of 2024.
The perfect name for the last summer newsletter, then, because progress doesn't go on holiday. Or does it?
Matt shows how, since the 80s, the words “progress” and “future” have become less and less frequent, replaced by risk and caution.
If you remove “future” from the synonyms of progress, the trend is even more obvious.
Mea culpa. By christening progress “futuro fortissimo”, I'm only messing up his analysis.
Below, two eye-opening interviews. Click the links for a fortissimo summary.

3.title: 🩸 ff.102.4 From blood to Amazon

Zipline, founded in 2016 to deliver blood in Rwanda and going on to cut post-partum deaths by 50%, is aiming to expand.

In short, more dematerialisation. But not of pizza.

0.title: 🍓 ff.103.1 Think before you speak
0.content:
I know, we're tired of pairing “intelligence” with “artificial”. But OpenAI's new model, o1 (aka Project Strawberry), opens up a futuro fortissimo. I couldn't let it pass.
GPT vs o1? The default on chatgpt.com, GPT-4 is the gossip's model, the quick answer, the bar-room chat. It isn't ideal where more elaborate answers are needed.
So here's the fruit of knowledge: a strawberry, o1.
o1 thinks before it speaks.
Think before you speak and judge, try to think Think that you can decide Stay just a moment, one moment more With your head in your hands Fabrizio Moro, Pensa
Learning to Reason with LLMs details the differences from the past. The most important thing is in the chart below.
More parameters and data “during training” give better results. We knew that.
With o1, the breakthrough comes after “training”: by increasing the resources allocated to the answer, the model explores internal "reasoning trees" (chain of thought) more deeply. With better results.
captions: o1's accuracy as training (left) and inference/thinking time (right) increase (via futuro fortissimo)

1.title: 🎓 ff.103.2 NASA, MENSA and IQ
1.content:
The new model's abilities are astonishing, especially in fields with a single right answer (science, maths, coding).
For example, in 5 minutes it built a black-hole filter that had cost the NASA researcher in this video 10 months of work. His initial reaction is worth the ticket alone.
@Maximlott gave o1 the MENSA test, using non-public questions to minimise the chance it had memorised them.
The result? o1 has the IQ of an “average” person, around 100. More than the number itself, what's striking is the IQ jump from the past (GPT-4 has an IQ of 60).
captions: The new o1 model takes an IQ test: much better than Claude 3.5 (via futuro fortissimo)

2.title: 🆕 ff.103.3 The new Era of Intelligence
2.content:
OpenAI applied deep learning (the same as AlphaGo, ♟️ ff.18.4 Artistic chess: the king of chess) to text generation. A new paradigm, so much so that OpenAI's CEO Sam Altman talks of an Age of Intelligence.
How did we get to the doorstep of the next leap in prosperity? In three words: deep learning worked. In 15 words: deep learning worked, got predictably better with scale, and we dedicated increasing resources to it. Sam Altman, The Intelligence Age
With the Ages of Fire and Iron we mastered energy and matter. Today we can combine them to generate knowledge.
Here is one narrow way to look at human history: after thousands of years of compounding scientific discovery and technological progress, we have figured out how to melt sand, add some impurities, arrange it with astonishing precision at extraordinarily tiny scale into computer chips, run energy through it, and end up with systems capable of creating increasingly capable artificial intelligence. We're seeing growing interest in longevity, supplements and diets. Or at least, the algorithms filtering my internet are.
And so futuro fortissimo veers a little into all that.

In his book Smarter Not Harder he proposes biohacking. His theory is that we often “stress” the body with insane workouts, in intensity and duration, without feeding it the food it needs to reap the benefits.
For example, through mineral deficiency (45% of Americans don't reach their daily magnesium)
In the book, Dave lists supplements, broken down by whether you want to optimise athletic performance, longevity or muscle mass.
And more. He gives the dosages. Crucial.

1.title: 🦸‍♂️ ff.104.2 The Fantastic 4
1.content:
I know. We're stressed and in a rush, pushed by social compromises into less-than-ideal food choices too.
Here are my fantastic 4, super-supplements to correct course a little.
Electrolytes Even eating well, hitting your magnesium and potassium needs isn't trivial. Especially in summer, when we sweat a bit more. And indeed Polase is on everyone's lips this season (and on Esselunga's shelves). The problem? As I said, the dosages. Let's look at an example: Soy strips Eating protein and fibre while minimising fat? Almost impossible. When I discovered texturized vegetable protein (the name is scary, but it's soy) I was amazed: €1.5 per 100g, delivering 50 g of protein, 15 g of fibre and only 7g of fat. Glycine Glycine supports longevity by aiding collagen turnover and boosting antioxidant defences (glutathione synthesis). We know that cutting a single protein, methionine (found in animal protein), promotes longevity. Glycine balances methionine's potential negative effects (for longevity). Siim Land, top 10 in the anti-ageing olympics, suggests a dose of 12-18 grams a day. Wheat germ In 🌶️ ff.99.2 Polenta and spermidine we discovered another molecule with a mystical name: spermidine extends life. 10 g of wheat germ (mixed into bread dough or morning porridge) is a good base. Then mango, soy and polenta!

2.title: 🤮 ff.104.3 The Abominable 5
2.content:
The best thing about life? To improve, you don't necessarily have to do stratospheric things. You just have to not do the wrong ones.
So here are 5 foods or ingredients to avoid. Always.
Margarine (trans fats) Of all fats, avoid trans fats above all: they raise the risk of heart disease and visceral inflammation by 30% (🍔ff.94.2 Good fats and bad fats). Processed puddings and yoghurts (polysorbate 80) This single emulsifier can reduce gut-barrier integrity by 50%, raising the risk of systemic inflammation. Jarred mayonnaise (oxidised seed oils on supermarket shelves) Commercial mayonnaise contains seed oils, which oxidise during their long stay in the jar. These oxidised seed oils increase inflammation and fat mass. Fizzy drinks (corn syrup) Consumption of high-fructose corn syrup is linked to a 20% drop in learning and memory abilities. Froot Loops (Red Dye 40) Here too, a single ingredient makes the difference: Red Dye 40 is associated with a 10% increase in ADHD (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder) in children and with markers of neuroinflammation in adults.

0.title: 🤴ff.105.1 Turning a frog into Prince Charming?
0.content:
Once upon a Volta, Galvani. In the late 1700s, Italy was at the centre of the electrical world. People wondered whether electricity was natural or belonged only to man-made materials, like metals.
Galvani backed the natural thesis: he threw himself into experiments with so many frogs that, in some areas, they almost disappeared.
Volta instead focused on metals, going on to invent the first battery and temporarily eclipsing Galvani's discoveries.
Anal electricity? A 60,000-franc prize for creating an "animal battery" drove scientists mad: Humboldt went as far as self-experimentation, inserting wires into his own rectum.
That's the historical digression that opens We Are Electric by Sally Adee, science writer for New Scientist and The Economist. The perfect book for today's newsletter, between brains, electricity and experiments worthy of Frankenstein.

1.title: 🧠ff.105.2 Frogs, brains and ion channels
1.content:
With the discovery of neurotransmitters (molecules, so chemistry), the role of electricity in the body (and brain) seemed eclipsed for good.
Electrifying comebacks. It took Hodgkin and Huxley (1952, Nobel 1963) to measure the action potential in neurons (using a giant squid) and Neher and Sakmann (Nobel 1991) to isolate ion channels.
Today the influence of electricity on biological processes is expanding even further. Let's see how.

Michael Levin is bypassing DNA to reprogram life through electricity.
For example, he grew a fully working eye on a frog's backside (yes, frogs and backsides are clearly popular).
By influencing sodium-potassium channels, electric fields can localise/extend a tumour. Or regenerate the leg of… wait for it… a frog.
And more. With AI he designs “artificial legs” optimised for certain movements. Then, with electric fields, he controls their growth: the birth of xenobots.

This tangle of computers, AI and biological substrates is fascinating (we talked about it in the early days of futuro fortissimo, 🦠 ff.4.5 Computational microbes?).

2.title: 🕊️ ff.106.3 Nexus and Harari
2.content:
Anthropic's Claude is named after Shannon, who invented the entropic theory of information.
Entropy, information and AI: a perfect logical thread that leads us to Harari and his latest book, Nexus.
The thesis: ChatGPT is the latest stage of a process that began with writing, technologies that “schematise” the world into tables and drawers, a completely non-human skill.
Bureaucracy tries to solve the problem of retrieving information by dividing the world into drawers, separate containers so that documents don't get mixed up. However, this principle comes at a cost. Instead of focusing on understanding the world as it is, bureaucracy is often busy imposing a new, artificial order. In short, bureaucracy sacrifices depth of understanding for the sake of organisational efficiency, creating a partial and distorted view of the world. Yuval Noah Harari, Nexus

3.title: 🐕 ff.106.4 A dog's life
3.content:
Back to Claude: in one of his most enigmatic prophecies, Shannon suggested that one day we would be "dogs for AI".
But, but, but. Look closely, and our four-legged friends, who started out as hungry wolves, now sleep on our designer sofas and eat gourmet food.
What if Shannon was right, but the other way round? Maybe dogs domesticated us: with a few tail wags they "hacked" evolution, scoring belly rubs and kibble.
Are we controlled by algorithms, or are we “domesticating” artificial intelligence (and the robots that will follow) to dodge the queues at Esselunga and the traffic between Pero and Cormano?
As Manzoni said, to posterity (and AI) the arduous verdict.

0.title: 🪣 ff.108.1 What's your Perfect Day?
0.content:
Today, a "dialectical" reflection, exploring the contradictions I face every day and in which, perhaps, many of you will recognise yourselves.
Whether it's COVID, a society obsessed with optimisation or the algorithms that increasingly run our lives, I live by ever more rigid, pre-set routines.
Figures like Bryan Johnson (and his "Don't Die" project, with standardised protocols for food and lifestyle choices) or Sahil Bloom, an entrepreneur the algorithms constantly recommend to me, push this message:
The boredom of routine is a tax on long-term success. All the successful people around me share one thing: they are really, really boring. We notice and envy their success, the gala dinners, the endless events and holidays. The reality hidden behind it all: long stretches of extreme discipline and boredom. Sahil Bloom, The Taxes of Life You Need to Pay
But does routine have to be boring? Or can every day be a perfect day?

1.title: 👶 ff.108.2 Through the eyes of the inner child
1.content:
In Wim Wenders's film Perfect Days (2023), the protagonist, Hirayama, finds novelty in the changing leaves on the trees, in the play of morning light, in the small variations of his methodical life cleaning Tokyo's public toilets.
Finding wonder in small things: a flight of fancy back to secondary school and Pascoli's Poetics of the little child:
There is a little child inside us […] Whoever thinks about it carefully understands that it is the poetic feeling that makes the shepherd content with his hut, the petty bourgeois with his little furnished flat, even if furnished without good taste Giovanni Pascoli, Il fanciullino
A little child who creates poetry in the simple, the ordinary; like a plough abandoned in an autumn field.
In the field, half grey and half black, a plough remains without oxen, which seems forgotten, amid the light mist. Giovanni Pascoli, Lavandare

2.title: ☯️ ff.108.3 Be water
2.content:
One element of variation in the film is the books the protagonist reads.
In one of the latest books that have marked my own daily life, Change Your Thoughts – Change Your Life, I found an illuminating answer to the method-versus-creativity conflict.
Wayne Dyer, analysing Taoist philosophy, offers the analogy of water. It does only one thing: it falls by gravity. It seeks the low ground, with a unique humility. And yet, without meaning to, it quenches thirst, waters plants, lets us ski and produces hydroelectric power.
In short, it sustains life. Without knowing what life is.
Wu-Wei? Water generates without any intention: a concept that extends to the whole Tao. To the universe. To ourselves. We must dissolve and flow, without the ego imposing itself, without goals or forcing.
Like children who haven't yet adapted to cultural and social expectations, showing their most spontaneous selves. […] When being was unaware of its ego-being. Wayne Dyer, Change Your Thoughts – Change Your Life
Pascoli's little child, again.
captions: The Chinese philosophy of “non-action”

3.title: 🚽 ff.108.4 Art in the toilets
3.content:
Tao = Creation (and creativity). The book also speaks of a mysterious force, feminine, creative; mother of novelty. It's up to us to notice it.
It's what, in 🎤 ff.101.1 Adele's manager, Rick Rubin calls "the creative act of noticing".
So in Perfect Days the protagonist invites us to see the romance and the art in Tokyo's public toilets.
The link to Fountain, Duchamp's ready-made, is immediate. If Pascoli's little child spots poetry in an abandoned plough, Duchamp forces us to reconsider everyday objects, transformed by attention.
So, routine or no routine? It's the same question that closes the film Perfect Days, in a long single take that captures the protagonist's conflicted emotions, alternating smiles and gazes lost in the void.
And that's all for today.

0.title: 👩 ff.109.1 LinkedIn's most influential woman
0.content:
Arianna Huffington (founder of the newspaper that bears her name) is the woman with the most followers on LinkedIn.
I discovered her in a recent podcast with Peter Diamandis (creator of the XPRIZE, the Nobel for technology that for 30 years has offered millions to whoever develops innovative technologies).
Arianna's story fascinated me: at the Huffington Post she tried to overturn the idea of sensationalist, negatively viral media by introducing the What's Working section, news centred on the positive.
An idealism shattered by the media business model, focused on maximising likes and engagement.

refs.0: Arianna Huffington (founder of the newspaper that bears her name) is the woman with the most followers on LinkedIn.

1.title: 🌱 ff.109.2 From media to digital wellbeing
1.content:
So she launched Thrive Global, to channel the power of algorithms with one priority: human psychophysical wellbeing.
The mountain comes to Muhammad. Integrated into Microsoft Teams, Slack and similar digital spaces, Thrive brings a release valve “to the workplace”, like meditation, mood check-ins and digital detox.

2.title: 🧶 ff.109.3 Untangling a ball of yarn in a minute
2.content:
Ariadne's thread. Let's look at an example of how Thrive uses AI to get out of the labyrinth of an algorithmic society. In one minute.
Control techniques like eye tracking to gauge a user's engagement are already widely used for commercial purposes; Arianna wants to use the same ones to gauge - during a meeting - an employee's stress level.
Just give me a minute A breath of air One more moment Pooh, Dammi solo un minuto
Thrive has a Reset feature: one minute with a user's favourite song, messages and images, to clear your head between one Zoom meeting and the next.
Or a password will do: Mauricio Estrella got over the depression of a betrayal and divorce by resetting his PC password to “Forgive@h3r”. He turned a boring work chore into a mantra, a moment of meditation and acceptance.

refs.0: eye tracking to gauge a user's engagement
refs.1: Or a password will do: Mauricio Estrella

3.title: 💲 ff.109.4 Alms from AI
3.content:
And if I share with you my story would you share your dollar with me? Aloe Blacc, I Need A Dollar
Our society is increasingly automated, algorithmic. It measures us and recommends purchases, diets, workouts. Human free will is cancelled out.
But, but, but. According to Harari, the problem isn't spending on artificial intelligence, but the failure to invest in human consciousness (Google spends more on data centres than on employee salaries, 🦖ff.82.1 Mass extinction?)
So Arianna's project is heading in the right direction: building algorithms to improve our self-awareness. It's encouraging that OpenAI's Sam Altman is among Thrive Global's investors.
Is this the right ball of yarn?

0.title: 🏛️ ff.110.1 All roads lead to Rome's potholes
0.content:
For two months, my home near Bergamo has been cut off. A hairpin bend gave way after heavy rain, closing the only road to Val Seriana.
The most optimistic forecasts put the end of works at late 2025. AGI might arrive first.
That bend is yet another example of how fragile Italian infrastructure is. World-class fragile.
In life as in infrastructure, new is more exciting: a new bike, a new outfit, a new Calatrava bridge. Going to the mechanic, the tailor, or calling the builder for a leak is far less glamorous, especially in the throwaway era.
But with infrastructure, we have to make the most of what already exists. Especially bridges. The Morandi in Genoa and the banknotes in our wallets remind us of that.

1.title: 🚧 ff.110.2 An endless construction site
1.content:
And yet the State struggles to fund maintenance of what's been built. Extreme weather events like the Valencia rains don't help.
And so around us there's an endless construction site, overseen by retired old men.
All that's left is to make a show of it, Big Brother style: the livestream of the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation's I-95 site.
The truth is we're in the middle of a productivity cliff. McKinsey points it out too: construction productivity has been stuck since the 2000s.
And yet America used to be efficient: 138 days after the idea, Apollo 8 reached the Moon.

refs.2: 138 days after the idea, Apollo 8 reached the Moon.

2.title: 💎 ff.110.3 Cryptocurrencies versus state obsolescence
2.content:
The US elections sent a clear message, however hard to swallow: the State is too slow, regulation suffocating.
SpaceX lands rockets again, Starlink brings internet where fibre doesn't reach. No coincidence that Musk himself proposes - with his usual irony - DOGE, the Department of Government Efficiency.
Trump's election and Bitcoin's spike: from 69,000 to 75,000 dollars in a few hours. A sign that we're moving beyond modern democracy? Are we about to 🎼 ff.52 Found a Nation in your garage?
According to Naval, yes: Bitcoin at all-time highs is the first sign of relief from the weight of the State, which gets heavier every day.
Meanwhile, remember that El Salvador's president has been buying one Bitcoin a day since November 2022: the strategic reserve is worth 600 million dollars today (at the start of 2024 it was worth 100).
But, but, but. Maybe decentralised democracy is an illusion too.

refs.1: El Salvador's president has been buying one Bitcoin a day since November 2022
refs.2: decentralised democracy is an illusion too.

3.title: 🤤 ff.110.4 Robots and AI: opportunities
3.content:
There is an alternative to digital anarchy: the State can save itself with the help of artificial intelligence and robots.
Sidewalk AI (Carlo Ratti, MIT Senseable City Lab) uses AI to map the condition of pavements.
The other technological piece is robots: they could speed up construction sites, cutting costs and boosting efficiency. On that note, the update on the collaboration between Figure AI and BMW.
While we wait for the robot revolution, all we can do is fix reality following the Japanese principle of Kintsugi (金継ぎ), or Kintsukuroi (金繕い): potholes turned into works of art by Ememem.

0.title: 🍊 ff.111.1 A life to squeeze
0.content:
On futuro fortissimo we also talk about time. We've converted it into bananas (⚖️ ff.61.1 Measuring pollution in hours of life) and slowed it down, noticing the variations in everyday life (📝 ff.65.3 Homework for life).
The end of the year is perfect for stopping, and stopping time. As I do with a recap video on YouTube, for whoever's left of the 50,000 subscribers who used to watch me shoot things up in Call of Duty.
Stopping isn't enough, though. First we have to turn our life energy, our work, into life: reckless, remembered.

1.title: 💯ff.111.2 A reckless life
1.content:
I want a reckless life I want a life like the ones in the movies I want an over-the-top life I want a life like Steve McQueen Vasco Rossi, Vita Spericolata
You don't need to be Vasco to live fully, you just need a method: Bill Perkins's, an engineer turned gas trader.
His book Die with Zero opens with a thought: if we die with €10,000 in the bank, we've lost 3 months of life at work; missing out on 5 trips, 50 dinners or 3 months of retirement.
captions: Bill Perkins's book, Die with Zero (via futuro fortissimo)

2.title: 🛡️ ff.111.3 Children, health and wasted years
2.content:
Bill asks us to “die with zero”. Clearly an impossible provocation (obviously nobody knows the day they'll die). But it reveals hidden inefficiencies in how we manage our finances:
Inheritance: children receive it at 60, when they're already financially settled. Better to help them between 25 and 35, when they can use it for a home, a business, a family or more experiences. Health: in case of serious illness, savings can't cover huge medical bills (especially in America). Better a good health insurance policy. Retirement: our estimates of post-work years are rough. Better life annuities.

3.title: 📈 ff.111.4 Experiences = investments
3.content:
Scandalous? With his hedonism, Bill seems to trample values like family, health and security for the future: to all intents and purposes a mental stumbling block (skàndalon), a stone on the main road.
A scandal first of all for himself, since Bill wants to remember the mental traps he fell into when young, saving €1,000 of a €16,000 salary. When his boss found out, he told him: "Are you an idiot? You're sacrificing 1/16 (22 days a year) of your life for money you'll make in 3 days in 10 years' time!".
So let's see how Bill, through an analogy between money, time and investments, makes us rethink life.
Memories as dividends? In finance, the earlier you invest, the more dividends you accumulate. The same goes for experiences: a trip to Italy at 20 generates 20+ more years of memories, lessons and knowledge than the same trip at 40.
Physical inflation. A dollar spent at 60 buys less life. Bill's example is a day on the slopes. In old age, physically slower, we do fewer runs, fewer experiences.
But, but, but. Fascinating as I find Bill's ideas, allow me some criticism:
without novelty, more experiences don't turn into more moments to remember (🆕 ff.65.1 Time = new experiences?) novelty depends on our attention (or distraction), regardless of how much happens around us; old age, even if it slows us down physically, brings out the value of things we took for granted when young
In short. A fine mess. A big bang. Happy end, better beginning.
P.S. Exercise for the 31st: maximise the next 365/22,000 days, in case you die (with zero) at 60.

0.title: 💸 ff.112.1 5 years to make money
0.content:
The start of the year means resolutions and predictions. Both doomed to crumble against the wall of an ever more unpredictable reality.
The COVID explosion taught us that our linear minds don't grasp exponential trends, says Neil deGrasse Tyson.
An example: o3, OpenAI's latest model, doubled its (already staggering) accuracy in a few months.
Faced with this acceleration, is Raoul Pal right to say that within 5 (6) years the current socio-financial system will completely lose its meaning/value?

1.title: 🙅 ff.112.2 We can't predict anything
1.content:
Putting a face on it? We don't understand reality, not just the future one but the present: Hollywood is scared of generative art recreating actors, yet half of box-office takings are already tied to non-human characters.
Instead of making predictions, Ved Sen invites us to replace “never” with “what if”.
Here are my 5 very personal what-ifs:
What if the robot population overtakes the human one? What if I live to 500? If I can't predict the next 5 years, how do I think about the next 100? What if a swarm of autonomous drones appeared on the horizon? If energy and money lose value, will biological health (measured in VO2max) be the new wealth?

2.title: 🏋️ ff.112.3 We can only prepare as well as possible
2.content:
Given an uncertain future, all we can do is refocus on the present, keeping good habits and making small investments.
I've kept a personal diary for 10 years. I thought it would be useless, given the jumble of text I'd hardly ever reread. This year, thanks to Google's NotebookLM, I turned it into a podcast episode about my life.
Hearing two “people” comment, not without some irony, on my very personal worries made me smile. Now I can't wait to generate a whole film of my life.

3.title: 🏞️ ff.112.4 Unexpected rivers
3.content:
The diary is just one example of how AI (we'll soon talk about Google Deep Research) processes the jumble of information we generate (♾️ ff.72.1 Digital infinity).
Research on the link between drinking-water hardness and lower cardiovascular risk has existed since the '60s. Only recently have we managed to rediscover and understand it more deeply.
A small example: I took the data on the mineral salts in Bergamo's water and, with a simple copy-paste into ChatGPT, generated a report on mineral salts in the water of various towns in the province, noticing that my village tops the chart for magnesium. Hooray!

4.title: 💧 ff.112.5 Water everywhere
4.content:
2025 isn't a blank slate, but the continuation of life's flow. So let's go back to the recent invitation to follow the Tao, to be water (☯️ ff.108.3 Be water).
Water that flows without resolutions or predictions, but with a direction: downwards. Following a single law: gravity.
Without knowing whether it'll end up in a sea, a lake, a toilet, a fruit or your mouth.

0.title: ⚖️ ff.113.1 Shall we throw away the scale?
0.content:
Say diet, and everyone thinks of the weight on the scale (or rather mass, to be scientifically precise).
Problems, problems, problems. That number can't guide our food and health choices:
every day the amount of water in our body can vary by 1 to 4 litres; muscle weighs more than fat for the same volume; few scales (bioimpedance ones included) properly measure visceral fat (the most dangerous kind)
In Good Energy, Casey Means starts from her mother's death to change course: pay attention to metabolism. And to “good energy”.
Casey left contemporary medicine: it pushes you to specialise and treat, instead of preventing and seeing the body as a whole.
With Levels too, she proposes personalised medicine (for example with continuous glucose monitoring 🕛 ff.35.2 Smartwatches and more).
She also points to new markers for telling whether we're truly “healthy”:
Fasting glucose: correlates with our metabolic health, optimal below 85 mg/dL. Insulin needed to keep sugars in check (HOMA-IR): the ratio of glucose to insulin in the blood, optimal below 2. Average blood sugar (3 months, HbA1c): measures haemoglobin glycation.
captions: Good Energy: why metabolism matters for health (via futuro fortissimo)

refs.0: amount of water in our body can vary by 1 to 4 litres
refs.1: muscle weighs more than fat for the same volume

1.title: 🥛 ff.113.2 The protein-milk trick
1.content:
Food as medicine. But we also need to focus on food, on good energy, precisely.
Hard, when food producers spend 10 times more on marketing and tempting (but unhealthy) formulations than goes into medical research.
Two personal anecdotes to prove it.
I came across a soy “protein milk”, with “10g of protein” printed in huge letters on the pack.
Knowing typical protein values in milk, those 10g intrigued me. So I read the label and did the maths: for the same amount of protein, the one on the left costs twice the kcal of the one on the right (!).
Similarly, after a friend of mine was told to cut potatoes from his diet (which are more filling 🤰🏻 ff.22.4 The most filling foods) but keep the pasta, I created buonGPT.
captions: Potatoes vs pasta, per 100 kcal, thanks to BuonGPT (via futuro fortissimo)

2.title: 💎 ff.113.3 A mineral diet?
2.content:
Swapping potatoes for pasta is debatable, since potatoes have 25x the potassium of pasta, and doubling potassium intake (4300mg/day) lowers the risk of cardiovascular disease by 40%.
These details pushed me all the way to Mineral Fix, a 1,000-page doorstop on the importance of minerals in food and human physiology.
A quick selection of interesting ideas:
Spa (the one with the Formula 1 circuit) was famous in Roman times for its thermal waters. An acronym of Salut Per Aqua, today's SPAs take their name from it. Too much iron can cause anaemia if not balanced by an adequate amount of copper (we'll come back to this “chemical” idea of ratios and normalising).
To get more copper, we should partly replace “muscle” meat with liver, heart and a vegetarian diet (which has 2x the copper density of an omnivorous one).
captions: Mineral Fix: why minerals matter for our health (via futuro fortissimo)

refs.0: doubling potassium intake (4300mg/day) lowers the risk of cardiovascular disease by 40%
refs.2: Spa (the one with the Formula 1 circuit) was famous in Roman times for its thermal waters
refs.3: vegetarian diet (which has 2x the copper density of an omnivorous one)

3.title: ➗ ff.113.4 Why ratios matter
3.content:
The iron/copper ratio (and BuonGPT) are examples of the complexity of our bodies and diets, made intrinsically of chemical reactions.
Which explains why:
Unprocessed foods are key to health, thanks to their balanced internal ratios. Single supplements can backfire, because they upset these natural balances (like putting 1kg of turmeric into 100g of chicken curry)
My favourite “ratios”:
Protein/kcal (for satiety) Sugar/protein (to flatten glucose spikes) Fibre/100kcal (for the microbiome)
And you, what's your relationship with food? Tell me in the comments?

I'm in China right now, and Chinese is DeepSeek, the open source model that makes free what OpenAI offered for €200/month (🍓 ff.103.1 Think before you speak).
The serpent of knowledge has slipped out.
Slytherin or evergreen? More the latter, since Chris Sacca (the 2,378th richest person in the world) backs climate-change solutions through Lowercarbon Capital (some portfolio companies):

He was recently on Tim Ferriss's show. Let's see what they talked about.

1.title: ❔ ff.115.2 What to study with ChatGPT around?
1.content:
As a good investor, Chris Sacca follows tech trends closely. With podcasts? No. By talking to ChatGPT for hours (after asking it to impersonate Buckminster Fuller, 🎼 ff.48 Resurrecting Aristotle).
Better Call Saul and Mr. Robot. It's no accident that the protagonists of these series, magnetic personalities, are a lawyer and a programmer: symbols of two professions any sane parent would have suggested to their kids. Until a year ago.
Today - in the age of AI - the best-paid jobs (actors, programmers and lawyers) are also the most at risk (you don't need McKinsey to tell you that).
We've already got used to it, but until recently coding the game Snake took years of study. Today DeepSeek does it bug-free from 6 words: “write the snake game in python”.

2.title: 🐍 ff.115.3 Exponential venoms
2.content:
Speaking of snakes. Artificial intelligence is slithering out of chatbots and into practical applications.
ProteinMNPP is a “ChatGPT” trained on protein structures (instead of internet text, ⚛️ff.98.4 Quantum systems). In Nature, a study shows how to find an antidote to snake venom in seconds instead of months.
From here, a reflection on human short-sightedness about exponentials, featuring the illustration by Tim Urban, who in 2015 wrote about the Artificial Intelligence revolution.
Chris points out that these trends are everywhere: he claims nuclear fusion (not fission!) is being achieved daily (with Q>1), precisely by using AI (☢️ ff.28.1 Artificial intelligence for nuclear fusion).
How do we avoid being squeezed by this boa of technology? We'll see in 10 days. Now back to eating bao.

0.title: 🏆 ff.117.1 Oscar-worthy days
0.content:
I tried to give this (and the next) newsletter a linear thread. But then I realised Newtonian linearity has been dead for a while (🍎 ff.64.2 From Newton to Einstein).
So hold on tight, because I'm taking you into the hallucinations and mental movies I witnessed in less than 24 hours. Fuelled by the “spice” of Hong Kong and Shenzhen.
Interstellar. The days felt eternal, as if near a black hole, forcing me to keep redefining concepts like:
freedom of movement: in the morning a run through the green of The Peak (Hong Kong), in the evening through the emptiness of straight, silent streets, red with flags, in Shenzhen (China). freedom of speech: listening to Cancelleria by Pinguini Tattici Nucleari while looking at Shenzhen, towered over by a huge penguin (the symbol of Tencent and WeChat, which control information in China) and a “fountain-pen skyscraper”.
The ballpoints, big bosses, tried to keep the pencils at the same social status as before, but the pencils now meant to abolish every class distinction, and at their marches in the squares they hailed the revolution […] In the free state of Cancelleria only the ballpoints remained, and they sang and celebrated their victory Pinguini Tattici Nucleari, Cancelleria
Inception. The vertigo of spaces that seem to fold in on themselves.
Black Mirror. Need I say more?
michelemerelli.ig A post shared by @michelemerelli.ig

1.title: 🍩 ff.117.2 Atomic doughnuts
1.content:
Premises:
Everything Everywhere All at Once hadn't particularly struck me. I never eat bagels. But in Shenzhen, looking for comfort, I went for a brunch as if I were in New York.
When, that same evening, back in Hong Kong, my subconscious connected these premises, these two dots, my brain nearly exploded.
In an instant, I saw my past (and future?) again: everything everywhere all at once.
The most absurd part is that I wasn't in a film, but in reality. Between Hong Kong and Shenzhen it feels like living inside a TikTok feed: here humanity is compressed into .zip format, condensed as in ChatGPT.
A reality so dense with concepts and contrasts that it becomes a black hole, where space and time lose meaning: where everything is everywhere at the same time, precisely.
captions: The (bagel) brunch in Shenzhen, Shenzhen's museum of contemporary art, a video of mine on black holes (2019), past listens and reads with “bagel”

2.title: 🧮 ff.117.3 Simulations and algorithms
2.content:
Disoriented and looking for meaning - needless to say - I opened a “medium”, YouTube. The algorithm recommended this review of the film:
In the video, more unexpected connections with my past: DALL-E, which can generate anything (🎼 ff.30 DALL-E: it makes art), and Bo Burnham's film Inside, which I watched during lockdown.
And so I realised we live in a simulation, generated by algorithms that spoon-feed our brains with connections. A brain that feeds on connections (pattern recognition) to make sense of the chaos out there.

3.title: 👨‍💻 ff.117.4 Breaking free from the algorithms' simulation?
3.content:
But how can we escape this simulation?
In the YouTube video, a possible cure for hypermodernism (the virtual one of social media and the real one of Hong Kong): pay attention to what's happening.
But then I wondered where that phrase came from.
It's from a book I'd bought before leaving. That book is from 1967 and is called - prophetically - The Medium is the Massage (let's not also connect neural stimulation, there's no time, 🎼 ff.75 Brain massages).
This extra dot made everything collapse again. Into the bagel. Into the simulation out there (or only in our brains?).
We'll come back to it.

0.title: 🌎 ff.118.1 Brave New World
0.content:
Almost everyone knows the book 1984, Orwell and Big Brother: controlling society by controlling information, through censorship.
But what if the “new world” were instead the one of Brave New World?
Back in 1932 Aldous Huxley painted another dystopian society: one where a “spice” mentally controls the population.
Here's the alternative to censorship: drown the truth in a chaos of content (AI-generated too); throw it back into the “simulacrum of stimuli” the brain has to make sense of (👨‍💻 ff.64.4 Matrix and matter).
A spice, a drug: that of the media, of TikTok feeds we can't take our eyes off, modern gladiators in the Colosseum (Juvenal's “panem et circenses” on steroids).

1.title: 🌶️ ff.118.2 Paprika - Dreaming a dream パプリカ (2006)
1.content:
Paprika (a spice) is the title of Satoshi Kon's masterpiece film, which I watched recently.
It connects other dots from last issue's mental journey, 🎼 ff.117 We live in a simulation.
The director portrays the danger of a digital world (but also modern society) in which everything can coexist: the internet (but also a skyscraper) where every tab (or floor) is a possibility.
Looking for a loo in Hong Kong, I walked into a skyscraper. At random, I pressed 17 in the lift. When the doors opened, my lungs were flooded with eugenol: I was on a floor full of nothing but dentists.
It was yet another confirmation of the non-linear, electronic, quantum reality we live in. Where parallel realities coexist, stacked like the floors of a skyscraper.
Here's the desert - a space with no landmarks - painted in Paprika, where all our myths and symbols parade past.
A desert of signs with no single meaning: umbrellas, for rain or for sun?

2.title: 🌳 ff.118.3 The cure: trees and silences?
2.content:
How do you “unplug” from this drug, this spice?
In Hong Kong, I reacted by running a marathon.
Not so much to cover the infamous 42.196 km, or for a medal; but to find the time I needed to get bored again.
To switch off from the city's constant stimuli (one giant social network) and listen to what was happening inside me.
In short, to find my “groundedness” again, the roots and fixed points of my being: running, podcasts and simple food (bananas).
And to listen again to the songs that matter most.
Where are you going, tree? So high That every shoot is less firmly rooted And every leaf is weaker And bound to fall just a little above the roots And all these arms flung open to the sky And those slender fingers, because they're fighting this gravity Because they're fighting this gravity Na na, against this gravity, na na Eugenio in Via di Gioia, Albero
And in all this music, to find silence again. Like John Cage's 273 seconds (also degrees Kelvin).

0.title: 🏃🏼‍♂️ ff.120.1 How much running to “outrun” death?
0.content:
Our future runs through health, movement and sport. That's why these topics are at home here.
How I METs your mother. In 🎼 ff.86 Burning oxygen is life we introduced the Metabolic Equivalent, a unit for measuring movement (basal metabolism = 1 MET).
It works even if you run a marathon in space:
runneralerts A post shared by @runneralerts
Using the Bruce test, a study sorted 750,000 people by their metabolic fitness (ranking them by the METs they could sustain).
Nerd corner. 10 METs equals running 10 km in an hour (6 min/km); the relationship between the Cooper test, VO2max and METs.
Back to the study: after 20 years, those who could sustain 14 METs died 4 times less than those who stopped at 5.

1.title: 🥗 ff.120.2 Diet or exercise?
1.content:
Movement is so good for you that it lengthens your life even if you eat junk.
Don't take my word for it, but another study's: if you move, you can even eat badly (and if you don't move, a good diet takes a back seat).
Let's look at one possible explanation.

2.title: 💕 ff.120.3 Matters of the heart
2.content:
Candy from strangers? If not burned off, blood sugar makes your vessels stiffer (like a Maillard reaction: Advanced Glycation Endproducts, AGEs).
That explains the link between sugar, blood glucose and heart problems.
When activated, muscles act like a sponge and “soak up the excess”. That's why VO2Max (a measure of oxygen and sugar consumption) is a longevity marker.

3.title: 🍼 ff.120.4 Lactate for the brain?
3.content:
Keeping arterial stiffening in check is one of the benefits of movement.
Moving also produces lactic acid (the stuff that turns stairs into our worst enemy the day after a mountain hike).
Mental energy. Yes, the brain burns 20% of the sugar we take in. But did you know that neurons prefer lactate? So much so that it's used to treat brain injuries.
So the lactic acid produced during sport promotes the growth of new nerve cells (sport and Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor, BDNF).

0.title: 🌊 ff.121.1 Flow basics
0.content:
I first came across the idea of flow a few years ago, reading Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi: it's that mental state of total immersion in an activity that makes us lose our sense of self and of time.
What encourages flow? Physical movement, risk, the complexity of a task (but not too much: the 4% rule), novelty, the absence of distractions.
When we play, we often slip into flow. No coincidence that it was first measured in chess players, with an increase in theta waves and activation of the "implicit system".

1.title: 💸 ff.121.2 Flow gives you wings
1.content:
Besides making us happy, it boosts our performance, with socio-economic effects:
McKinsey: managers in flow are five times more productive. DARPA (the US defence agency): military snipers acquiring targets 2 times faster. Red Bull: the North America's High-Performance Center led by Leslie Sherlin
