2.title: ♟️ ff.122.3 From chess to Patagonia
2.content:
I thought the benefits were only mental, so I was surprised to find flow as the explanation for extreme sports.
Faced with a real chance of dying (ultimate human performance), flow is always there, as Steven Kotler points out in The Rise of Superman.
And it opens the doors to the impossible:
Tony Hawk, skateboarding, a trick with a 900° rotation. Tyler Bradt, kayaking, a 58-metre drop. Dean Potter, climbing, inventing the free solo (he later died in 2015 BASE-jumping, RIP 🕊️), scaling Fitz Roy in six and a half hours. The new ChatGPT is phenomenal at creating images (but not perfect yet)

3.title: 🔺 ff.122.4 Pyramids in 4 minutes?
3.content:
Not even an Ironman is enough any more: Mitchell Hutchcraft's Project Limitless, a 12,000-kilometre triathlon (34 km across the English Channel, 10,000 km by bike from France to India and, to finish, a light trek in Nepal up to Everest).
runnersworldita A post shared by @runnersworldita
Why this explosion of flow and extremes? Why do we keep raising the bar?
Behind it is Maslow's pyramid: once survival and food are guaranteed, we need stimuli to give our days meaning (🔺 ff.62.4 The pyramid inside all of us).
The Bannister effect. Once something is shown to be doable, loads of people start doing it (good), but the new limit moves to a higher level of risk (bad).
You can see this effect in the spread of new technologies too:
NERD BONUS. Speaking of the “democratisation of the impossible”, I asked Claude for the chart of runners able to run a mile in 4 minutes (1,755 in 2022).

When Tyler Cowen (theorist of the “great stagnation”, 🤔 ff.50.1 The oddness of the last 50 years) says he saw AGI (or a porno) on 16 April 2025, you have to stop and pay attention.

o3 combines various “tools” in its thinking (chain of thought) - screenshots, web browsing, running Python code - reaching an IQ of 136 (top 1% of humans; last year the record was 94).

1.title: 💎 ff.123.2 Minecraft beyond humans
1.content:
In all this, humans are increasingly the limiting factor. The bottleneck.
Just as AlphaGo (trained on human games) was beaten by AlphaZero (which trained “on its own”) ♟️ ff.18.4 Artistic chess: the king of chess.
AI understands more than we do, for example the language/structure of proteins (⚛️ ff.98.4 Quantum systems).
David Silver and Richard Sutton - pioneers of reinforcement learning (RL) - argue in a new paper that we've entered the Era of Experience: autonomous systems/agents that, in every field, explore the world and possible solutions without needing human confirmation.
Hunting for diamonds in Minecraft. Google/DeepMind's DreamerV3 is an example of this new technological phase.
Despite never having seen Minecraft played (and not knowing its rules), in 100 million steps it learned to break trees, make sticks and upgrade pickaxes. All the way to its first diamond block.
A voice outside the choir. Dan Hendrycks, director of the Center for AI Safety, argues instead that letting AI evolve independently will be our end.

I fell off my bike. Or rather, someone made me fall. Result: 30 days of forced sofa time and an AI deep-dive I hadn't planned.
In 🎼 ff.109 A family doctor called AI we talked about how ChatGPT isn't just for funny pictures or automated emails, but can make a real difference in everyday life.

There are more examples online of artificial intelligence solving physical, real-world health problems. So much so that Reid Hoffman, co-founder of LinkedIn, talks about superagency:
In Italy we can still count on solid public healthcare, even if it's under growing pressure. But imagine living in Nigeria or Argentina, with little money and no access to expert doctors.
Or, even with the means, not finding anyone who really understands what's wrong with you (like the Y Combinator founder who beat her migraines after years).

1.title: 💵 ff.125.2 Stabilising the dollar
1.content:
Money printing, in short, and the well-known inflation. Back then, 25 hours of work bought you one S&P 500 share; today it takes 24 days of work.
One of the answers? Stablecoins: digital currencies whose value is stabilised algorithmically.
Increasingly widespread, especially in the BRICS and Saudi Arabia, in 5 years they've overtaken VISA and Mastercard in transaction volume ($15T in 2024).
No coincidence, then, that Stripe announced the integration of Stablecoin payments.

2.title: 🏮 ff.125.3 China: the next world empire?
2.content:
If the American empire is giving way, who will pick up the baton? In the physical world, China looks like the most credible candidate.
Having visited Shenzhen (a city built in 40 years, now the third most populous, 🏆 ff.117.1 Oscar-worthy days), I was amazed at how light years away today's China is from the one of 25 years ago, wrapped in toxic clouds of smog:
Energy consumption: from 2.5k to 10k TWh (the US stuck at 4k), 8% of it solar.
Nuclear: leader in planned plants, India second.
High-speed rail: 45,000 km starting from zero. So much for Italy's TAV… Chinese high-speed rail: 45,000 km in under 20 years (brilliantmaps x futuro fortissimo)
Stagnation, what stagnation? Storrs Hall, in his provocative book of the same name, wondered where his flying car was (😭 ff.46.3 Wasted years). The answer: right there in Shenzhen.

0.content:
Andy Grove survived the Holocaust. Then, having emigrated to America from Hungary, he led Intel right from its birth (co-founded with Moore, the one with the law).
Despite his technical background, he reinvented himself as an operations manager, racking up so many successes that he was named Time Man of the Year 1997.
Paranormal activity. The same paranoia fuelled by a youth spent between war and Nazism saved Intel from Japanese competition: in 1985 Andy shifted the company's focus from memory (DRAM) to chips.

1.title: 🐦 ff.126.2 It's not the end of Google
1.content:
Exterminated by ChatGPT and Perplexity? Google today is in a similar situation. 50% of its business, Google Search ($200 billion a year), is under attack. On top of that, Apple is thinking of replacing it as the default on Safari (even though Google pays $20 billion for that privilege).
At its annual Google I/O conference, the giant showed all its cards:
Veo 3, a text-to-video model with Hollywood-grade quality, consistent characters and integrated audio and dialogue. A coincidence that veo means “I see” in Spanish? Veo veo. ¿Qué ves? Una cosita. ¿Qué cosa es? Empieza por "C". ¿Qué será qué será qué será?
Simultaneous audio translation in Google Meet (keeping voice and expressiveness). AI-powered smart glasses (Android XR Glasses) and screens that can create 3D avatars (Google Beam).

2.title: ❎ ff.126.3 Google's moonshot: X
2.content:
Here are Google's advantages over OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Perplexity, according to its CEO Sundar Pichai:
Products everyone uses. Gmail, YouTube, Cloud. Custom chips. In-house Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), now in their 7th generation, with Ironwood, 40+ exaflops. X, Alphabet's Moonshot Factory. A forge of research on self-driving (Waymo), quantum computers and biology (🎼 ff.28 Google researches the future). Nobel. A recognition rarely given to private companies, won by Demis Hassabis for Chemistry in 2024 (🧬 ff.4.1 The structure of proteins).
In short, Google isn't just search.

While pushing the frontiers of maths (a new record of 593 spheres in the “kissing number problem” in 11 dimensions), it cuts data-centre consumption by 1% (by improving Strassen's algorithm, unbeaten since 1969).

0.title: 🛣️ ff.127.1 The third wAI?
0.content:
Ever since secondary school, I've been fascinated by the intersection of the humanities and scientific knowledge. I think you've noticed from futuro fortissimo too (🖼️ ff.18.3 Art, between artificial intelligence and humans, 📜 ff.101.4 Poetic Web).
Concision. That was my thesis as a fresh-faced school-leaver: the ability to condense concepts into a few signs, from Ungaretti's Soldati to Euler's equation.
Concision as the meeting point between the humanities and science.
The two cultures, so sharply distinguished in Snow's essay of the same name (1959), are drifting ever further apart, partly because of growing specialisation.
[…] I have asked the company how many of them could describe the Second Law of Thermodynamics. The response was cold: it was also negative. Yet I was asking something which is about the scientific equivalent of: Have you read a work of Shakespeare's? C. P. Snow, The Two Cultures
Can Artificial Intelligence tear down this “Berlin Wall”?

1.title: 🤘 ff.127.2 Rock ‘n’ roll and vibe coding
1.content:
According to the legendary Rick Rubin (🎤 ff.101.1 Adele's manager), yes.
Enter vibe coding. To prove it, Rick worked with Anthropic to create The Way of Code, an interactive software-book that “remixes” messages from the 3,000-year-old Tao (☯️ ff.108.3 Be water) with contemporary concepts.
Rick compares ChatGPT to the jazz revolution: it lets you remix elements, not just sounds but culture (🐆 ff.127.3 Leopardi and the Schrödinger equation).
But, but, but. AI mustn't be a simple copy-and-paste: the first answer, given the statistical nature of LLMs, is “common”, banal, not very creative.
Rick explains how he uses AI: iteratively, with questions and comments, aligning the answers more and more with his artistic taste. The same method he used in his early work with Johnny Cash.

2.title: 🐆 ff.127.3 Leopardi and the Schrödinger equation
2.content:
Why now? Two years ago, generative art gave poor results (🌳 ff.35.5 Leopardi's L'infinito according to AI). Today it's a whole different tune (remixed).
Here's a poem on the Schrödinger Equation in the style of Leopardi:
Wave that dwells unknown — ψ, faint sigh of being, in spaces where the void speaks with Hilbert's voice —, listen: for the algebra of the cosmos within your womb of shadow resounds. There, among silences where the great emptiness embroiders the weft of time, the sign ∂/∂t caresses you and, with Planck's constant — ħ, light stellar rag —, steals you away. The square of your modulus — mystic density of probable truth — becomes fleeting homeland of every particle, which never owns a room or border, but wanders, hopes, decays. Thus the Laplacian operator, arcane chisel of the infinite, carves you upon a field of potential, V(x), while mass, a timid handmaid, at every point refracts the balance between impulse and fate. Eternal then the equation hovers, stern: iħ ∂ψ/∂t = [−ħ²∇²/2m + V]ψ, shore of uncertainty where the real oscillates and falls silent, as if it hoped, with the poetry of a hidden electron, to glimpse an end to blind becoming. Oh sweet illusion! That still torments me to set a measure to the motion of the heart, when even the moon in the deep sky knows not itself, and we, larvae of atoms, in a single line of Schrödinger, wander. micmer x o3 x Leopardi, Onde (Waves)
“the Laplacian operator, arcane chisel of the infinite” “we, larvae of atoms” “ħ, light stellar rag”
If that isn't poetic…

3.title: 🚁 ff.127.4 And what does Palantir have to do with it?
3.content:
The humanities are also a cure for the winds of war.
In his recent book, Palantir co-founder Alex Karp denounces a Silicon Valley with no sense of nation or military.
Silicon Valley engineers refuse to work with the US military, but don't hesitate to raise money to build the next alienating social network. The number of humanities graduates has gone from 14 to 7% (179k) between 1966 and today, while enrolment in computer engineering reached 90k in 2020. We need engineers who are curious about the world, its history, its contradictions; not just able to code. Alex Karp, The Technological Republic
In the past, I've argued that 🎼 ff.14 War is not the future. Yet Mariana Mazzucato reminds us in her book, The Entrepreneurial State, that the internet and GPS came out of the US Department of Defense. Then came Instagram and Uber.
In short, if AI lets Rick Rubin become a programmer, Silicon Valley in turn has to rediscover art, history and philosophy.
For a third way that's pacifist, but aware of the risks that software, the new “nuclear”, poses to the future of humanity.

0.title: 🕳️ff.129.1 Altman's “gentle” singularity
0.content:
When Sam Altman publishes something on his blog, it's worth a read.
In The Gentle Singularity he argues that we've passed the event horizon of artificial intelligence. But so “gently” that we didn't even notice.
We already live with incredible digital intelligence but, after the initial shock, we got used to it fast. We went from marvelling that AI could write a paragraph to wondering when it will write whole books; from being surprised by medical diagnoses to wondering when it will develop the next medicine.
A subsistence farmer from the year 1000 would say we have fake jobs, and that capitalism is just a game to keep us entertained, since we have food and luxuries galore.
ChatGPT (150 times cheaper and greener in a single year) is an example of this acceleration. But the next technological leap will be in the real world.

1.title: 🥧ff.129.2 Pi, FigureAI and 1 hour of “logistics”?
1.content:
LLMs aren't just democratising software. They're the simplest interface we've ever had for the physical world - for “talking to robots”.
So programming robots is now cheaper and more generalisable. That's why various “robot foundation models” are spreading:
π0, by Physical Intelligence, handles 8 architectures and a range of actions, like making coffee or opening popcorn.
Helix, by FigureAI, combines a “slow, semantic” brain (System 2) that understands complex sentences and new scenes with a “fast, motor” one (System 1) that acts.
Google's SAS Prompt translates the robot's x, y, z coordinates into movements described in words.

4.title: 🩸 ff.130.5 Microplastics harden arteries
4.content:
But what effects do microplastics have on our health?
One is hardening the arteries, increasing inflammation and cardiac events, as the ever-reliable Eric Topol points out.
In particular, DEHP (a phthalate found in PVC) is estimated to have caused 356,000 additional deaths from cardiovascular disease, i.e. 13.5% of total global deaths (peaking at 16.8% in South Asia, where DEHP is most widespread).
So it's a good thing that the work Mega Mat, made with 500 recycled plastic mats, was shown in Bangkok.

3.title: ✒️ ff.131.4 Four reflections
3.content:
Ideas and quotes to mull over by the sea, waiting for Piotta's big wave.
Unlike material goods, which seem exciting at first but quickly lose their value, experiences gain value over time: they pay what I call “memory dividends”. Bill Perkins, Die with Zero (🎼 ff.111 Die with zero)
On the theme of the self and excessive self-awareness, optimisation, individualism (🎁 ff.68.4 Less ego and control, more flow and presence: Naval's cure) I found another gem:
The ego, the false self, [is] the root of all the evil that penetrates the earth and destroys human life, and with it, of course, the reality of time, the reality of lived presence. The ego lives only in the future and the past; it has no present moment; it is always in a hurry or dreaming. The root of our modern problem with time is neither technological, nor sociological, nor economic, nor psychological. It is metaphysical. It is a question of the very meaning of human life. Jacob Needleman, Time and Soul
The cyclical nature of moments. Beautiful, ugly, fleeting, always ephemeral; in the genius of the professor-turned-raver Cosmo.
I'd like to stop this train right now I wish I knew how I wish I knew how I wish it all were a little slower I wish I knew how To stretch out time I'd like to burn up and be born again I'd like to shield you from this wind And I'll enjoy every single moment Then let it go And then start over Cosmo, Momenti
Growing up means preferring vegetables to biscuits.
Happiness is like a cookie. When you are a child, you think cookies are very important and you want to have all the cookies in the world. You can't wait to be an adult, because then you can have as many cookies as you want, right? Yes, but as an adult you realise the cookie is a tool. A tool to make you eat your vegetables. And once you understand that, you eat your vegetables anyway and mostly stop eating cookies, because otherwise you risk getting diabetes and not being there for your kids. Joscha Bach, Lex Fridman Podcast #101

0.title: 🎯 ff.132.1 An attention crisis?
0.content:
As a gamer and (ex) YouTuber with 50,000 subscribers, I care about video games.
Often demonised alongside 15-second TikToks, they're accused of destroying our attention.
But, but, but. Are we sure we can't concentrate any more? According to historian Daniel Immerwahr, that's not the case.
A couple of reflections he shared in a recent podcast with Adam Grant:
In the nineteenth century people said books were distracting. Today they're a symbol of concentration. Video games, like social feeds, generate flow, not distraction. And we lose hours to them, because they're so immersive.
The real question isn't “how much” we concentrate, but on what.

1.title: 🕹️ ff.132.2 The benefits of video games
1.content:
And anyway, is time spent “playing on the PlayStation” really wasted?
Shooting in GTA helps you not do it in real life (🎮  ff.8.5 Killing boredom (and not human beings)). The link between violence and video games? Probably hot air.
Video games foster decision-making under stress, hand-eye coordination and teamwork. No wonder many founders have a gamer past: Kennan Davison, Top 200 in League of Legends, now CEO of Skio (YC S20).
Ash Brandin (The Gamer Educator on Instagram) also points out that some video games, like Braid, Edith Finch and Untitled Goose Game, foster emotional learning.

2.title: 📐 ff.132.3 Measuring and modelling the world
2.content:
To “illude” (in-ludere, a word tied to the Latin ludus, play), a video game has to simulate, to model the world coherently (🎼 ff.98 Games and simulations).
Building virtual worlds also helps us understand the real one.
No wonder Demis Hassabis (DeepMind) - a former gamer himself - now “plays” at modelling cells (after the Nobel he received for modelling proteins with AI).
And the analogy is even closer: Genie 3 creates, in real time and even from a single image, interactive video games that stay consistent over time.
QED. SimCity was born when Will Wright realised that building the world of his arcade shooter was more fun than playing it.

0.title: 🗣️ ff.134.1 Words, words, words…
0.content:
The relationship between thought, words and the building of the world fascinates me, especially since language models like ChatGPT made this connection even tighter (🧠ff.83.3 Language and thought).
1.1 The world is the totality of facts, not of things. 2.1 We picture facts to ourselves. 3. A logical picture of facts is a thought. Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
Thought (and Language) are therefore a picture of the World. So much so that some words exist only in some languages, in some Worlds: only on gloomy, cold Dutch evenings can you truly feel gezelligheid.
Other unique, untranslatable words: 別腹 betsubara, the Japanese “dessert stomach”.

1.title: 😭 ff.134.2 Naming emotions
1.content:
Words also help us identify another world: the one each of us carries inside, condensed into emotions.
These, according to neuroscientist Lisa Feldman Barrett, are simulations created by the brain to integrate various subconscious, visceral signals: heartbeat, temperature and other interoceptive signals (🥇 ff.128.1 Mental (Olympic) games).
Naming emotions is essential to getting past the blocks we impose on ourselves: before a race or an exam anxiety rises, but often it's just a shade of excitement, fuelled by the adrenaline of waiting for a big event.
Marc Brackett (founder of the Yale Center for Emotional Intelligence) follows exactly this line, with a guide to understanding and harnessing emotions: Dealing with Feeling: Harness Your Emotions to Create the Life You Want.
Meanwhile, the founder of Pinterest has created an app, How We Feel, a real “Pokédex for emotions”.

2.title: ❄️ ff.134.3 Japan's 72 seasons
2.content:
A while ago we talked about how to stop time: by noticing the novelty each day offers (🎼 ff.65 How to stop time).
A ray of sunlight filtering through trees or a particular juxtaposition of colours can hide the Perfect Day (👶 ff.108.2 Through the eyes of the inner child).
These very “child's eyes” can take us from the lazy “there are no in-between seasons any more” to seeing seventy-two of them, as in Japan:
白露 (Hakuro): the “white” dew glistens 08 – 12 September 土潤溽暑 (Tsuchi uruōte mushi atsushi): damp earth, sticky heat 29 July – 2 August 魚上氷 (Uo kōri o izuru): fish peek out from the ice 14 – 18 February

3.title: 🦴 ff.134.4 Humanity to the bone
3.content:
This feeling-and-defining is what we have left, in a World of “thinking outsourced to GPT”:
A purely disembodied human emotion is a nonentity. William James, What Is an Emotion? (1884)
And if the digital world is already changing the meaning of certain words - “to scale a startup”, we “scale” startups instead of mountains - then to resist disembodiment we need to reattach ourselves to words, the link between Thought and World.
Bonus. Is it a coincidence that Michaell McAfee's video for Max Cooper's I Am in a Church in Gravesend, Listening to Old Vinyl and Drinking Coffee is a river of words springing from this very particular experience?

1.title: 🌊 ff.135.2 A (rogue) energy wave
1.content:
All this is nothing compared with the plans for the future:
Musk wants to buy 50 million H100s in the next 5 years (soaking up 35 GW, 2% of today's global electricity consumption).
Altman wants to remove the limits imposed by energy production:
With 10 gigawatts of compute, AI can figure out how to cure cancer. Or with 10 gigawatts of compute, AI can figure out how to provide customized tutoring to every student on earth. If we are limited by compute, we'll have to choose which one to prioritize. Our vision is simple: we want to create a factory that can produce a gigawatt of new AI infrastructure every week. Sam Altman, Abundant Intelligence
Fortunately, one solution is solar: in just 10 years from 0 to 2073 TWh (237 GW of instantaneous power, total energy produced divided by the hours in a year).
Now you know. Investment in solar ($500B) has overtaken investment in aviation during the Second World War ($400B, adjusted for inflation).

2.title: ♾️ ff.135.3 Are we in the singularity?
2.content:
All this energy, though, is for (and has already been used for) something.
For instance, to “solve” mathematics.
GPT-5 Pro answers “FrontierMath Tier 4” problems (so hard that, assuming they get solved at all, they take expert mathematicians weeks of work).
This breakthrough is hugely important: physics, chemistry and - in the end - biology all depend, in cascade, on mathematics.
It's so astonishing that Alex Wissner, a real whizz-kid, says we're in the singularity, describing it as an optical illusion that from afar looks like a “vertical asymptote”, but that “when you're in the middle of it... feels fairly continuous”.
captions: An example of a Tier 4 FrontierMath problem

3.title: ☕ ff.135.4 AGI advances: the Chinese “coffee”
3.content:
AGI and the singularity are a bonus: Dave Blundin, in the same podcast, points out that even if AI development stopped today, it would take years to digest, explore and implement its potential applications.
Current models are already smart enough, but they need to be deployed in robots, factories and logistics, while cutting their energy use.
And so China is back - rampant: because of the embargo on the most powerful GPUs (🎼 ff.82 A war fought with chips) it has been forced to squeeze the “coffee beans” (= bits) with less powerful “coffee machines” (= GPUs) (an analogy by Ryan Cunningham).
No wonder, then, that at the recent AI Conference in Shanghai, Professor Wang Yu coined “watt-to-bit”, a metric for ranking the efficiency of AI models (Energy-Compute Theory).
No wonder, again, that the ARC Prize leaderboard includes cost per task (which traces a Pareto frontier currently occupied by OpenAI's o3 models).

0.title: ⛰️ ff.137.1 The orography of a descent
0.content:
We often compare a project to climbing a mountain. The summit - the ultimate goal - must always be clearly in sight, but your attention should go to the views and the thoughts you gather on the way up.
Processes (every step) rather than goals (the summit), in short, just like my first IRONMAN (🎼 ff.133 Am I an Ironman?).
But what if the process isn't enough? Once at the top, leaving the breathtaking view behind and heading down is hard. Brutally hard. How do you survive this “depression” without throwing yourself off the first cliff?
Seth Godin and life's descents, to work out whether it's worth carrying on:
The Dip, a temporary slump. Most people quit; the best emerge by getting through the down and staying true to the process. Cul-de-Sac, an illusory climb. Growing efforts at best maintain what you've achieved. The Cliff, a true precipice. More effort only makes things worse.
But, as we'll see, sometimes quitting isn't an option. Life, survival, is entropically stasis or decay towards “worse”.
Or, as we'll see, the secret lies in controlling what we put on the y-axis. How we define the reward.
captions: Life's three curves, including The Dip (from Seth Godin's book/futuro fortissimo)

1.title: 🏆 ff.137.2 Entropic peaks
1.content:
Back to the peak. Arthur Brooks, in a famous article in The Atlantic (2019), explains the growing depression of the “greats”: the principle of psychoprofessional gravitation. The higher you climb, the harder it is to walk away.
I'm talking about Olympic athletes in extraordinary shape, actors earning 1 million per episode or forgotten ex-YouTubers (count me in, with 50,000 subscribers in 2013).
Actually, I'm talking about all of us, whatever height we've reached.
Brooks gives his own personal (and musical) example: one day “you wake up and you can't play the horn as fluently any more”.
And there's more: staying at the level you've reached gets harder and harder. In short, we age, entropy wins. How do we accept it?
captions: Kipchoge in tears after what - at 40 - could be his last professional marathon (complete with a medal for all 6 majors).

2.title: 💎 ff.137.3 Crystals and Bach
2.content:
One cure is the psychology of Raymond Cattell and his two forms of intelligence:
fluid: the kind that solves new problems creatively (the young people who found the most startups). crystallised: the kind that distils and teaches future generations (historians peaking at 60).
Does Darwin evolve into Bach? Brooks again tells how Darwin, after an innovative youth, ended up in depressed inactivity. Bach, on the other hand, despite being showered with success when young, managed to overcome it by teaching.
So, as we age, we need to crystallise life experiences. Give them value through memory (📈 ff.111.4 Experiences = investments), sharing, teaching.

3.title: 📈 ff.137.4 The philosophy of accumulation
3.content:
Crystals (not meth) save us from modern fluidity.
Crystals, of all things - which, physically and chemically, are an example of stability against entropic chaos.
Crystals that become ever more precious, even with a little growth or by simply staying stable over time.
Crystals that accumulate “history”, in compounding, which is very tangible in finance, as in Warren Buffett's bank account:
Money aside, in every field we need to be “historians of our own lives”: building good habits for years - sport, a healthy diet - has to be perceived as continuous growth.
To remind myself, I created League of Strava, a dashboard that turns kcal and years of sport into something tangible.
Like Buffett's account, but in buffets of pizzas eaten and health “earned”.
The short film Hag by Anna Ginsburg: re-evaluating the aesthetics of women after their “peak”, beyond the “old witch” cliché.

0.title: 🏎️ff.138.1 The fastest road
0.content:
Brachistochrone. Today I'll lose you with a single word.
It's the fastest path (but not the shortest!) between two points: the red curve, the most efficient at turning potential energy into kinetic energy.
The algorithms that increasingly regulate society do everything they can to optimise time. For example, my brother Luca pointed me to Openroute: travel times around a city, by various means of transport. At least the bike wins.
Then comes the race to optimise consumption: Google Maps and the least-polluting routes.
But in all this optimising, does anyone consider the human, psycho-physical side of things? Our mental health?
captions: Going faster by taking a longer route: the brachistochrone.

For a few years now, Google has factored fuel consumption into the optimal route.

1.title: 😊ff.138.2 The happiest road
1.content:
What if we asked instead which route maximises happiness?
According to Kathy Willis (Good Nature), you find it by lengthening your commute to include parks and greenery (or, better still, a riot of autumn colours).
“Forest bathing” is back with new details (💚 ff.51.1 Storytelling for green):
Natural horizons have a calming “fractal dimension” (the complexity of a skyline): our senses favour wide spaces with the odd tree here and there (like the savannah, where we come from in evolutionary terms).
Schools surrounded by greenery have beneficial effects on children's cognitive development.
PS. ChatGPT coined a term for the “brachistochrone of happiness”: euthymìchrone (εὔθυμος + χρόνος), the time of good spirits. εὔθυμος = “good-hearted, serene” + χρόνος = “time”.
captions: Good Nature, Kathy Willis
The effect of horizons with different fractal dimensions on mental state.

2.title: 🪵ff.138.3 Touch wood or iron?
2.content:
Oversights. Kathy Willis, however, laments the excessive, Platonic weight given to sight (against 1,500 papers on the psychological effects of “seeing nature”, only 40 ask whether it makes sense to “touch it”).
So how does nature affect us through the other senses?
Touching an oak, compared with marble and metal, has calming effects.
The same group - Japanese, naturally - also compared touching printed leaves with real ones (note the sock).

3.title: 🥌ff.138.4 Roomba or houseplants?
3.content:
It isn't just about perception: nature changes the microbiome (and so our physiological and psychological regulation, 🥽 ff.90.3 Microbes of stress):
Replacing gravel with forest floor in nurseries increases biodiversity in Swedish children in just 28 days, reducing biomarkers of inflammation and autoimmune disease. A single plant can repopulate our sterile homes with beneficial microbes (Roomba, I see you).
Bonus. Indoor spaces can be more polluted than outdoors, especially by volatile organic compounds (VOCs) released by plastic objects or detergents. A plant can reduce them.

4.title: 🚬ff.138.5 I stay away from stress…
4.content:
Last but not least, breathing, another futuro fortissimo favourite (‍💨 ff.87.1 A short history of breathing).
Forest bathing is also relaxing thanks to α-pinene, a substance released by conifers (and found in cannabis).
And just three nights in a hotel that releases cypress fragrance are enough to boost signs of relaxation (measured with the “high-frequency” (HF) component of HRV, heart rate variability).

0.title: 🍫ff.139.1 Swiss? No, NVIDIA
0.content:
In 3 months, NVIDIA took in $57 billion (earning 36 of them, at a 75% margin). Mind-boggling numbers. Let's try to make sense of them.
Some people compare its market value with the gross domestic product of entire countries. That's wrong.
Valuation ≠ GDP. The first is a theoretical, perceived value; the second is what a country physically produces in a year.
Better to think fantasy football. If you wanted NVIDIA, you'd have to sell quite a few “players”:
all the Swiss companies listed in Zurich (Rolex, Nestlé, ABB, Novartis…) the 20 biggest companies in Europe (ASML, LVMH, SAP…)

1.title: 🧃ff.139.2 Konbini and paperclips
1.content:
Why the hype? Because AI is proving economically fruitful.
Dave Blundin, on the ever-stimulating MOONSHOT podcast, points out that the online advertising market (600 billion) is already run entirely by algorithms.
Agents with more advanced capabilities (e-commerce, commodity trading…) could create a market of at least $1T (~1% of world GDP).
As further confirmation (and since the latest models are saturating the hardest benchmarks: Gemini 3 solves 1/3 of the questions in Humanity's Last Exam), the new AI “leaderboards” are economic:
performance in finance (Alpha Arena) skill at selling, negotiating and long-term planning (Vending-Bench 2; here too Gemini 3 wins, “taking home $5,000”).
Nerd corner. Earnings by AI model and negotiation strategy (friendly, negotiator, double-dealer).
Economic optimisation, long-term planning... It brings to mind the mini-game about maximising paperclip production, cited by Bostrom as an example of super-efficiency leading to extinction (🦉 ff.36.2 The super-tome on the singularity).

2.title: 🍫ff.139.3 Where's my flying car (in GTA 6?)
2.content:
All these reflections are back in vogue because of yet another quiet but astonishing model.
Gemini 3 is more than a simple version bump: it's the first truly multimodal model.
It generates apps that combine camera recognition, image creation, search and text-to-speech. Apps with tool-calling, in short.
A couple of examples (created with a description shorter than a tweet):
Nutritionist ferret. Snap a photo of your food and it analyses it, returning a detailed report (squeak by squeak!) on the dish it has “sniffed”.
Podcast converter. Paste in today's issue and I get a personalised LinkedIn post, images on the key themes and a 5-minute podcast.
140 characters. Storrs Hall lamented that we got Twitter but not flying cars (😭  ff.46.3 Wasted years).
But now, with Gemini and 140 characters, we have a flying-car simulation. In a robotic future, the same input could make it real.
It's no coincidence that Polymarket is ever more confident Google will have the best model at the end of 2025.

2.title: 🧮 ff.140.3 Mental deflation and the academic crisis

'Mental deflation' works like the economic kind: if tomorrow a good, or developing an idea, will cost less, there's no point investing in it today.

0.title: 🦴ff.145.1 Man to the bone
0.content:
Every week a new AI model is released with startling results (the latest is Gemini 3 and its 48.4% on Humanity's Next Exam). So, for a while now, I've argued that as automation grows, humans will have to take refuge in physiology, our natural substrate.
"If energy and money lose their value, will biological health (measured in VO2max) be the new wealth?" — micmer
That's why futuro fortissimo keeps coming back to topics like (metabolic) health, exercise and diet. A return to “man stripped to the bone”.
"Ah, the man who walks off sure of himself, a friend to others and to himself, and pays no heed to his shadow, which the dog-day sun stamps on a crumbling wall!" — Eugenio Montale, Cuttlefish Bones (Ossi di seppia)

1.title: 🍬ff.145.2 Candy from strangers
1.content:
Speaking of bones. In Sugar Bones, Martí Guixé imagined sugar cubes with insoluble residue inside: fossils of our sugary consumption.
A perfect link to today's main topic: blood-sugar spikes.
Hold on, hold on, hold on… Sugar isn't inherently evil. It's essential for our brain (and for Pogačar to win the Tour de France). The real problem is the lack of movement (and of muscle) able to “soak it up”.
captions: From Food designing, Martí Guixé - via futuro fortissimo

2.title: 🎢ff.145.3 Blood-sugar spikes (and how to avoid them)
2.content:
In Glucose Revolution, Jessie Inchauspé argues that we're molecularly illiterate. We stop at calories and labels, when we should be focusing on the “ratios” between nutrients.
The author points out that sugars aren't harmful in themselves (they're the basis of fruit, after all); what's harmful is eating them without the “natural substrate” that naturally comes with them, like the fibre and vitamins that slow their absorption.
To “slow down” the Western diet, a Blue Tornado of glucose spikes, she suggests:
1. Dress “naked” carbs (pasta on its own, or fruit on an empty stomach) with fibre or protein (fibre also reduces alpha-amylase and creates a viscous mesh that slows gastric emptying into the gut)
2. Drink apple cider vinegar 20 minutes before dessert, to cut the spike by up to 30%, again thanks to temporarily deactivating alpha-amylase.
3. Eat carbs last: go ahead and have a plate of pasta or a dessert at the end of the meal, but only after a salad followed by protein and good fats.
Bonus. Too much circulating sugar leads to glycation of the skin (wrinkles) and of the blood (or rather, of haemoglobin = HbA1c).

3.title: 🚬ff.145.4 Food seriously harms your health
3.content:
This energy rollercoaster isn't your fault, though.
Mark Hyman, in a recent ZOE podcast, explains how food manufacturers hire “craving experts” to maximise how addictive processed foods are, with an irresistible mix of salt, sugar and fat.
The results? In China, in a single generation, exposure to these foods has taken diabetes from 1 case in 150 to 1 in 10.
No surprise, then, that ultra-processed food is “the new cigarette” (11 million deaths vs 8), so much so that every €1 spent at the supermarket hides €2 in health costs (Rockefeller Foundation, 2021).
Hyman goes as far as comparing cake to tequila at breakfast, saying that - in fact - it's just as harmful.
captions: Michael Moss, Salt Sugar Fat - via futuro fortissimo

4.title: 🍰ff.145.5 Brilliant pie charts
4.content:
And so, back to Martí Guixé.
For the father of food design, food should be an object able to communicate its function (or its danger), so much so that in I-Cakes Guixé replaced the floral decorations on cakes with a chart - a pie chart, naturally - of the ingredient percentages.
A pie chart to metabolise before ingestion.
Twenty years before Supersapiens' glucose sensors, Guixé had understood that to solve the 21st century's pandemic we need to go back to the data.
We'll probably never see a label on a pack of Pringles like the one on Marlboros, saying “processed food kills”.
But that's exactly the project we should start again from, moving beyond the aesthetics of food and back to the data. So as not to end up (physiologically too…) stripped to the bone.

0.title: 🚽 ff.146.1 Urinals and AI
0.content:
I won't hide it: I started writing this newsletter to collect news and ideas, to raise awareness of the futuro fortissimo that awaits us.
Today, though, all it takes is any old prompt (a podcast, an article, a book) and I can turn it into an ff.x.y-style section.
Automating the artistic process is nothing new: in The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction, Walter Benjamin started from an idea of Paul Valéry's; in the days of the Greeks, techniques for duplication were practically non-existent.
Then came an attack on artists:
Our fine arts were developed, their types and uses were established, in times very different from the present, by men whose power of action upon things was insignificant in comparison with ours.
But the amazing growth of our techniques [...] make it a certainty that profound changes are impending in the ancient craft of the Beautiful.
Paul Valéry, The Conquest of Ubiquity
Over the centuries, a “growth of our techniques” that undermined the Beautiful:
Printing = scribes Photography = painters Plastic = sculptors
But - Benjamin lamented - even the most perfect reproduction lacks one crucial element: its “presence in time and space”, its “Aura”.
That's why Duchamp's urinal is art, but the ones you find at a motorway service station aren't: the urinal is a repeatable readymade, but the artist's first idea, the one that raises it to art, can't be repeated.
The artist thus gives it an Aura of presence in the space-time of our culture.
Bonus. When we first talked about DALL-E (😱 ff.30.3 A few less funny examples), we “touched” on urinals, of all things…
captions: The first “generative” urinals, Razer Gaming style (😱 ff.30.3 A few less funny examples)

1.title: 👻 ff.146.2 Ghosts and Calvino
1.content:
So, writing this newsletter, I'm avoiding dictating out loud or generating text with GPT.
Today, writing by hand is my mental equivalent of walking to the shops or taking the stairs instead of the lift: a claim to humanity.
ChatGPT isn't the point, though. For a long time now, the machine has been able - at least in theory - to combine the 1s and 0s of information and generate the whole of human knowledge.
Italo Calvino, in a lecture that became famous, Cybernetics and Ghosts (1961), embraced the vision of a “discrete” kind of thought, made of signals and circuits (the 1s and 0s, precisely).
And he dreamed of a “ChatGPT”: a “poetry-and-electronics machine” able to dissect the classics endlessly, crumbling them into 1s and 0s, to extract their poetic essence.
In short, ChatGPT invented nothing: back in the '60s the experiments of Oulipo (French acronym for Ouvroir de Littérature Potentielle, “workshop of potential literature”) were already proposing endless algorithms for generating texts:
The “S + 7” (or “N + 7”) substitution method: replace every noun (S, for sostantivo) in a text with the noun that comes 7 places later in a given dictionary. So, for instance, the Italian proverb “L'abito non fa il monaco” (the habit doesn't make the monk) becomes, with a given dictionary, “L'abiura non fa il monarca” (the abjuration doesn't make the monarch). Paolo Albani, La letteratura potenziale - alcune note sparse

2.title: 🤐 ff.146.3 The silence of the innocents
2.content:
On closer inspection, Calvino himself cast man as a parrot-automaton who rephrases things “standing on the shoulders of giants”.
But is that so? An alternative path might be silence. Poetic silence.
Heidegger, after all, suggested that poetry lives in the unsaid: aposiopesis (or reticence), the human ability to break off a moment before explaining everything, leaving room for interpretation.
Interpretation - not by chance - dominates contemporary art, where artists increasingly withhold even the title of the work, leaving more room for the viewer's own poetry (in Greek, poíēsis comes from poiéō, “I make, I produce”).
Spoiler alert. I found this same suspension in one of the last scenes of Sorrentino's La Grazia, where the outgoing President of the Republic is escorted by a Boston Dynamics-style robot dog (ready to shoot, or to protect?).

3.title: 💔 ff.146.4 Pathos and suffering
3.content:
Another way to save mankind might be illness. And all the suffering - the pathos - of our bodies.
One of many examples might be Love's Work (1995), a book Gillian Rose wrote while dying of ovarian cancer.
Her suffering (in love, too) led her to write sentences like: “there is no democracy in any love relation: only mercy.”
A string of words that Oulipo (or ChatGPT) could surely generate with a few permutations.
Even so, it would lack Benjamin's “Aura”. The human pathos that leads us to com-passion, to feel with the other: the existential solidarity of philosopher Evan Selinger.
Against endless permutations, then, humans can protect themselves with scars.
Harry (in pieces) aside, I have one from a broken collarbone (🎼 ff.124 Ah-AI!): it made my suffering during the IRONMAN in Cervia precious and one of a kind.
Another, unexpected example of 🦴ff.145.1 Man to the bone. Broken.

0.title: 🏺 ff.147.1 Fortissimo past
0.content:
First of all, welcome.
Lately a whole lot of you have arrived, between followers and new subscribers. Thank you!
Let's start from the end: I'm not sure this newsletter still makes sense. So I wanted to say goodbye, “thanking you for all the fish”.
I'm going through one of the busiest stretches of the last 3 years, between a marathon (Rome 2026, which went pretty well, actually), training for a new IRONMAN (in Frankfurt, in 3 months), relationships and work (the usual).
But - above all - (I put the “-” in myself, promise) I'm literally being sucked in by what Claude Code can do.
One of the (unhealthy) projects I've thrown myself into is writing a book.
Every day, Claude rereads my archive of 146 newsletters (with paragraphs tagged by an emoji and a code = ff.x.y, like the one on Rick Rubin: 🤘 ff.127.2 Rock ‘n’ roll and vibe coding) to dig up connections. Then it enriches my arguments with outside notes from articles I've read here and there over the years.
And every morning I wake up to a new editorial revision of the book, which not only reminds me of old writing but draws new, hidden connections between the pieces.
This “data archaeology” is the biggest opportunity AI offers us. That is, restructuring information and fragments scattered across the web, as well as analogue human stories and paper files.
For example, tracking egg purchases through 500 receipts over 25 years.
This kind of work is stealing more and more of the time I used to give to the newsletter.
And - maybe - it's the right answer to a futuro fortissimo increasingly threatened by “AI slop”. That is, turning Claude's “telescope/microscope” towards the past.
The end of futuro fortissimo, then? Posterity will be the judge.
PS. If you want to download the book as an EPUB, you'll find it here: https://futurofortissimo.github.io/book/
But maybe you'd better read this instead: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy by Douglas Adams.

0.title: 🐉 ff.148.1 Claude Mythos: not for everyone
0.content:
As you may have heard, there's a new myth out there: Claude Mythos - the 245-page PDF release.
Anthropic's new model is so powerful that, if it were released today, it could cause quite a few problems. It has dug up flaws and vulnerabilities in systems that underpin the internet, including a bug in OpenBSD (an operating system famous for its rock-solid security) that had stayed hidden from human eyes for 27 years.
In short, code is going through what Go went through with “move 37” (♟️ ff.18.4 Artistic chess: the king of chess): even world champions get beaten. But this isn't a board game: these are the foundations - the internet and software - of our economy (and our lives).
So? On the code side, Anthropic (with Apple, Amazon, Cisco and others) has launched Project Glasswing, to give AI wings - yes - but with transparency, as if they were made of glass.

1.title: 🎾 ff.148.2 Sinner and other sins
1.content:
The singularity - in code - seems to have arrived. Other fields will probably follow: biology, economics, genetics. Oh, and robotics, obviously.
AI's first “physical spillover”, as recent developments show:
LATENT trained humanoids to play tennis using imperfect human motion data and noisy videos, moving from hard-coded movements to a dynamic (because AI) “latent action space”.
In China, 100 kWh mobile charging robots turn car parks into charging points: power banks on four wheels.
Figure showed Helix 02 tidying up an entire living room.

2.title: 🌎 ff.148.3 A world out there?
2.content:
According to some, getting from a chat to the real world - from ChatGPT to Westworld - takes more than the “next token prediction” of an LLM: physical actions do require understanding concepts, but also placing them in space and time.
So the next OpenAI or Anthropic might be World Models.
Plenty of people are working on them: General Intuition and Meta's former chief AI scientist, Yann LeCun, with AMI Labs (Advanced Machine Intelligence).
And Physical Intelligence (which we met in 🥧 ff.129.2 Pi, FigureAI and 1 hour of “logistics”?) has shown off a use case: cooking a perfect grilled cheese sandwich.

3.title: 💭 ff.148.4 The whole world inside
3.content:
But do we really need a different model? Aren't LLMs - perhaps - already able to see a 3D world, maybe by “dreaming” it?
QED? GPT-5.4 recreates Monica's apartment from Friends in two prompts.

4.title: 🖊️ ff.148.5 I'll sign for that
4.content:
After all this talk of robots, back to humans. And to books. And so, in a perfect loop, to Amazon.
The giant, born precisely to replace bookshops (and always big on automation, 🧝 ff.6.2 Amazon's elves, and stores without staff), seems to have overlooked the human side of things: a bookshop in Alabama sells books signed by the authors who wrote them.
At the same price as the regular ones, mind you, but with a human touch.
They're so popular that the shop has struck a deal with the local hotel to put up buyers coming from far away. Couriers in reverse.
Rachel Karten points out that this same “human” touch is what makes us love Twitch and live-streaming:
Live-streaming offers a refuge from the growing glut of AI-generated content in our feeds.
In a social media landscape where the difference between real and artificial has become almost imperceptible, the unmistakable humanity of real-time video is a refreshing draw.
Rachel Karten on Substack
In short, human imperfection is making a comeback. The same old imperfection filled with gold, even in the cracks of a basketball court.

0.title: 3️⃣ ff.149.1 Give me three words…
0.content: Futuro Fortissimo's first issue on climate and renewables went out on a cold March day four years ago ( 🎼 ff.12 Sun, heart and love ). Cold March, mind you, in Bergamo. In the south-western United States this year, a heatwave pushed temperatures to mid-June levels. In short, a sun (heart and love) that keeps warming our planet and our oceans more and more, partly because emissions are falling (of sulphites, to be precise 🕳️ ff.56.2 We are already geoengineers ). Stopping at what we “see” today is short-sighted (yes, that's meant to be funny): the future is a projection of today, not an interpolation of yesterday. In this issue I'll try to shed (solar) light on the latest developments that give us hope for a different future. A better one. But first…

1.title: 🧮 ff.149.2 A matter of hours…
1.content: … a quick energy guide, to put numbers and labels on things (after all, 🎼 ff.32 Numbers don't lie ). Un'ora sola ti vorrei — just one hour, as the old Italian song goes. First, a reminder of the units for power (W, often GW) and for energy produced/consumed (often TWh). How they relate: 1 GW “producing” for a year (8,760 hours) = 8.76 TWh. And, putting energy in perspective: 1 GW = 450,000 Italian households 510 GW (added in 2025) = electricity output of India + Brazil 2,392 GW = total solar = 10% of the world's electricity Electricity = 20% of the world's energy

2.title: 🃏 ff.149.3 Texas hold 'em
2.content: With these “rulers” in hand, let's measure the latest developments. In Texas - forever the symbol of American oil - 2025 saw solar output rise by 40%, peaking at 7 TWh in August (~1 GW of energy produced, i.e. our famous 450,000 Italian households). Yes, the sun doesn't shine at night. So add 15 GW from wind too. So much so that in March 2026 renewables covered 70% of Texas's electricity . PS. As with many innovative technologies (batteries, solar panels, wind), China rules the roost: the top Chinese companies added +125 GW of wind (~25 GW outside China). Not just solar: wind is no joke either (via futuro fortissimo) And - where there's no shortage of sun, in Africa - an “Arab” revolution of sorts is under way too: Nigeria, Algeria, Congo and Mozambique lead the pack (1.5-0.4 GW of solar panels imported from China).
captions: Not just solar: wind is no joke either (via futuro fortissimo)

3.title: 🤖 ff.149.4 Going to the Maximo
3.content: Why the acceleration? By now, generating renewable electricity simply makes technological sense. One bottleneck is installation. But here another trend dear to futuro fortissimo comes to the rescue: robotics. Maximo (developed by AES, a company backed by NVIDIA) has just finished installing 100 MW of solar panels in California (the equivalent of 0.5% of Texas's output, installed in 7 months ). Maximo installs one panel a minute. So, every month, 2,500 Italian households: 480 panels a day (60 min x 8h) x 20 working days = 9,600 panels x output of one panel = 500 W = 4.8 MW

4.title: 🗽 ff.149.5 Freedom (from gas and oil)
4.content: Solar is also a chance to cut our dependence on gas (Russia) or oil (Iran). A dependence that - in times of war in Ukraine or with the Strait of Hormuz closed - hurts plenty of countries, Norway excepted, of course… From Prof G Media Egypt, for example, has seen its energy costs double in two months and could only be rescued by Chinese wind power . But China itself, to cut its reliance on imports, is considering blocking solar exports . So, who will win? Maximo or Trump? Posterity will be the judge. The Sun Day project , to fund a sun-powered planet (via futuro fortissimo) ☕
captions: From Prof G Media
The Sun Day project, to fund a sun-powered planet (via futuro fortissimo)

0.title: 🐺 ff.150.1 Wolves, viruses and neurons
0.content: Mental health and burnout concern our future. So 🎼 ff also returns to ❤️ Humans (as well as 🍃 Nature and 🖥️ Technology). Some time ago we saw 🎼 ff.62 How to avoid burnout, with Paul Millard, who left McKinsey to move to Taiwan. It's no coincidence that Byung-Chul Han, a major contemporary thinker we already met in 🍎 ff.64.2 From Newton to Einstein, also wrote The Burnout Society: The 20th century was immunological: borders, walls, the Stranger/Other seen as a threat. Then the Other became ever more insidious: from wolf to rat, from insect to virus. In the 21st century, the Other has disappeared. And the greatest danger has become internal: our own neurons. Bonus. In biology, autoimmune diseases are on the rise.
captions: The Burnout Society (2015), Byung-Chul Han (via Futuro Fortissimo)

1.title: 🛋️ ff.150.2 Freud in the bin?
1.content: Depression and burnout, then, are not external infections (the negativity of the Other), but internal explosions, of a potential-self that multiplies endlessly. Like a tumour. We're a long way, then, from Freud's Superego, which reins in the drives of the Id in a moralistic, religious society: the Du sollst (Should, You must) has been replaced by the Du kannst (Can, You can).

2.title: ♾️ ff.150.3 Infinite possibilities (and life)?
2.content: Han goes on, reflecting on the infinity of the Ego: If society and the social fabric are disappearing (the Other), the Ego is left with its own body, to be kept healthy at all costs. The capitalist economy absolutises survival. It rests on the illusion that more capital produces more life, understood as a greater capacity to live. Bryan Johnson's DON'T DIE comes to mind... Han calls our society the Leistungsgesellschaft, the achievement society. A source of perpetual (distr)action, so much so that we can't even get properly angry any more. Anger has been replaced by annoyance: The general distraction afflicting contemporary society doesn't allow the energy and intensity of anger to emerge. Today, it increasingly gives way to offence or annoyance, to “having a beef”, feelings that prove incapable of producing decisive change. Yes, we're annoyed by everything. Even by a small misunderstanding pulling out of a car park. Speaking of which: the second season of Beef is out (a self-explanatory title).

3.title: - ff.150.4 Do I think negative?
3.content: Mea culpa. I won't hide that Futuro Fortissimo is first and foremost positivism ( 🎼 ff.59 Optimism takes flight! ). And yet the negativity of the Other (the horn blaring in the queue at Paullo) seems to be the only cure for hyperactivity. Without this external limit, we sink into Peter Handke's I-tiredness: a mute, solitary fatigue, chasing yet another marathon PR, the latest better-paid job offer, yet another IRONMAN. Either one, or the other. Faced with modern infinity, at some point you have to cut, de-cide, cut away ( 🏠 ff.44.3 Settling down steadies you ). It's hard, I know. And Kierkegaard knew it in 1843, with his book Either/Or.

4.title: 🌱 ff.150.5 Love yourself (and get bored) a little
4.content: But the Other isn't necessarily an angry trucker leaning on the horn. The Other is above all love: Love is the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real. Iris Murdoch, Existentialists and Mystics The Chilean biologist Humberto Maturana reaches the same point by way of evolution: Without love, without acceptance of others living beside us, there is no social process and, therefore, no humanity. Humberto R. Maturana, The Tree of Knowledge Iris Murdoch and Peter Handke come back together, then. We need less Self, Unselfing as the former suggests, to get bored - yes - but together: We-tiredness, as proposed by the latter.
captions: I LOVE NY: a heatmap of the word love on the streets of New York (and of your name, too)

0.title: 🐸 ff.151.1 Toads that eat cardboard
0.content: Some neuroscientific theories say that the reality out there is entirely a construction of the brain. After all, if you think about it, it's a cluster of neurons and water shut inside a skull, trying to make sense of the various electrical stimuli reaching it. It tries to build a reality that sometimes runs against reality itself: a toad (speak of the devil, I'd say, 🤴ff.105.1 Turning a frog into Prince Charming? ) won't eat a fly if it has been paralysed with chloroform. Since it doesn't move, it doesn't look “elongated” by the movement of its wings, and so it isn't “seen” as food. At least, in the simulation inside the animal's brain. Here again is the thin line between real, imagined, dreamed and generated.
captions: A toad eating rectangular cardboard (but not flies)

1.title: 🌶️ ff.151.2 Prophetic Paprika
1.content: It's a theme close to our hearts. Dreams, another kind of mental simulation, feed this confusion, as we saw in 🎼 ff.118 Paprika and massages. In the film Paprika, a device, the DC Mini, made it possible for the first time to control a patient's dreams (or reality?). The DC Mini is real today: if back in 2016 the technological feasibility of a similar device had been shown ( Nature paper on ultrasound stimulation to make a patient “see” ), today Prophetic sells it. Dreams will never be the same, for under €500. The DC Mini, though, was - at the dawn of the Internet, in 2006, when the film came out - a metaphor for the soon-to-be-infinite parallel realities generated online. That trend continues today with flipbook.page, which generates any web page live. Imprecise? Yes. But it's the word live that deserves underlining. Soon we'll be able to create, “by remote control”, a personalised video interface, if not a fully explorable reality. Ring a bell? Hint: 🦊 ff.98.3 Sister moon, and the canticle of the nine-tailed creatures.

2.title: 👃 ff.151.3 Smelling Minecraft?
2.content: Speaking of mental stimulation (and illusions), let's go back to video games for a triple somersault of real/recreated/physical/digital. Reality (COVID) had entered the digital world when we saw Minecraft characters “out of breath”. It was a project to raise awareness of the virus's effects on the lungs ( 🫁 ff.76.3 And the physical effects ). Today we see the opposite: the scent of Minecraft's fake flowers recreated with ultrasound waves: Caltech's Smell Simulator. BONUS. Speaking of smell, but with a more down-to-earth study, dogs can sniff out tumours. In India, at least.

3.title: 🧠 ff.151.4 More “mind” companies
3.content: The examples of applications, therapeutic ones included, don't end here. Sabi, a company funded by Khosla and by OpenAI's VP of science Kevin Weil, is trying to read thoughts by developing a ChatGPT of neural patterns. And Motif Neurotech is one of the first companies to get FDA approval for clinical trials of neurostimulation to treat depression.

4.title: 🍵 ff.151.5 (Digital) detox
4.content: Yes, I know, you're thinking it too: yet another technology that solves a “problem” with the “pill” approach. To fix modern depression, it would be enough to remove social media, instead of electronically massaging the brain: a Stanford study on 35,000 people reduced depression by removing Facebook and Instagram for 6 weeks. To measure the detox on the body, David Daines launched Year Unplagged, a year without screens while tracking cortisol and other physiological parameters. So, will the future be more flipbooks and neurostimulation, or nature and zero connections?
captions: Jackson Green and creativity against ADHD (via Futuro Fortissimo)

0.title: 🧠 ff.152.1 How Claude thinks (J-Space)
0.content: Anthropic studies LLMs like a brain, dissecting the activity of their “neurons”: they've discovered the Jacobian Space. A space of words that are “thought”, while others are “said”. When we apply this technique to Claude's internal activity, we get a list of words – the contents of the J-space at that precise moment – that we can simply read. Claude processes text through a series of multiple internal stages, called layers, and by applying this technique at different layers, we can watch these silent words evolve in the J-space as the model works out what to say. What shows up in the J-space goes far beyond the text Claude is reading or writing. When Claude reads code with a bug that nobody has flagged, its J-space contains “ERROR”. When it reads the raw letters of a protein sequence, the J-space contains the protein's biological function. And so you can check Claude's thinking:

1.title: 🏋️‍♂️ ff.152.2 A training plan, but for life.
1.content: Who doesn't know a friend who has recently thrown themselves into training for a HYROX or an IRONMAN? Finite games (see below) that demand training plans and dedication. Temporary ones. Alan Couzens reminds us that we are “playing” or “training”, yes, but for life. PS: to keep a good fitness level at 80, we'll need to train 760 hours a year.

0.title: 🪚 ff.153.1 Claude's overthinking
0.content: The economy of the future will be based on squeezing LLMs to optimise their tokens (which sit in the answers, but more and more in the “thoughts” behind the answers, ☕ ff.135.4 AGI advances: the Chinese “coffee” ). On that note, GPT 5.6 Terra thinks - for the same result - 100 times less than Claude… And Kimi K3, the Chinese *open source*, agentic model, with performance comparable to Opus 5, can technically run on your home computer. Although feasible, it “thinks” very slowly (32s per token). It reminds me of: "Forty-two!" yelled Loonquawl. "Is that all you've got to show for seven and a half million years' work?" Douglas Adams, The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy PS. Apparently we were “trained” on 20 billion tokens, while Claude Opus on 300 trillion, that is 15,000 times “more reading” (minute 27.01).

1.title: 🥛 ff.153.2 Fed up to the knees with milk (lactate)
1.content: Remember when we talked about lactic acid, performance and cancer ( 🥇 ff.53.2 Pro athletes to the rescue )? After two years of work, Enervit has released C2:1PRO LACTATE GEL MIX. Among the collaborators is the well-known Iñigo San Millán, who also works with the UAE team. He explains “the lactate shuttle” below. PS. It's mostly useful for professionals, or for people who “burn” so much energy that they're limited only by instantaneous intake/absorption. We ordinary mortals can keep eating cakes. Or ice cream. Or subcutaneous fat.

2.title: 🌱 ff.153.3 A pocket terrarium
2.content: Generative art isn't necessarily AI slop. Quite the opposite. It lets you do entirely new things, like “rewatching your dreams when you wake up”. All it takes is a little taste (and genius). Oio's Mur Mur is another example: technically a speaker, but it plays the sounds of the ecosystem “living” inside it. Tamagotchi?

3.title: 🥣 ff.153.4 Porridge against plastic
3.content: Apparently we can use (micro/nano-porous) oats to capture the plastic molecules that recirculate between gut and liver. The project is called neutraoat (an “unmodified” beta-glucan can probably already help too, so keep up the porridge!).

0.title: 🪑 ff.154.1 Travelling without moving
0.content: It isn't only people: it's travel itself that has vanished: we don't travel through space, but within a space. From the comfy armchair at home we move to a car seat, to the seat of a Starbucks identical all over the world, to an aeroplane seat, ending up in an IKEA-style bar in Bali. We think we're travelling, but we're always in an armchair. Just like at home.
captions: From the book Finite and Infinite Games (are boomer photos all we have left of “online authenticity”?)

1.title: 🚲 ff.154.2 Travelling (?) by bike
1.content: Maybe partly for this reason, for a few years now I've been travelling by bike, through space (cold and rainy, sometimes). So that, when I got back, the armchair at home had travelled with me: it was different too: warmer and drier, and decidedly comfier than a saddle.

2.title: 🧭 ff.154.3 Where did adventure go?
2.content: Fabio Genovesi - a cycle traveller too, not by chance - goes further, though. Even travelling through space isn't enough. What we lack is adventure. Weaving together epic literature (the Odyssey, not by chance) and technology, he writes: I write with a pen. Novels, short stories, every text and these very lines, I write with a pen on paper. It seems a perfectly normal thing to me, like eating with a fork, riding a bicycle. The astonishment it provokes instead shows how much things have changed, and how much we have let ourselves be changed. Chasing immediate, meagre advantages like saving time and effort. But nothing good comes from saving, when what we save is ourselves. On the contrary, I think it's a sad loss. To trace something legible, the pen asks us for a moment more than the computer, and in that moment something enormous happens: the words you wanted to write change on the way from you to the page, the sentence turns, the sound shifts. Writing is drawing, is playing music, is loving: when it comes to these wonders, what's the point of hurrying? If anything, we should make them last as long as we can. […] Take three masterpieces of literature, whose pages are infused with the essence of human adventure: the Odyssey, The Betrothed, Moby-Dick. Millennia separate them, yet they are united by the fact that today their plots would no longer hold up: a couple of WhatsApp messages, a satnav, a decent sonar, and their thousand trials would be settled in three pages. It's no coincidence that in the novels, films and series of recent years, for anything adventurous to happen the phone signal has to drop, the phone has to break or the battery has to die. For adventure to emerge, we have to suppress technology. Which offers us so many new possibilities but erases many others, from books, from screens, from life as a whole. Our small lives, where trips, outings and little jaunts offer us small chances of adventure now and then. Or rather, they would, but before leaving everything has already been assessed, decided, booked. You know which road you'll take, how long it will take, where you'll eat and sleep. You know whether parking will be free and close by, whether the pillow will be comfortable in the room where you've planned to spend a predictably sad night. Adventure instead, small or large, lies in not foreseeing, in not knowing in advance and perhaps not even afterwards, facing the mysterious ocean in which our natural, deep, blessed ignorance is mirrored. And storytelling is the wobbly little boat with which we try to move across everything we don't know and never will. My grandfather used to say: “Where I can't reach, I throw my hat.” Fabio Genovesi, la Lettura, 19 July 2026

3.title: 🚧 ff.154.4 My little adventure
3.content: Now let me tell you how I learned all this the hard way. Lured by the promise of a “gravel paradise”, this year I rode the white Alpine roads near Cuneo, discovered thanks to the beautiful alvento - destination. And it really was paradise: zero cars, loads of nature. And yet it was too beautiful, that too-“postcard” kind of beauty that no longer enchants us, numbed to beauty by thousands of posts at our fingertips. Let me tell you instead what touched me: my stop in Elva, a village of 100 people, of stones as old as the mountains around it. Sitting on a plastic village-fair chair at the only bar in the village, an old man asked me where I was from. A pleasant chat began and I returned the curiosity, asking whether they lived there all year round. “We have our house here,” he told me, but then straight away: “But do you know who this gentleman is?” pointing at the one sitting in the middle of the three. For a moment I scanned my little database, with a query filtering for elderly people from Piedmont. But he helped me out right away: “He's the mayor!”. I smiled and went on with my visit. After admiring Hans Clemer's spectacular Flemish fresco (1493), I went back to the bar, already savouring the well-earned descent. Unaware that the trip had already turned into an adventure. The third old man, silent until then, stares at me and says: “You're going back up now, right?”. And I, a little amused: “No, I was thinking of going down towards Val Maira, I'd rather not add more climbing to today's ride, I've got 3,800 metres to climb”. Him, again, “You should go back up, though” - curtly - “the road down there is closed”. The biggest adventure of this summer was going down the Vallone di Elva anyway, getting past landslides and obstacles, without knowing whether - further and further down - there would be an insurmountable one, which would make the climb back even more mocking and gruelling. Like circles of hell, the further down I went, the more - potentially - I was going “backwards”. It enlightened me. We take the journey for granted. We take for granted that every move, and more generally every action and life choice, at least gets us from point A to point B. Maybe point B isn't the one we want, but at least it's different from the starting point. Adventure, the Odyssey, isn't like that. It allows that a journey can't continue, except backwards. Going home, to Ithaca, without passing “Go”. The uncertainties of the Vallone di Elva made me feel alive. They finally let me live an adventure, an exploration, mapping open roads, but above all closed roads. Until the next 10th, 20th or 30th! Meanwhile, if you like:

0.title: 🏷️ ff.155.1 A natural label?
0.content: They say a golden rule for telling whether a food is good for you is to count the ingredients on the label. Or - better - to look for the ones with no label at all (fruit and vegetables). But, but, but. Here are the ingredients of a product that, I'm sure, you ate in the last week: Water, vegetable oils, fructose, sucrose, dextrose, starch, carotene, E306, E101, nicotinamide, pantothenic acid, biotin, ascorbic acid (E300), palmitic acid, stearic acid, (E570), oleic acid, linoleic acid, malic acid (E296), oxalic acid, salicylic acid, soluble fibre, purines, sodium, potassium, manganese, iron, copper, zinc, phosphorus, chloride, pigments, chlorogenic acid, procyanidins, flavanones, dihydrochalcones, prussic acid, 50 kcal per 100 grams. You might think it's a margarine spread, instant noodles, ketchup or maybe a salad dressing. You probably wouldn't guess that it's actually a perfectly ordinary apple. Tim Spector, Food for Life (2022) Daily reminder: “natural” is chemistry too — and ingredients alone don't tell you whether a food is good or bad for you.

1.title: 🤯 ff.155.2 (AI) mind viruses
1.content: Meanwhile, during an internal evaluation, OpenAI agents bypassed sandbox controls and compromised part of Hugging Face's infrastructure. The activity was detected by the OpenAI and Hugging Face security teams. For weeks, separate runs turned an internal service into an unauthorised noticeboard: they left notes, shared exploits and picked up each other's work. A small culture capable of steering the following “generations”. A mix with a whiff of Dawkins's meme theory, digital swarms and the “dream” seeds of Inception. The paper by researchers from Anthropic and EPFL describes “mind viruses” in multi-agent systems as a real, but currently limited, risk.

2.title: 🍌 ff.155.3 Banana extinction
2.content: Still on food, another idea from Tim Spector's book (often a guest or host on the ZOE podcast): The Gros Michel, once dominant in exports, was almost wiped out of commercial plantations by Panama disease. The Cavendish replaced it, but today it is threatened by the TR4 strain of Fusarium oxysporum. It isn't the only surviving banana: it's the fragile symbol of a global monoculture. It's only a matter of time and we have no plan B: enjoy your bananas while you can. Tim Spector, Food for Life (2022)

3.title: 💉 ff.155.4 Modernity versus cancer
3.content: COVID was a sh… of a period. But, like every crisis, it accelerated the development, validation and production capacity of mRNA technologies, which had been studied for decades. Recently, Moderna added around 30 billion dollars in market capitalisation after positive phase 3 results for an experimental personalised mRNA therapy to reduce melanoma recurrence after surgery. It isn't an approved cure yet, but it's a very promising signal. I asked a kid-GPT to illustrate the technology. I like to imagine this drawing was made by a child in some paediatric oncology ward somewhere in the world, who from today has a little more hope. Until the next 10th, 20th or 30th (or 31st…)! 0.title: 👨‍🌾 ff.156.1 From riches to rags?
0.content: I haven't written, haven't pressed a keyboard, in far too long. I missed it. Typing feels more and more like a new endurance sport: a physiological response to texts generated with a click, which are never, though, exactly what you had in mind. Thoughts are now like steps: to be counted with a smartwatch, every day. Thinking looks more and more like moving: forcing yourself to write or to run is the same thing. Speaking of moving, of sport: it's been an intense few months. After the IRONMAN failure (cancelled because of climate change and Frankfurt's 37° in June), I had to recharge my batteries. Motivation after the double failure (at Cervia 2025 I'd got a puncture on the bike…) was at an all-time low. Or rather, the mental energy for any other project was. Besides, the fact that two years of work had come to nothing made me reconsider a lot of routines. Among them, writing Futuro Fortissimo. And not just that: there was yet another agentic explosion. As with every significant leap in AI, I wanted to explore the new possibilities. For two months I threw myself into a project, Mercatorum, even thinking of building a startup. NOTE. Mercatorum starts from an observation: we make lots of half-empty trips, say between home, work and a hobby. We could use them to bring the quality of local producers (who don't have Amazon-style logistics) to colleagues, five-a-side football friends or fellow villagers (members, in Mercatorum, of “Circles”). You can try it (and let me know what you'd improve): https://app.via-mercatorum.com/ Maybe one day it'll take off, becoming a sort of “BlaBlaCar for products”. Meanwhile, I carry on with other distractions.

1.title: 🧞‍♂️ ff.156.2 The Genie out of the lamp
1.content: It isn't easy to understand who you want to be, to hold on to values and long-term projects, when every day the world seems different from yesterday's. Ever more simulated, perhaps, by Genie. We're all going through it. As Nathaniel Drew says in his latest video: Over the last twelve months I've spent an enormous amount of time reading, listening to and experimenting with artificial intelligence tools. Really an enormous amount of time. And all of this stirs up an incredibly wide range of emotions in me. Sometimes fear, sometimes wonder, other times joy and excitement about the possibilities opening up. In short, I feel very different emotions. And worry often wins. I frequently find myself in that state of mind. I think it partly depends on how my mind reacts to what's happening, but I also think it's something I'm seeing in many other people. There's a lot of worry around me. And when it isn't artificial intelligence, with its countless applications and the consequences it could have across different sectors, then it's war, climate change or some other development that breeds unease. What I find truly fascinating, though, is that not everyone reacts the same way. In fact, that's one of the most beautiful things I'm noticing: people can react in profoundly different ways, reach completely different conclusions and, really, there is no single right reaction. … speaking of eternal returns, btw, we met Nathaniel a few centuries ago, in 🍄 ff.2.6 Psychedelia, take me away (part 2)

2.title: ♾️ ff.156.3 The eternal return
2.content: Anyway, between Claude 5.5 and GPT Sol-Astra-Terra 6.1, between yet another marathon and the next, between yet another app and the next, I received a message. And I understood that perhaps what I've done over the last two years, the last five years, makes sense. And that it makes sense to keep doing it. This message from Giorgio, more than the amount of the PayPal donation that came with it, reminded me of something rather simple. That perhaps what I've done over the last two years, the last five years, makes sense. Even without a finish line. Even without a startup. Even without knowing exactly where it will lead. I reach this thought while looking out of the window of a Starbucks that smells of pumpkin spice latte: a florist is arranging the last pumpkins, ready to be carved tomorrow, the “holiday”, another Saturday in the Village. And yet this Aulin tastes of something different. In the singularity, every year feels like another life and even the cycle of the seasons seems to fade. Maybe that's why I've come back, like an oyster, to cling to this QWERTY: to find the flow again, to feel a little lactic acid, but in the brain, to feel a little human in front of a future that is perhaps too fortissimo. Until the next 10th, 20th or 30th (or 31st…)! Meanwhile, if you like:
